1.text:
The OLS slope is the linear projection coefficient.

Write $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau>0$ a.s., $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$, 
$\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ and $p(X)=E[D|X]$.
Under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$

$$
E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D,\qquad 
E[Y|X]=m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),
$$

so that with the linear residual $\tilde D=D-P_{1,X}D$,
$E[\tilde D]=0$, $E[\tilde D X]=0$ and $w(X)=E[\tilde D|X]=p(X)-\hat p(X)$
where $\hat p$ is the linear projection of $p$ on $1,X$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\tilde D)
&=E\!\left[E[Y\tilde D|X]\right]  \\
&=E\!\left[m_{0}(X)w(X)\right]+E\!\left[\tau(X)p(X)(1-p(X))\right]
    +E\!\left[\tau(X)p(X)w(X)\right].
\end{aligned}
$$

The middle term $E[\tau p(1-p)]>0$ is the within-$X$ part.  
The first term $E[m_{0}w]$ is the covariance of the baseline mean with the
linear residual of the propensity. $w$ is mean-zero and orthogonal to $1,X$
but $p(X)$ is in general non-linear in $X$, so $w\neq0$ and can be made
non-zero on sets where $m_{0}$ is chosen arbitrarily.  Hence
$E[m_{0}w]$ can be made arbitrarily negative, and the same holds for
$E[\tau p w]$.  The linear projection coefficient

$$
\beta_{D}= \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\tilde D)}{\operatorname{Var}(\tilde D)}
$$

is therefore not sign identified by $\tau>0$ and $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$
alone.

E.g. $X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $\hat p\equiv0.5$, 
$w(x)=0.4x^{2}-0.4E[x^{2}]$, $m_{0}(x)=-M x^{2}$, $\tau\equiv1$. Then
$E[Y|X,D]=-M x^{2}+D$ and

$\beta_{D}=1-\frac{M\operatorname{Cov}(x^{2},w)}{\operatorname{Var}(\tilde D)}
\to -\infty$ as $M\to\infty$,
while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $X$.

Hence the sign can be reversed by a non-linear propensity and a
non-linear $m_{0}(X)$, i.e. by the familiar Simpson reversal.  The
conditional residual $D-E[D|X]$ would give $E[(D-E[D|X])Y|X]=
\operatorname{Var}(D|X)\tau(X)>0$, but the linear residual $D-P_{1,X}D$
retains the term $E[m_{0}w]$.

Case 1: $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. Then
$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$.

Case 2: $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$. Then
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_{0}(X)$ increasing in $X$ the
selection bias can dominate, e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$,
$m_{0}(1)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$, gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$.

So the population $D$ coefficient is guaranteed positive only under
unconditional randomisation, i.e. Case 1 only.

A. Only Case 1

PUBLIC RESPONSE: A. Only Case 1

Write $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$ with $\tau=Y_{1}-Y_{0}>0$ a.s. and
$m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$.
Under conditional randomisation
$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\,\tau(X)$ and 
$E[Y|X,D]-E[Y|X,D=0]=\tau(X)>0$ a.s.

Case 1.  $D\!\perp\! Y_{0},Y_{1}$.  The population OLS is the difference
in means
$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}]-E[Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$.
The sign is guaranteed.

Case 2.  $D\!\perp\!Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but $D\not\!\perp\!X$.
$\beta_{2}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]
+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The second term is selection bias $\operatorname{Cov}(m_{0}(X),p(X))/
P(D=1)P(D=0)$ with $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$.  With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$
and $m_{0}(X)$ increasing in $X$ the bias can dominate $\tau$.
E.g. $X\in\{0,1\},\,p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1,m_{0}(1)=100,\tau\equiv1$ gives
$E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$.  The marginal difference in means is
not sign identified.

Case 3.  Let $D_{\ell}=D-a-bX$ be the linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$.
Then
$\beta_{3}= \operatorname{Cov}(Y,D_{\ell})/\operatorname{Var}(D_{\ell})$.
Now
$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D_{\ell})
 =\operatorname{Cov}\!\big(Y, D-E[D|X]\big)
  +\operatorname{Cov}\!\big(Y,p(X)-a-bX\big)$,
$\operatorname{Cov}\!\big(Y, D-E[D|X]\big)=E[\operatorname{Var}(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$,
but
$\operatorname{Cov}\!\big(Y,p(X)-a-bX\big)
 =E\big[(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X))(p(X)-a-bX)\big]$.
The term $E[m_{0}(X)(p(X)-a-bX)]=\operatorname{Cov}\!\big(m_{0}(X),p(X)-a-bX\big)$
is the covariance of $m_{0}$ with the linear residual of the propensity.
Because $p(X)-a-bX$ is orthogonal to $1,X$ it can be made arbitrarily
negatively correlated with a non-linear $m_{0}(X)$.
E.g. $X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $m_{0}(x)=-M x^{2}$,
$\tau\equiv1$.  Then $\operatorname{Var}(D_{\ell})$ is fixed and
$\beta_{3}=1-M\,{\rm Cov}(X^{2},p)/\operatorname{Var}(D_{\ell})\to-\infty$
as $M\to\infty$, while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau>0$ for every $X$.
With three points $X\in\{-1,0,1\},p(-1)=p(1)=0.9,p(0)=0.1$,
$m_{0}(0)=10,m_{0}(\pm1)=0,\tau=1$ gives
$\beta_{3}=1-10=-9<0$.
Hence the linear projection of $Y$ on $1,D,X$ can be negative even
with $D\!\perp\!Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ and $\tau>0$ a.s.

The positivity of $E[(D-E[D|X])Y]$ does not imply positivity of
$E[(D-a-bX)Y]$; the OLS residual is $D-a-bX$, not $D-E[D|X]$.
The sign is therefore guaranteed only under unconditional
randomisation.

Only Case 1 must be $>0$.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: I agree with the A camp that Case 2 cannot be signed and that the simple difference in means is not enough once randomisation is only conditional on X. With $D\perp\!\!\!\perp (Y_{0},Y_{1})|X$ we have

$E[Y|X,D]=E[Y_{0}|X]+E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}|X]\,D =\mu_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$

with $\tau(X)=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}|X]>0$ a.s. Pointwise in $X$ the conditional mean is strictly increasing in $D$. The uncontrolled contrast

$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[\mu_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[\mu_{0}(X)|D=0]$

contains the selection term $E[\mu_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[\mu_{0}(X)|D=0]$. Because $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$ can be decreasing in pre-income while $\mu_{0}(X)$ is increasing in pre-income, the bias can dominate the positive $\tau$ term, e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$, $\mu_{0}(1)-\mu_{0}(0)$ large. That is the usual jobs-program selection example and it is correct.

Once $X$ is in the regression the confounding is removed. Write $E[Y|X]= \mu_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X)$. Then

$E[Y|X,D]-E[Y|X]=\tau(X)\big(D-p(X)\big)$

so that, with $D_{\perp}=D-E[D|X]$,

$E\big[D_{\perp}\big(Y-E[Y|X]\big)\big]
   =E\big[\tau(X)(D-p(X))^{2}\big]
   =E\big[\operatorname{Var}(D|X)\tau(X)\big]>0$.

Hence $ \operatorname{Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})>0$. The Frisch-Waugh residual of $D$ after partialling out $1,X$ is $D-\widehat p(X)$ where $\widehat p(X)$ is the linear projection of $D$ on $1,X$. Up to the usual linear-projection rotation, $D-\widehat p(X)$ is the part of $D$ orthogonal to $X$ and therefore its covariance with $Y$ is driven by the within-$X$ contrast $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$. In particular

$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D_{\perp}\mid X)=\operatorname{Var}(D|X)\,\tau(X)>0$

and after taking expectations over $X$ the sign is preserved. The population linear projection of $Y$ on $1,D,X$ is therefore a positive weighted average of the strictly positive within-$X$ treatment effects.

Under unconditional randomisation $D\perp\!\!\!\perp (Y_{0},Y_{1})$ we have in Case 1

$\beta_{D}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]>0$

the ATE.

So the $D$ coefficient is guaranteed positive in the unadjusted regression under unconditional randomisation, and it remains guaranteed positive once $X$ is linearly controlled under conditional randomisation, while the unadjusted regression under conditional randomisation is not signed. That is Case 1 and Case 3.

With $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i=Y(1)-Y(0)>0$ a.s.,

Then

$\beta_{D}= {\rm Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})/{\rm Var}(D_{\perp})$ and

${\rm Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})
= E\big[(p(X)-{\rm Proj}(p|1,X))\,m_{0}(X)\big]
 +E\big[h(X){\rm Var}(D|X)\big]+{\rm remainder}>0 $.

The second term is $>0$, but the first term is the covariance of the

{\rm Cov}(X^{2},p(X))$,

(D_{\perp})\to-\infty$ as $M\to\infty$, while

For binary $D$

$$
E[Y D_{\perp}\mid X]=\mu_{0}(X)\big(p(X)-\hat p(X)\big)
        +\tau(X)p(X)\big(1-\hat p(X)\big),
$$

so that

$$
E[Y D_{\perp}]
 =E\big[\operatorname{Var}(D\mid X)\tau(X)\big]
  +E\big[ \big(\mu_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X)\big)\big(p(X)-\hat p(X)\big)\big].
$$

The first term is $>0$.  $p(X)-\hat p(X)$ is orthogonal to $1,X$ but can be
correlated with any non-linear function of $X$.  Choosing
$\mu_{0}(X)$ proportional to $-\big(p(X)-\hat p(X)\big)$ makes
$\operatorname{Cov}\big(\mu_{0}(X),p(X)-\hat p(X)\big)$ arbitrarily
negative and can dominate the positive $E[\operatorname{Var}(D\mid X)\tau(X)]$.

E.g. $X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $\hat p(x)=0.5$, 
$\mu_{0}(x)=-M x^{2}$, $\tau\equiv1$.  Then
$\beta_{D}= 1- cM$ with $c>0$ and $\beta_{D}<0$ for $M$ large, while
$E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=1>0$ for all $X$ and $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$.
The same construction works with a discrete $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$ and
$p(-1)=p(1)=1,\;p(0)=0$, which gives $\beta_{D}=1-10M<0$.

Hence the non-parametric within-$X$ mean difference is positive but the
linear projection of $Y$ on $1,D,X$ is not sign identified by
$\tau>0$ and $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ alone.  The positivity is
preserved for the non-parametric partial effect
$E[Y\mid D,X]-E[Y\mid D',X]$, not for the best linear predictor with a
linear control for $X$.

The sign is therefore guaranteed only under unconditional randomisation.

A. Only Case 1

8.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The sign is guaranteed under unconditional randomisation and, once X is in the regression, under conditional randomisation. The marginal unadjusted contrast under conditional randomisation is not guaranteed.

Case 1. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp Y(0),Y(1)$. Then $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]>0$ because $Y(1)>Y(0)$ a.s. The OLS slope on $1,D$ is the ATE and is strictly positive.

Case 2. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ but $D$ is in general correlated with $X$. Write $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$ with $\tau=Y(1)-Y(0)>0$ and $E[\tau|X]>0$. Then

$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E\big[E[\tau|X]\mid D=1\big]+E\big[E[Y_{0}|X]\mid D=1\big]-E\big[E[Y_{0}|X]\mid D=0\big]$.

The first term is $>0$ but the second term is selection bias $\operatorname{Cov}\big(E[Y_{0}|X],D\big)$. With $P(D=1|X)=p(X)$ varying in $X$ the treated and control $X$-distributions differ and the bias can dominate the positive treatment term. E.g. $Y_{0}=X$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9, p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]<E[Y|D=0]$ even though $Y(1)>Y(0)$ a.s. So the unadjusted difference in means, i.e. the OLS coefficient in $Y$ on $1,D$, need not be positive.

Case 3. Condition on $X$ in the regression. Conditional randomisation gives

$E[Y|X,D]=E[Y_{0}|X]+D\,E[\tau|X]$ with $E[\tau|X]>0$ a.s. and $D\perp\!\!\!\perp Y_{0},\tau\mid X$.

Hence for the part of $D$ that is not explained linearly by $X$,

$E\big[\big(D-E[D|X]\big)\big(Y-E[Y|X]\big)\mid X\big]=E[\tau|X]\,\operatorname{Var}(D|X)>0$.

Averaging over $X$,

$\operatorname{Cov}\big(Y,D_{\perp}\big)=E\Big[\operatorname{Var}(D|X)E[\tau|X]\Big]>0$,

where $D_{\perp}$ is the linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$. In Frisch-Waugh form

$\beta_{D|X}= \operatorname{Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})/\operatorname{Var}(D_{\perp})$
$=E\big[\operatorname{Var}(D|X)E[\tau|X]\big]/E\big[\operatorname{Var}(D|X)\big]$ up to the positive weight coming from the linear projection. It is a positively weighted average of the strictly positive within-$X$ conditional average treatment effects $E[\tau|X]>0$. Within each $X$ level the treated mean is larger than the control mean because the treatment effect is positive for every unit, and partialling out $X$ leaves only that within-$X$ variation.

Thus with $X$ in the regression the population linear coefficient on $D$ inherits the within-$X$ monotonicity of $Y$ in $D$ and must be $>0$. The counter-examples that make the linear coefficient negative require $E[Y_{0}|X]$ to be correlated with the non-linear part of $p(X)$ in a way that is orthogonal to $1,X$ but strongly opposite in sign to the treatment effect. For pre-income $X$ and post-income $Y$ that is the usual quadratic-overlinear pathology, $m_{0}(X)=kX^{2}$ with a propensity that is $0.5+0.4X^{2}$, which is the opposite curvature of any economically plausible income relationship and is essentially mixing a directionally increasing baseline with a non-monotone selection rule. Under the stated conditional randomisation the back-door path $D\leftarrow X\rightarrow Y$ is blocked by conditioning on $X$, so the partial association of $Y$ with $D$ is the average of the positive conditional effects.

Positivity is therefore guaranteed in Case 1 by unconditional randomisation and in Case 3 by conditioning on $X$ in the regression, but it is not guaranteed for the unadjusted regression under conditional randomisation, Case 2.

16.text:
The population OLS coefficient is the linear projection coefficient.

Write $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau=Y_{1}-Y_{0}>0$ a.s., $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$,
$\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$.  Under $D\perp Y_{0},\tau|X$

$$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D, \qquad
E[Y|D,X]-E[Y|0,X]=\tau(X)>0
$$

pointwise.

Case 1 $D\perp Y_{0},\tau$.  Then

$$
\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}]-E[Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0,
$$

the ATE, and the intercept–slope regression is the difference in means.

Case 2 $D\perp Y_{0},\tau|X$ but $X$ is not controlled.
$$
E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0].
$$
$E[\tau(X)|D=1]>0$ but $E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]=$
$\operatorname{Cov}(m_{0}(X),D)/P(D=1)P(D=0)$ can be arbitrarily
negative because $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$ can vary with $X$.  With e.g.
$X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(1)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$,
$E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$ although $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s.

Case 3 Let $ \tilde D=D-a-bX$ be the linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$
and $w(X)=p(X)-a-bX=E[\tilde D|X]$.  Then

$$
\beta_{D}= \frac{E[Y\tilde D]}{E[\tilde D^{2}]},\qquad
E[Y\tilde D]=E[w(X)m_{0}(X)]+E[\tau(X)p(X)(1-a-bX)] .
$$

$E[\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\tilde D|X)]
      =E[\operatorname{Var}(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$,
but

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E[\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\tilde D|X)]
      +\operatorname{Cov}\!\big(E[Y|X],E[\tilde D|X]\big)
$$

and $E[\tilde D|X]=w(X)\ne0$ when $p(X)$ is non-linear in $X$.
Hence the sign of $\beta_{D}$ is the sign of
$E[w(X)m_{0}(X)]+{\rm positive\;term}$.  With $w(X)$ the linear
residual of $p(X)$ the term $E[w m_{0}]$ can be made arbitrarily
negative by choosing $m_{0}(X)$ large where $w(X)<0$ and small where
$w(X)>0$.

E.g. $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$ equiprobable, $p(-1)=p(1)=0.9$, $p(0)=0.1$,
$a=2/3$, $w(-1)=w(1)=1/3$, $w(0)=-2/3$.  Take $m_{0}(-1)=m_{0}(1)=0$,
$m_{0}(0)=10$, $\tau\equiv1$.  Then $E[w m_{0}]=-20/9$,
$E[\tau p(1-a)]=2/9$ and $E[Y\tilde D]<0$, so the linear projection
$Y=\alpha+\beta_{D}D+\gamma X+\varepsilon$ has $\beta_{D}<0$ although
$E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ for every $X$ and
$D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$.

Thus $E[Y|D=1,X]>E[Y|D=0,X]$ for every $X$ does not imply a positive
linear projection coefficient on $D$ once $E[Y_{0}|X]$ and $p(X)$ are
non-linear in $X$.  Positivity of the individual effect is therefore
preserved in the population OLS coefficient only under unconditional
randomisation.

A. Only Case 1

18.text:
The population OLS coefficient is the linear projection coefficient.
Write $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau_{i}$ with $\tau_{i}>0$ a.s. and under conditional
randomisation

$$
E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\,\tau(X),\qquad 
m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X],\;\; \tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0,
$$

and $E[Y|X]=m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X)$ with $p(X)=E[D|X]$.

Case 1. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$.  Then

$$
\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}]-E[Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0,
$$

the ATE, so the intercept–slope projection is strictly positive.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$.  Then

$$
E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]
 =E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0],
$$

i.e. the usual selection bias $E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
With $p(X)$ non-constant the $X$ distribution of the treated and the
untreated differ and the bias can dominate the positive
$E[\tau(X)|D=1]$.  E.g. $X\in\{0,1\},m_{0}(1)=100,m_{0}(0)=0,\tau\equiv1$,
$p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$ although
$Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s.  Hence the unadjusted difference in means, i.e. the
OLS coefficient on $D$ alone, is not signed.

Case 3.  Let $\hat p(X)=\alpha+\beta X$ be the linear projection of $D$
on $1,X$ and $D_{\perp}=D-\hat p(X)$.  Put $r(X)=p(X)-\hat p(X)$,
$E[r]=E[rX]=0$.  With $\eta=D-p(X)$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
E[Y D_{\perp}]
&=E\big[m_{0}r\big]+E\big[\tau p r\big]+E\big[\tau\eta^{2}\big]  \\
&=E\!\left[r\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X)\big)\right]
  +E\!\left[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)\right].
\end{aligned}
$$

The second term is $>0$.  The first term is
${\rm Cov}\big(E[Y|X],r(X)\big)$.  $r(X)$ is the linear approximation
error of the propensity score.  With no linearity restriction on
$m_{0}(X)$ or $p(X)$ the error $r(X)$ can be made negatively correlated
with $m_{0}(X)$ while keeping $E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\tau(X)$ and
$\tau(X)>0$.  Then ${\rm Cov}\big(E[Y|X],r\big)$ can be made
arbitrarily negative and dominate $E[\tau{\rm Var}(D|X)]$.

A classic example is $X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$,
$m_{0}(x)=-Mx^{2}$, $\tau\equiv1$.  Then $E[Y|X,D]=-Mx^{2}+D$ and
$E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $X$, yet the Frisch–Waugh
coefficient

$$
\beta_{D}= \frac{E[Y D_{\perp}]}{E[D_{\perp}^{2}]}
        =1-M\,\frac{{\rm Cov}(X^{2},p)}{{\rm Var}(D_{\perp})}\to-\infty
$$

as $M\to\infty$.  The same construction works in discrete form, e.g.
$X\in\{0,1,2\}$, $p(0)=p(1)=0.9$, $p(2)=0.1$ and $m_{0}(2)$ large, gives
$E[Y D_{\perp}]<0$ while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau>0$.

Hence the sign of the $D$ coefficient in the linear projection on
$1,D,X$ is not implied by $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ and $\tau_{i}>0$ alone;
it requires a linear conditional mean restriction which is not assumed.
With the exact residual $D-E[D|X]$ the covariance would be
$E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$, but OLS uses the linear residual
$D-\hat p(X)$.  In the non-parametric setting positivity is guaranteed
only under unconditional randomisation.

So the population $D$ coefficient is necessarily $>0$ only in Case 1.
A. Only Case 1

17.text:
The population $D$ coefficient is the linear projection coefficient. Write
$Y=Y_{0}+D\tau_{i}$ with $\tau_{i}>0$ a.s. and under conditional
randomisation

$$E[Y\mid X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D,\qquad 
\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0,\;\;m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}\mid X],$$
so that $E[Y\mid X,D]-E[Y\mid X,D-1]=\tau(X)>0$ pointwise in $X$.

Case 1  $D\perp Y_{0},\tau$. Then

$$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]>0,$$
the ATE, so the intercept–slope projection is strictly positive.

Case 2  $D\perp Y_{0},\tau\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$. 

$$\beta_{2}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
 =E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0].$$

The second term is selection on the baseline $m_{0}(X)$. With
$p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_{0}(X)$ increasing,
$E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]<0$ can dominate the
positive $E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]$.  E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$,
$p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(1)-m_{0}(0)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$, then
$E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=1+10-90<0$ although $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s.

Case 3  is the linear projection on $1,D,X$. Let $a+bX$ be the linear
projection of $D$ on $1,X$ and $w(X)=p(X)-a-bX$, $D_{\perp}=D-a-bX$.
Then

$$E[Y D_{\perp}\mid X]=w(X)\bigl[m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)p(X)\bigr]
+\tau(X){\rm Var}(D\mid X),$$

so that with $E[D_{\perp}]=E[D_{\perp}X]=0$

$$\beta_{D}= \frac{E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D\mid X)]+
E[w(X)\{m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)p(X)\}]}{E[D_{\perp}^{2}]}.$$

The first term is $>0$.  The second term is $E[w(X)m_{0}(X)]$ up to a
term in $\tau$.  $w(X)$ is the linear residual of the propensity
$p(X)$ and is orthogonal to $1,X$ but not to arbitrary functions of $X$.
Choosing $m_{0}(X)$ non-linear in $X$ and negatively correlated with
$w(X)$ makes $E[w m_{0}]$ arbitrarily negative.  For instance with
$X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $m_{0}(x)=-M x^{2}$,
$\tau(x)\equiv\tau_{0}>0$,

$$E[Y\mid X,D]=-Mx^{2}+\tau_{0}D,\qquad D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X,$$

and the Frisch–Waugh coefficient on $D$ is 
$\beta_{D}= \tau_{0}-cM$ with $c>0$.  For $M>\tau_{0}/c$,
$\beta_{D}<0$ even though $E[Y\mid X,D=1]-E[Y\mid X,D=0]=\tau_{0}>0$
for every $X$.

The same phenomenon occurs on a discrete support, e.g.
$X\in\{-1,0,1\}$ equiprobable, $p(-1)=p(1)=1,p(0)=0$, 
$m_{0}(-1)=m_{0}(1)=0,m_{0}(0)=M$, $\tau\equiv1$, where the linear
projection of $Y$ on $1,D,X$ has $\beta_{D}=1-10M<0$ for large $M$.
Hence the linear coefficient on $D$ after a linear control for $X$
need not inherit the within-$X$ positivity.  The non-parametric
partial effect $E[Y\mid X,D]-E[Y\mid X]$ is positive, the linear
projection is not.

The sign is therefore guaranteed only under unconditional randomisation.
That is Case 1 only.

A. Only Case 1

public_text.4:
The population OLS coefficient is the linear projection coefficient, not the
population regression function.  Write $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_{i}>0$ a.s.,
$m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$ and $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$.

*Case 1.*  $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y_{0},Y_{1})$.  Then
$$
\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}]-E[Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0 ,
$$
the difference in means is the ATE. Sign is guaranteed.

*Case 2.*  $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y_{0},Y_{1})|X$, $E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\tau(X)$.
$$
E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0].
$$
The first term is $>0$ but $E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$
$=Cov\!\big(m_{0}(X),D\big)/\operatorname{Var}(D)$ can be made arbitrarily
negative by letting $p(X)$ be decreasing in $m_{0}(X)$.  E.g.
$X\in\{0,1\}$, $m_{0}(1)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$
gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$. The uncontrolled difference in means,
i.e. the $1,D$ projection, is not sign identified.

*Case 3.*  The population linear projection is
$\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,D_{\perp})/Var(D_{\perp})$ with
$D_{\perp}=D-\operatorname{Proj}(D|1,X)$.  With $E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\tau(X)$,
$$
Cov(Y,D_{\perp})=E[\operatorname{Var}(D|X)\tau(X)]
   +Cov\!\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),\;p(X)-\operatorname{Proj}(p(X)|1,X)\big).
$$
The first term is $>0$ but the second term involves the covariance of
$m_{0}(X)$ with the non-linear part of the propensity.  Because
$p(X)-\operatorname{Proj}(p(X)|1,X)$ is orthogonal to $1,X$ it can be
made arbitrarily positively correlated with $m_{0}(X)$ where the linear
projection over-predicts $p(X)$ and negatively correlated where it
under-predicts it.  Hence $Cov(Y,D_{\perp})$ can be made negative.

E.g. $X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $Y_{0}=-Mx^{2}$, $\tau>0$.
Then $\operatorname{Proj}(D|1,X)$ is linear in $X$ and
$\beta_{D}= 1-M\,Cov(X^{2},p)/Var(D)\to-\infty$ as $M\to\infty$.
With $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$ equiprobable, $p(-1)=p(1)=1,\;p(0)=0$,
$m_{0}(0)=10,\;m_{0}(\pm1)=0$, $\tau=1$, the linear projection gives
$\beta_{D}=-9<0$ although $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau>0$ a.s. and
$D\perp(Y_{0},Y_{1})|X$.

Thus positivity of $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]$ does not carry over to the
linear residual $D-\operatorname{Proj}(D|1,X)$.  The sign is guaranteed
only under unconditional randomisation.

A. Only Case 1
public_text.9:
I think the sign is guaranteed in Case 1 and in Case 3, and not in the uncontrolled regression under conditional randomisation.

Case 1 is the usual randomised experiment.  With $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y_0,Y_1)$,
$\beta_D =E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_1-Y_0]>0$ because $Y_1>Y_0$ a.s.  So the
intercept-slope regression is the ATE and is strictly positive.

Conditional randomisation is $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y_0,Y_1)\mid X$ so that
$E[Y\mid X,D]=E[Y_0\mid X]+D\,E[Y_1-Y_0\mid X]$.
Put $\mu_0(X)=E[Y_0\mid X]$ and $\tau(X)=E[Y_1-Y_0\mid X]>0$ a.s.
Then

$E[Y\mid X,D]-E[Y\mid X]=\tau(X)\big(D-E[D\mid X]\big)$

and

$\operatorname{Cov}\big(Y,D\mid X\big)=\operatorname{Var}(D\mid X)\,\tau(X)>0$
pointwise.

Hence the within-$X$ association of $Y$ with $D$ is strictly positive for
every $X$.  Let $D_{\perp}=D-E[D\mid X]$ be the part of $D$ orthogonal to
$X$.  Then

$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})=E\!\left[\operatorname{Var}(D\mid X)\,\tau(X)\right]>0$

and the population linear projection of $Y$ on $1,D,X$ is

$\beta_D=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})}{\operatorname{Var}(D_{\perp})}
       =\frac{E\big[\operatorname{Var}(D\mid X)\,\tau(X)\big]}
              {E\big[\operatorname{Var}(D\mid X)\big]+E\big[(E[D\mid X]-P_XD)^2\big]}>0,$

a variance-weighted average of the strictly positive conditional average
effects $\tau(X)$.  Frisch–Waugh is just this: after partialling out $X$,
the residualised $D$ is a mean-zero function of $X$ and the covariance
with $Y$ is driven by $\operatorname{Var}(D\mid X)\tau(X)>0$.  Within each
$X$-level $Y$ is increasing in $D$ and the linear projection inherits that
monotonicity, so the partial coefficient on $D$ in $Y\sim1+D+X$ is
necessarily positive under $D\perp(Y_0,Y_1)\mid X$.

Case 2 is different.  The uncontrolled coefficient is

$E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
 =E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]+E[\mu_0(X)\mid D=1]-E[\mu_0(X)\mid D=0]$

so the selection bias $\operatorname{Cov}(\mu_0(X),D)$ remains.  With
$P(D=1\mid X)$ varying in $X$ the $X$-distribution of the treated and the
control can be reversed relative to $\mu_0(X)$.  E.g. $Y_0=X$, $Y_1=Y_0+1$,
$P(D=1\mid X=0)=0.9$, $P(D=1\mid X=1)=0.1$ gives
$E[Y\mid D=1]<E[Y\mid D=0]$ even though $Y_1>Y_0$ a.s.  The sign of the
simple difference in means is therefore not guaranteed.

So positivity is guaranteed for the unadjusted regression under
unconditional randomisation and for the regression that controls for $X$
under conditional randomisation, but not for the unadjusted regression
under conditional randomisation.  That is Case 1 and Case 3.

$\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,D_{\perp})/Var(D_{\perp})$.

$Cov(Y,D_{\perp}|X)=\tau(X)Var(D|X)>0$ so
$E[Cov(Y,D_{\perp}|X)]>0$, but

$Cov(Y,D_{\perp})=E[Cov(Y,D_{\perp}|X)]+Cov(E[Y|X],E[D_{\perp}|X])$
$=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov\big(m(X)+p(X)\tau(X),r(X)\big)$.

The second term is $Cov(m(X),r(X))+Cov(p(X)\tau(X),r(X))$ and is
unrestricted under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ alone. $r(X)$ is the linear
residual of the propensity.  With a non-linear $p(\cdot)$ we can make
$m(X)$ arbitrarily large and negatively correlated with $r(X)$, or
make $\tau(X)$ arbitrarily small where $r(X)$ is large, while keeping
$\tau(X)>0$.  E.g. $X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$,
$m(x)=-Mx^{2}$, $\tau\equiv1$,

$\beta_{D}=1-M\,Cov\big(x^{2},p(x)\big)/Var(D_{\perp})\to-\infty$
as $M\to\infty$.

though $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ for every $X$ and
$D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$.  The sign is preserved only when $p(X)$ is
linear in $X$, i.e. under a parametric restriction that is not allowed.

So a strictly positive population $D$ coefficient is guaranteed only
under unconditional randomisation.

I’m with E — Only Case 1 and Case 3 must be positive.

Case 1 is the usual RCT: D ⟂ (Y0,Y1) so the OLS slope is E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y1-Y0]>0. No issue.

Case 2 is the classic selection problem. With D ⟂ (Y0,Y1)|X we have 
E[Y|X,D]=m0(X)+τ(X)D with τ(X)=E[Y1-Y0|X]>0 a.s., so 
E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=τ(X)>0 pointwise.  Marginally
E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[τ(X)|D=1]+E[m0(X)|D=1]-E[m0(X)|D=0].
The second term is the X-composition bias Cov(m0(X),D).  Because P(D=1|X)=p(X) can be monotone in X, e.g. p(0)=0.9, p(1)=0.1 with m0(1)≫m0(0), the bias can dominate the positive τ term. The uncontrolled difference in means is therefore not signed.

Case 3 adds X to the linear projection.  Write Y=m0(X)+τ(X)D+u with E[u|X,D]=0 and τ(X)>0.  Conditional on X, D is mean independent of m0 and τ, so
Cov(Y,D|X)=Var(D|X) τ(X)>0 for every X.

Let D⊥ be the part of D orthogonal to the linear space spanned by 1,X, i.e. the Frisch-Waugh residual from the linear projection D=a+bX+ D⊥.  Then

Cov(Y,D⊥)=E[ Cov(Y,D|X) ] + E[ (E[Y|X]-E[Y]) (E[D|X]-a-bX) ].

The first term is E[Var(D|X) τ(X)]>0.  The second term is the covariance of the X-dependent part of the mean with the part of E[D|X] that is not captured linearly in X.  After projecting out the linear span of 1,X, the variation left in D⊥ is precisely the within-X variation in D.  By construction E[D⊥|X]=p(X)-a-bX has mean zero and is orthogonal to 1,X, and

E[Y D⊥|X]=m0(X)E[D⊥|X]+τ(X)E[D D⊥|X]=τ(X)E[D D⊥|X].

Hence, conditional on X, Y is increasing in D and the residual covariance is a positive weighted average of the strictly positive within-X gaps τ(X)Var(D|X).  With τ(X)>0 a.s. the numerator E[Y D⊥] is strictly positive and

β_D = Cov(Y,D⊥)/Var(D⊥)= E[ w(X) τ(X) ]/E[w(X)] >0,

with w(X)=Var(D|X)>0.  In words, once X is in the regression the only variation identifying D is within-X variation, and within every X-stratum Y is strictly increasing in D by conditional randomisation.  A linear best predictor therefore inherits that within-stratum monotonicity.

The sign reversals quoted for the linear projection are obtained by replacing the linear residual D⊥=D-a-bX with the non-parametric residual D-p(X).  The object Cov(Y,D-p(X))=E[Var(D|X)τ(X)]>0 is the non-parametric partial covariance, i.e. controlling for X non-parametrically.  The population OLS in Case 3 controls for X only linearly.  The examples with p(x)=0.5+0.4x² and m0(x)=-Mx² are perfectly valid for non-parametric control – with p(X) partialled out non-parametrically the coefficient is positive – but they do not change the sign of the best linear predictor on 1,D,X, which is the average of the positive within-X contrasts.

So positivity is guaranteed under unconditional randomisation, not guaranteed for the marginal regression under conditional randomisation, and it is restored once X is included in the regression.

I think the sign is preserved once X is in the regression, and the objection about a non-linear propensity is a confusion between $D-E[D|X]$ and the linear residual $D-\hat p(X)$.

Write $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$ with $\tau>0$ a.s. and under conditional randomisation
$D\perp Y_{0},\tau\mid X$, so that

$$E[Y\mid X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D,\qquad \tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0,$$
$$E[Y\mid X]=m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),\qquad p(X)=E[D\mid X].$$

Then

$$Y-E[Y\mid X]=\big(D-p(X)\big)\tau(X).$$

Hence with the $X$-mean-centred residual

$$E\big[(D-E[D|X])\,(Y-E[Y|X])\big]
 =E\Big[\tau(X)(D-p(X))^{2}\Big]
 =E\big[\,\operatorname{Var}(D\mid X)\tau(X)\big]>0.$$

The linear projection of $Y$ on $1,D,X$ is the projection on the space
spanned by $1,X,D$.  Frisch-Waugh is $ \beta_{D}= \operatorname{Cov}(Y,\tilde D)/
\operatorname{Var}(\tilde D)$ with $\tilde D$ the linear population residual of
$D$ on $1,X$.  Up to the linear part in $X$,
$\tilde D$ is $ (D-p(X))$ plus a term that is $X$-measurable and hence
orthogonal to the part of $Y-E[Y|X]$ that is mean zero given $X$.
Consequently

$$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E\big[\tau(X)\,\operatorname{Cov}(D,\tilde D\mid X)\big]>0,$$

a positive weighted average of the strictly positive conditional effects
$\tau(X)>0$ with weights $\operatorname{Var}(D\mid X)\ge 0$.  In other words,
after removing the linear part of $X$ the remaining variation in $D$ is
still mean independent of $Y_{0}$ given $X$, and within every $X$-stratum
$E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$.  The population partial
coefficient is therefore a positive average of those within-$X$ gaps.

Case 1 is the usual unconditional experiment:
$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]>0$.

Case 2 is the uncontrolled mean difference under conditional
randomisation,

$$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D)=E[\operatorname{Var}(D\mid X)\tau(X)]
      +\operatorname{Cov}\!\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),p(X)\big),$$

so the composition term $\operatorname{Cov}(m_{0}(X),p(X))$ can dominate
the positive first term.  With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_{0}(X)$
increasing in $X$, e.g. $Y_{0}=100X$, $\tau\equiv1$, $P(D=1|X=0)=0.9$,
$P(D=1|X=1)=0.1$, we get $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]<0$ even though $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$
a.s.  The sign is not guaranteed without $X$ in the regression.

Hence positivity is guaranteed for the unadjusted regression under
unconditional randomisation, and for the regression that controls for $X$
under conditional randomisation, but not for the unadjusted regression
under conditional randomisation. That is Case 1 and Case 3.

The first term is $>0$ but the selection term $E[E[Y_{0}|X]|D=1]-E[E[Y_{0}|X]|D=0]=\operatorname{Cov}(E[Y_{0}|X],D)/P(D=1)P(D=0)$ can be made arbitrarily negative. $E[(D-E[D|X])(Y-E[Y|X])\mid X]=E[\tau(X)(D-E[D|X])^{2}\mid X]=\operatorname{Var}(D|X)\tau(X)>0$,

so unconditionally

$E[(D-E[D|X])(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[\operatorname{Var}(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$.

The population linear projection of $Y$ on $1,D,X$ is the projection on $1,X$ followed by projection on the residual. The Frisch-Waugh coefficient is

$\beta_{D|X}= \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})}{\operatorname{Var}(D_{\perp})}
          =\frac{E[\operatorname{Var}(D|X)\tau(X)]}{\operatorname{Var}(D_{\perp})}>0.$

E[Y|X]=m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),
$$

$E[\tilde D]=0$, $E[\tilde D X]=0$ and $w(X)=E[\tilde D|X]=p(X)-\hat p(X)$
where $\hat p$ is the linear projection of $p$ on $1,X$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\tilde D)
&=E\!\left[E[Y\tilde D|X]\right]  \\
&=E\!\left[m_{0}(X)w(X)\right]+E\!\left[\tau(X)p(X)(1-p(X))\right]
    +E\!\left[\tau(X)p(X)w(X)\right].
\end{aligned}
$$

The middle term $E[\tau p(1-p)]>0$ is the within-$X$ part.  
The first term $E[m_{0}w]$ is the covariance of the baseline mean with the
linear residual of the propensity. $w$ is mean-zero and orthogonal to $1,X$
but $p(X)$ is in general non-linear in $X$, so $w\neq0$ and can be made
non-zero on sets where $m_{0}$ is chosen arbitrarily.  Hence
$E[m_{0}w]$ can be made arbitrarily negative, and the same holds for
$E[\tau p w]$.  The linear projection coefficient

$$
\beta_{D}= \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\tilde D)}{\operatorname{Var}(\tilde D)}
$$

A. Only Case 1

Write $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$ with $\tau=Y_{1}-Y_{0}>0$ a.s. and
$m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$.
Under conditional randomisation
$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\,\tau(X)$ and 
$E[Y|X,D]-E[Y|X,D=0]=\tau(X)>0$ a.s.

Case 1.  $D\!\perp\! Y_{0},Y_{1}$.  The population OLS is the difference
in means
$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}]-E[Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$.
The sign is guaranteed.

Case 2.  $D\!\perp\!Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but $D\not\!\perp\!X$.
$\beta_{2}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]
+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The second term is selection bias $\operatorname{Cov}(m_{0}(X),p(X))/
P(D=1)P(D=0)$ with $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$.  With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$
and $m_{0}(X)$ increasing in $X$ the bias can dominate $\tau$.
E.g. $X\in\{0,1\},\,p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1,m_{0}(1)=100,\tau\equiv1$ gives
$E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$.  The marginal difference in means is
not sign identified.

Case 3.  Let $D_{\ell}=D-a-bX$ be the linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$.
Then
$\beta_{3}= \operatorname{Cov}(Y,D_{\ell})/\operatorname{Var}(D_{\ell})$.
Now
$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D_{\ell})
 =\operatorname{Cov}\!\big(Y, D-E[D|X]\big)
  +\operatorname{Cov}\!\big(Y,p(X)-a-bX\big)$,
$\operatorname{Cov}\!\big(Y, D-E[D|X]\big)=E[\operatorname{Var}(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$,
but
$\operatorname{Cov}\!\big(Y,p(X)-a-bX\big)
 =E\big[(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X))(p(X)-a-bX)\big]$.
The term $E[m_{0}(X)(p(X)-a-bX)]=\operatorname{Cov}\!\big(m_{0}(X),p(X)-a-bX\big)$
is the covariance of $m_{0}$ with the linear residual of the propensity.
Because $p(X)-a-bX$ is orthogonal to $1,X$ it can be made arbitrarily
negatively correlated with a non-linear $m_{0}(X)$.
E.g. $X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $m_{0}(x)=-M x^{2}$,
$\tau\equiv1$.  Then $\operatorname{Var}(D_{\ell})$ is fixed and
$\beta_{3}=1-M\,{\rm Cov}(X^{2},p)/\operatorname{Var}(D_{\ell})\to-\infty$
as $M\to\infty$, while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau>0$ for every $X$.
With three points $X\in\{-1,0,1\},p(-1)=p(1)=0.9,p(0)=0.1$,
$m_{0}(0)=10,m_{0}(\pm1)=0,\tau=1$ gives
$\beta_{3}=1-10=-9<0$.
Hence the linear projection of $Y$ on $1,D,X$ can be negative even
with $D\!\perp\!Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ and $\tau>0$ a.s.

The positivity of $E[(D-E[D|X])Y]$ does not imply positivity of
$E[(D-a-bX)Y]$; the OLS residual is $D-a-bX$, not $D-E[D|X]$.
The sign is therefore guaranteed only under unconditional
randomisation.

Only Case 1 must be $>0$.

I agree with the A camp that Case 2 cannot be signed and that the simple difference in means is not enough once randomisation is only conditional on X. With $D\perp\!\!\!\perp (Y_{0},Y_{1})|X$ we have

$E[Y|X,D]=E[Y_{0}|X]+E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}|X]\,D =\mu_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$

with $\tau(X)=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}|X]>0$ a.s. Pointwise in $X$ the conditional mean is strictly increasing in $D$. The uncontrolled contrast

$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[\mu_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[\mu_{0}(X)|D=0]$

contains the selection term $E[\mu_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[\mu_{0}(X)|D=0]$. Because $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$ can be decreasing in pre-income while $\mu_{0}(X)$ is increasing in pre-income, the bias can dominate the positive $\tau$ term, e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$, $\mu_{0}(1)-\mu_{0}(0)$ large. That is the usual jobs-program selection example and it is correct.

Once $X$ is in the regression the confounding is removed. Write $E[Y|X]= \mu_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X)$. Then

$E[Y|X,D]-E[Y|X]=\tau(X)\big(D-p(X)\big)$

so that, with $D_{\perp}=D-E[D|X]$,

$E\big[D_{\perp}\big(Y-E[Y|X]\big)\big]
   =E\big[\tau(X)(D-p(X))^{2}\big]
   =E\big[\operatorname{Var}(D|X)\tau(X)\big]>0$.

Hence $ \operatorname{Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})>0$. The Frisch-Waugh residual of $D$ after partialling out $1,X$ is $D-\widehat p(X)$ where $\widehat p(X)$ is the linear projection of $D$ on $1,X$. Up to the usual linear-projection rotation, $D-\widehat p(X)$ is the part of $D$ orthogonal to $X$ and therefore its covariance with $Y$ is driven by the within-$X$ contrast $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$. In particular

$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D_{\perp}\mid X)=\operatorname{Var}(D|X)\,\tau(X)>0$

and after taking expectations over $X$ the sign is preserved. The population linear projection of $Y$ on $1,D,X$ is therefore a positive weighted average of the strictly positive within-$X$ treatment effects.

Under unconditional randomisation $D\perp\!\!\!\perp (Y_{0},Y_{1})$ we have in Case 1

$\beta_{D}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]>0$

the ATE.

So the $D$ coefficient is guaranteed positive in the unadjusted regression under unconditional randomisation, and it remains guaranteed positive once $X$ is linearly controlled under conditional randomisation, while the unadjusted regression under conditional randomisation is not signed. That is Case 1 and Case 3.

$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\,h(X)$ with $m_{0}(X)=E[Y(0)|X]$ and

$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)]-E[Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$,

so the intercept–slope projection of $Y$ on $1,D$ is the ATE and is $>0$.

Case 2. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$ in general.
$E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=h(X)>0$, yet

$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[h(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.

With $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$ decreasing in $X$ while $m_{0}(X)$ is increasing in $X$
the selection term $E[m_{0}|D=1]-E[m_{0}|D=0]$ can dominate $E[h|X]$.
E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $m_{0}(1)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=1+10-90<0$ although $Y(1)>Y(0)$ a.s.  The uncontrolled
difference in means is not signed.

Case 3. The population OLS coefficient is the linear projection on
$\operatorname{span}\{1,D,X\}$.  Write $D_{\perp}=D-{\rm Proj}(D|1,X)$.
Then

$\beta_{D}= {\rm Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})/{\rm Var}(D_{\perp})$ and

${\rm Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})
= E\big[(p(X)-{\rm Proj}(p|1,X))\,m_{0}(X)\big]
 +E\big[h(X){\rm Var}(D|X)\big]+{\rm remainder}>0 $.

The second term is $>0$, but the first term is the covariance of the
linear residual of the propensity $p(X)$ with $m_{0}(X)$.  Because the
OLS residual of $D$ is only the linear residual of $p(X)$,
$w(X)=p(X)-a-bX$ with $E[w]=E[wX]=0$, $E[w(X)m_{0}(X)]$ can be made
arbitrarily negative by choosing a non-linear $m_{0}(X)$ that is strongly
negatively correlated with $w(X)$.  With e.g. $X\sim U[-1,1]$,
$p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $m_{0}(x)=-M x^{2}$ and $h(x)\equiv\tau>0$,

${\rm Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})=\tau {\rm Var}(D_{\perp})-M\,
{\rm Cov}(X^{2},p(X))$,
${\rm Cov}(X^{2},p(X))>0$, so $\beta_{D}= \tau-M\,{\rm Cov}(X^{2},p)/{\rm Var}
(D_{\perp})\to-\infty$ as $M\to\infty$, while
$E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau>0$ for every $X$.

$m_{0}(X)$; the linear residual of $D$ can be correlated with the
non-linear component of $E[Y(0)|X]$.  The sign reversal is the usual
linear-projection Simpson phenomenon.

randomisation.  That is Case 1, and Cases 2 and 3 are not guaranteed
positive without parametric linearity of $E[Y(0)|X]$ and $p(X)$.

$E[Y\mid X,D]= \mu_{0}(X)+D\,\tau(X)$ with $\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$
under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ and

$E[Y\mid D,X]-E[Y\mid D',X]=\tau(X)>0$ for every $X$.

*Case 1.* $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$.  Then
$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]>0$.
The population intercept-slope projection is the ATE.

$p(X)=E[D\mid X]$ and $\mu_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}\mid X]$.  Then

$$
E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
=E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]+E[\mu_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[\mu_{0}(X)\mid D=0] .
$$

The second difference is $\operatorname{Cov}(\mu_{0}(X),D)/P(D=1)P(D=0)$
and can dominate the first positive term.  With e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$,
$p(0)=0.9,\;p(1)=0.1$, $\mu_{0}(1)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$,

$E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$ although $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s.

$D_{\perp}=D-\hat p(X)$.  The population linear coefficient is

$$
\beta_{D}=\frac{E[Y D_{\perp}]}{E[D_{\perp}^{2}]}.
$$

For binary $D$

$$
E[Y D_{\perp}\mid X]=\mu_{0}(X)\big(p(X)-\hat p(X)\big)
        +\tau(X)p(X)\big(1-\hat p(X)\big),
$$

so that

$$
E[Y D_{\perp}]
 =E\big[\operatorname{Var}(D\mid X)\tau(X)\big]
  +E\big[ \big(\mu_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X)\big)\big(p(X)-\hat p(X)\big)\big].
$$

The first term is $>0$.  $p(X)-\hat p(X)$ is orthogonal to $1,X$ but can be
correlated with any non-linear function of $X$.  Choosing
$\mu_{0}(X)$ proportional to $-\big(p(X)-\hat p(X)\big)$ makes
$\operatorname{Cov}\big(\mu_{0}(X),p(X)-\hat p(X)\big)$ arbitrarily
negative and can dominate the positive $E[\operatorname{Var}(D\mid X)\tau(X)]$.

E.g. $X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $\hat p(x)=0.5$, 
$\mu_{0}(x)=-M x^{2}$, $\tau\equiv1$.  Then
$\beta_{D}= 1- cM$ with $c>0$ and $\beta_{D}<0$ for $M$ large, while

$p(-1)=p(1)=1,\;p(0)=0$, which gives $\beta_{D}=1-10M<0$.

linear projection of $Y$ on $1,D,X$ is not sign identified by
$\tau>0$ and $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ alone.  The positivity is
preserved for the non-parametric partial effect
$E[Y\mid D,X]-E[Y\mid D',X]$, not for the best linear predictor with a
linear control for $X$.

The sign is therefore guaranteed only under unconditional randomisation.

The sign is guaranteed under unconditional randomisation and, once X is in the regression, under conditional randomisation. The marginal unadjusted contrast under conditional randomisation is not guaranteed.

Case 1. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp Y(0),Y(1)$. Then $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]>0$ because $Y(1)>Y(0)$ a.s. The OLS slope on $1,D$ is the ATE and is strictly positive.

Case 2. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ but $D$ is in general correlated with $X$. Write $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$ with $\tau=Y(1)-Y(0)>0$ and $E[\tau|X]>0$. Then

$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E\big[E[\tau|X]\mid D=1\big]+E\big[E[Y_{0}|X]\mid D=1\big]-E\big[E[Y_{0}|X]\mid D=0\big]$.

The first term is $>0$ but the second term is selection bias $\operatorname{Cov}\big(E[Y_{0}|X],D\big)$. With $P(D=1|X)=p(X)$ varying in $X$ the treated and control $X$-distributions differ and the bias can dominate the positive treatment term. E.g. $Y_{0}=X$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9, p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]<E[Y|D=0]$ even though $Y(1)>Y(0)$ a.s. So the unadjusted difference in means, i.e. the OLS coefficient in $Y$ on $1,D$, need not be positive.

Case 3. Condition on $X$ in the regression. Conditional randomisation gives

$E[Y|X,D]=E[Y_{0}|X]+D\,E[\tau|X]$ with $E[\tau|X]>0$ a.s. and $D\perp\!\!\!\perp Y_{0},\tau\mid X$.

Hence for the part of $D$ that is not explained linearly by $X$,

$E\big[\big(D-E[D|X]\big)\big(Y-E[Y|X]\big)\mid X\big]=E[\tau|X]\,\operatorname{Var}(D|X)>0$.

Averaging over $X$,

$\operatorname{Cov}\big(Y,D_{\perp}\big)=E\Big[\operatorname{Var}(D|X)E[\tau|X]\Big]>0$,

where $D_{\perp}$ is the linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$. In Frisch-Waugh form

$\beta_{D|X}= \operatorname{Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})/\operatorname{Var}(D_{\perp})$
$=E\big[\operatorname{Var}(D|X)E[\tau|X]\big]/E\big[\operatorname{Var}(D|X)\big]$ up to the positive weight coming from the linear projection. It is a positively weighted average of the strictly positive within-$X$ conditional average treatment effects $E[\tau|X]>0$. Within each $X$ level the treated mean is larger than the control mean because the treatment effect is positive for every unit, and partialling out $X$ leaves only that within-$X$ variation.

Thus with $X$ in the regression the population linear coefficient on $D$ inherits the within-$X$ monotonicity of $Y$ in $D$ and must be $>0$. The counter-examples that make the linear coefficient negative require $E[Y_{0}|X]$ to be correlated with the non-linear part of $p(X)$ in a way that is orthogonal to $1,X$ but strongly opposite in sign to the treatment effect. For pre-income $X$ and post-income $Y$ that is the usual quadratic-overlinear pathology, $m_{0}(X)=kX^{2}$ with a propensity that is $0.5+0.4X^{2}$, which is the opposite curvature of any economically plausible income relationship and is essentially mixing a directionally increasing baseline with a non-monotone selection rule. Under the stated conditional randomisation the back-door path $D\leftarrow X\rightarrow Y$ is blocked by conditioning on $X$, so the partial association of $Y$ with $D$ is the average of the positive conditional effects.

Positivity is therefore guaranteed in Case 1 by unconditional randomisation and in Case 3 by conditioning on $X$ in the regression, but it is not guaranteed for the unadjusted regression under conditional randomisation, Case 2.

$$

 =E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0],
$$

i.e. the usual selection bias $E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
With $p(X)$ non-constant the $X$ distribution of the treated and the
untreated differ and the bias can dominate the positive
$E[\tau(X)|D=1]$.  E.g. $X\in\{0,1\},m_{0}(1)=100,m_{0}(0)=0,\tau\equiv1$,
$p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$ although

OLS coefficient on $D$ alone, is not signed.

on $1,X$ and $D_{\perp}=D-\hat p(X)$.  Put $r(X)=p(X)-\hat p(X)$,
$E[r]=E[rX]=0$.  With $\eta=D-p(X)$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
E[Y D_{\perp}]
&=E\big[m_{0}r\big]+E\big[\tau p r\big]+E\big[\tau\eta^{2}\big]  \\
&=E\!\left[r\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X)\big)\right]
  +E\!\left[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)\right].
\end{aligned}
$$

The second term is $>0$.  The first term is
${\rm Cov}\big(E[Y|X],r(X)\big)$.  $r(X)$ is the linear approximation
error of the propensity score.  With no linearity restriction on
$m_{0}(X)$ or $p(X)$ the error $r(X)$ can be made negatively correlated
with $m_{0}(X)$ while keeping $E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\tau(X)$ and
$\tau(X)>0$.  Then ${\rm Cov}\big(E[Y|X],r\big)$ can be made
arbitrarily negative and dominate $E[\tau{\rm Var}(D|X)]$.

$m_{0}(x)=-Mx^{2}$, $\tau\equiv1$.  Then $E[Y|X,D]=-Mx^{2}+D$ and

$$
\beta_{D}= \frac{E[Y D_{\perp}]}{E[D_{\perp}^{2}]}

$$

as $M\to\infty$.  The same construction works in discrete form, e.g.

so that $E[Y\mid X,D]-E[Y\mid X,D-1]=\tau(X)>0$ pointwise in $X$.

Case 1  $D\perp Y_{0},\tau$. Then

$$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]>0,$$
the ATE, so the intercept–slope projection is strictly positive.

Case 2  $D\perp Y_{0},\tau\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$. 

$$\beta_{2}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
 =E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0].$$

The second term is selection on the baseline $m_{0}(X)$. With
$p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_{0}(X)$ increasing,
$E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]<0$ can dominate the
positive $E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]$.  E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$,
$p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(1)-m_{0}(0)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$, then
$E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=1+10-90<0$ although $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s.

Case 3  is the linear projection on $1,D,X$. Let $a+bX$ be the linear
projection of $D$ on $1,X$ and $w(X)=p(X)-a-bX$, $D_{\perp}=D-a-bX$.
Then

$$E[Y D_{\perp}\mid X]=w(X)\bigl[m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)p(X)\bigr]
+\tau(X){\rm Var}(D\mid X),$$

so that with $E[D_{\perp}]=E[D_{\perp}X]=0$

$$\beta_{D}= \frac{E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D\mid X)]+
E[w(X)\{m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)p(X)\}]}{E[D_{\perp}^{2}]}.$$

The first term is $>0$.  The second term is $E[w(X)m_{0}(X)]$ up to a
term in $\tau$.  $w(X)$ is the linear residual of the propensity
$p(X)$ and is orthogonal to $1,X$ but not to arbitrary functions of $X$.
Choosing $m_{0}(X)$ non-linear in $X$ and negatively correlated with
$w(X)$ makes $E[w m_{0}]$ arbitrarily negative.  For instance with
$X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $m_{0}(x)=-M x^{2}$,
$\tau(x)\equiv\tau_{0}>0$,

$$E[Y\mid X,D]=-Mx^{2}+\tau_{0}D,\qquad D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X,$$

and the Frisch–Waugh coefficient on $D$ is 
$\beta_{D}= \tau_{0}-cM$ with $c>0$.  For $M>\tau_{0}/c$,
$\beta_{D}<0$ even though $E[Y\mid X,D=1]-E[Y\mid X,D=0]=\tau_{0}>0$
for every $X$.

The same phenomenon occurs on a discrete support, e.g.
$X\in\{-1,0,1\}$ equiprobable, $p(-1)=p(1)=1,p(0)=0$, 
$m_{0}(-1)=m_{0}(1)=0,m_{0}(0)=M$, $\tau\equiv1$, where the linear
projection of $Y$ on $1,D,X$ has $\beta_{D}=1-10M<0$ for large $M$.
Hence the linear coefficient on $D$ after a linear control for $X$
need not inherit the within-$X$ positivity.  The non-parametric
partial effect $E[Y\mid X,D]-E[Y\mid X]$ is positive, the linear
projection is not.

The sign is therefore guaranteed only under unconditional randomisation.
That is Case 1 only.

A. Only Case 1

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The potential-outcome model is $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_i=Y_{1i}-Y_{0i}>0$ a.s., $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, $p(X)=E[D|X]$ and under conditional randomisation $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ so $E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$ and $E[Y|X,D]-E[Y|X,D=0]=\tau(X)>0$ pointwise.

*Case 1.* $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. Then the OLS intercept-slope projection is the difference in means
$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}]-E[Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$. Unconditional randomisation forces the sign.

*Case 2.* $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$. 
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_{0}|D=1]-E[m_{0}|D=0]=Cov(m_{0}(X),D)/Var(D)$ can dominate the positive $\tau$ term. E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $m_{0}(1)\gg m_{0}(0)$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$. Uncontrolled difference in means is not sign identified.

*Case 3.* Linear projection $Y=\alpha+\beta D+\gamma X+\varepsilon$. With $D_{\perp}=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}(D)$,
$\beta_{3}=Cov(Y,D_{\perp})/Var(D_{\perp})$.
$Cov(Y,D_{\perp}|X)=\tau(X)Var(D|X)>0$ so $E[Cov(Y,D_{\perp}|X)]>0$, but
$Cov(Y,D_{\perp})=E[Cov(Y,D_{\perp}|X)]+Cov(E[Y|X],E[D_{\perp}|X])$
$=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),\,p(X)-\hat p(X)\big)$
where $\hat p(X)$ is the linear projection of $p(X)$ on $1,X$ and $r(X)=p(X)-\hat p(X)$ is orthogonal to $1,X$ in the $L^{2}$ sense.
The term $Cov(m_{0}(X),r(X))$ is unrestricted under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ alone. With a non-linear propensity $p(\cdot)$ the linear residual $r(X)\neq0$ and can be made arbitrarily negatively correlated with $m_{0}(X)$ while keeping $\tau(X)>0$. Then $Cov(Y,D_{\perp})$ can be made negative.

Standard examples: $X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $\hat p\equiv0.5$, $m_{0}(x)=-M x^{2}$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives $\beta_{D}=1-M\,Cov(x^{2},p)/Var(D_{\perp})\to-\infty$ as $M\to\infty$; discrete $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$ with $p(\pm1)=0.9$, $p(0)=0.1$, $m_{0}(0)=M$, $m_{0}(\pm1)=0$ yields $\beta_{D}=1-10M<0$. The non-parametric partial covariance $E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$ is positive, but OLS uses the linear residual $D-\hat p(X)$, not $D-p(X)$. Hence the linear projection can suffer the usual Simpson/linear-sign-reversal.

The colleagues arguing for E/Only Case1 and Case3 conflate $D-E[D|X]$ with the linear residual $D-{\rm Proj}(D|1,X)$ and assume positivity of the Frisch-Waugh coefficient is inherited from the within-$X$ positivity. That requires linearity of $p(X)$ and $m_{0}(X)$ in $X$, which is not allowed.

Thus under the stated non-parametric assumptions positivity of the population OLS coefficient on $D$ is forced only by unconditional randomisation. Case 2 is false by selection bias, Case 3 is false by non-linear $p(X)$ and $m_{0}(X)$ interacting with the linear projection residual. Current belief: A. Only Case 1.

4.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The population OLS coefficient is the linear projection coefficient, not the conditional mean coefficient. Write $Y=Y_0+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., $m_0(X)=E[Y_0|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, $p(X)=E[D|X]$. Under $D\perp Y_0,Y_1|X$, $E[Y|X,D]=m_0(X)+\tau(X)D$ and $E[Y|X]=m_0(X)+p(X)\tau(X)$.

Case 1. $D\perp Y_0,Y_1$. Then $\beta_1=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_1-Y_0]=E[\tau]>0$. Unconditional randomisation makes the intercept–slope regression the ATE, sign is guaranteed.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_0,Y_1|X$ but $D\not\perp X$. $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$. The selection term $\operatorname{Cov}(m_0(X),D)$ can dominate. With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_0(X)$ increasing, e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $m_0(1)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$, $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$. The uncontrolled difference in means is not sign identified.

Case 3. Linear projection on $1,D,X$. Let $\hat D=\operatorname{Proj}(D|1,X)$, $D_\perp=D-\hat D$, $w(X)=p(X)-\hat p(X)$ with $E[w]=E[wX]=0$. Then $\beta_D=\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D_\perp)/\operatorname{Var}(D_\perp)$ and

$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D_\perp)=E[\tau(X)\operatorname{Var}(D|X)]+E[w(X)\{m_0(X)+p(X)\tau(X)\}]$.

The first term $>0$, but $E[w(X)m_0(X)]$ is the covariance of $m_0(X)$ with the linear residual of the propensity. With a non-linear $p(X)$ $w(X)\neq0$ and can be made arbitrarily negatively correlated with $m_0(X)$ while keeping $\tau(X)>0$ and $D\perp Y_0,Y_1|X$. E.g. $X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^2$, $m_0(x)=-M x^2$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives $\beta_D=1-M\,{\rm Cov}(x^2,p)/\operatorname{Var}(D_\perp)\to-\infty$ as $M\to\infty$, while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for all $X$. Discrete examples $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$ with $p(-1)=p(1)=1,p(0)=0$, $m_0(0)=10$, $\tau=1$ give $\beta_D=-9<0$.

The non-parametric partial covariance $E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[\tau(X)\operatorname{Var}(D|X)]>0$ would be positive, i.e. controlling for $X$ non-parametrically preserves sign. The OLS residual is $D-\hat p(X)$, not $D-p(X)$. The confusion in the E camp is the replacement of the linear residual by the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$. Without a linearity restriction on $m_0(X)$ and $p(X)$ the linear projection on $1,D,X$ does not inherit pointwise positivity.

Hence positivity is guaranteed only under unconditional randomisation. Case 2 and Case 3 can be negative despite $\tau_i>0$ a.s. and $D\perp Y_0,Y_1|X$. Current belief: A. Only Case 1. The split in the room is between those using $D-E[D|X]$ and those using $D-\operatorname{Proj}(D|1,X)$.

10.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The core objects are Y = Y0 + D τ with τ_i = Y1(i)-Y0(i) >0 a.s., m(X)=E[Y0|X], τ(X)=E[τ|X]>0, p(X)=E[D|X] and D⊥ Y0,Y1 |X.

Case 1 unconditional randomisation D⊥Y0,Y1. Then E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y1]-E[Y0]=E[τ]>0 so the OLS of Y on 1,D is strictly positive. Unanimous.

Case 2 D⊥Y0,Y1|X but D not ⊥ X.
E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=τ(X)>0 pointwise, but
E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[τ(X)|D=1]+E[m(X)|D=1]-E[m(X)|D=0].
Selection term E[m(X)|D=1]-E[m(X)|D=0]=Cov(m(X),p(X))/... can dominate. Example X∈{0,1}, m(1)=100,m(0)=0, τ≡1, p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1 gives E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]. Accepted by all.

Case 3 linear projection of Y on 1,D,X. Let \hat p(X)=Proj(p|X) be linear projection, r(X)=p(X)-\hat p(X) with E[r]=E[rX]=0, \tilde D=D-\hat p(X). Then
β_D = Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D).
Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[τ(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov(m(X)+p(X)τ(X),r(X)).
E[τ Var(D|X)]>0, but Cov(m(X),r(X)) is unrestricted because r(X) is orthogonal to 1,X but generally non-zero when p(·) is non-linear. By making m(X) large and negatively correlated with r(X) and/or τ(X) small where r(X) is large, Cov(Y,\tilde D) can be made negative. Canonical counterexamples: X~U[-1,1], p(x)=0.5+0.4x², m(x)=-M x², τ≡1 gives β_D=1-M Cov(X²,p)/Var(\tilde D)→-∞ as M→∞; discrete X∈{-1,0,1} with p(-1)=p(1)=1,p(0)=0 and m0(0)=10 gives β_D<0.

The mistaken claim that E[D̃|X]=0 and thus Cov(Y,D̃)=E[Var(D|X)τ(X)]>0 holds for the non-parametric residual D-E[D|X], not for the linear residual D- Proj(D|1,X). OLS uses the linear residual, so sign reversal is possible without parametric linearity of p(X) or m(X). Several colleagues invoke the non-parametric residual argument and conclude Case3 must be positive, e.g. E. Only Case1 and Case3. That is the disagreement in round1.

Given no parametric assumptions beyond D⊥Y0,Y1|X and τ>0, the linear projection coefficient is not sign-identified. Only unconditional randomisation guarantees positivity. Current best belief remains A. Only Case 1.

Unresolved: the exact phrasing about “regress Y on a constant, D and X” is linear OLS, so the counterexample stands. If the question intended non-parametric control of X, answer would be E, but as stated it is A.

7.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The core structure is Y = Y0 + D τ with τ_i = Y1i-Y0i >0 a.s., m0(X)=E[Y0|X], τ(X)=E[τ|X]>0 and under conditional randomisation D ⟂ Y0,Y1 | X so E[Y|X,D]=m0(X)+τ(X)D and E[Y|X,D]-E[Y|X,D=0]=τ(X)>0 pointwise.

Case 1. D ⟂ Y0,Y1 unconditionally. Then the population regression of Y on 1,D is the difference in means β1 = E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y1]-E[Y0]=E[τ]>0. Sign is guaranteed.

Case 2. D ⟂ Y0,Y1|X but D is correlated with X marginally. 
E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[τ(X)|D=1]+E[m0(X)|D=1]-E[m0(X)|D=0].
The selection term E[m0|D=1]-E[m0|D=0]=Cov(m0(X),p(X))/… can be made arbitrarily negative by letting p(X)=P(D=1|X) decrease in X while m0(X) increases in X. Example X∈{0,1}, p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1, m0(1)=100, τ≡1 gives E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0] despite τ>0 a.s. So the unadjusted difference in means / OLS on 1,D is not sign identified.

Case 3. Population linear projection Y = α+β D+γ X+ε. Frisch-Waugh β = Cov(Y,D⊥)/Var(D⊥) with D⊥=D- Proj(D|1,X). Write p(X)=E[D|X]. Then
Cov(Y,D⊥)=E[Var(D|X)τ(X)]+Cov(m0(X)+p(X)τ(X), p(X)-Proj(p|1,X)).
The first term is >0. The second term is Cov(m0(X), p(X)-a-bX)+ … . 
p(X)-a-bX is the linear residual of the propensity. It is mean zero and orthogonal to 1,X but can be non-zero when p(X) is non-linear in X. By choosing m0(X) non-linear and strongly negatively correlated with that linear residual, E[m0(X)w(X)] with w(X)=p(X)-a-bX can be made arbitrarily negative and dominate the positive within-X term.

Concrete examples:
X~U[-1,1], p(x)=0.5+0.4 x², m0(x)=-M x², τ≡1. Then Proj(D|1,X)=0.5, w(x)=0.4(x²-E[x²]), β =1 - M Cov(x²,w)/Var(D⊥) → -∞ as M→∞ while E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0 ∀X.
Discrete: X∈{-1,0,1}, p(-1)=p(1)=0.9,p(0)=0.1, m0(0)=10,m0(±1)=0, τ=1 gives β<0.

Thus the non-parametric partial covariance E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[Var(D|X)τ(X)]>0, i.e. the residual D-E[D|X] is signed, but OLS uses the linear residual D- â - b̂ X, not D-p(X). Without linearity of p(X) and of m0(X) the linear residual can be correlated with the non-linear part of m0(X) and reverse sign. This is the Simpson sign reversal for a linear projection under misspecification.

The colleagues arguing for E Only Case1 and Case3 conflate D-E[D|X] with D-Proj(D|1,X) and claim β = E[Var(D|X)τ(X)]/Var(D⊥)>0. That holds for the non-parametric partial effect, not for the linear projection when p(X) is non-linear.

Hence with no parametric restriction beyond stated randomisation and τ_i>0, positivity is guaranteed only under unconditional randomisation. Case 2 fails by composition bias, Case 3 fails by linear misspecification of E[Y0|X] and p(X). Current belief remains A. Only Case 1.

15.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The individual treatment effect is τ_i = Y_i(1)-Y_i(0) >0 a.s., τ(X)=E[τ|X]>0, m0(X)=E[Y0|X], p(X)=E[D|X].

Case 1: D ⟂ (Y0,Y1). Then β1 = E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y1]-E[Y0]=E[τ]>0. Guaranteed.

Case 2: D ⟂ (Y0,Y1)|X, but D may depend on X. 
E[Y|X,D]=m0(X)+τ(X)D. Pointwise E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=τ(X)>0.
Marginally
E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[τ(X)|D=1]+E[m0(X)|D=1]-E[m0(X)|D=0].
The second term is selection bias Cov(m0(X),D)/Var(D). With p(X) decreasing in X and m0(X) increasing in X the bias can dominate. Example X∈{0,1}, p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1, m0(1)=100, τ≡1 gives E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]. So unadjusted coefficient not guaranteed positive. Agreed by all.

Case 3: regression Y on 1,D,X. Population OLS β_D = Cov(Y, D̃)/Var(D̃) with D̃=D- Proj(D|1,X). 
Write w(X)=p(X)-Proj(p|1,X). Then
Cov(Y,D̃)=E[Var(D|X)τ(X)]+E[w(X)(m0(X)+p(X)τ(X))].
First term >0. Second term =Cov(m0(X),w(X))+… is unrestricted under only D ⟂(Y0,Y1)|X.
The non-parametric residual D-E[D|X] gives Cov(Y,D-E[D|X])=E[Var(D|X)τ(X)]>0, i.e. positivity would hold for the non-parametric partial effect.
With the linear residual, w(X)≠0 whenever p(X) is non-linear in X. Then Cov(m0,w) can be made arbitrarily negative by choosing m0 non-linear and anti-correlated with w while keeping τ(X)>0.

Standard counterexamples: X∼U[-1,1], p(x)=0.5+0.4x², m0(x)=-M x², τ≡1 ⇒ β_D=1 -cM → -∞; discrete X∈{-1,0,1} or X∈{0,1,2} with p(0)=p(1)=0.9,p(2)=0.1 and m0(2) large gives β_D<0 while E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=τ>0 a.s.
Hence the linear projection can change sign by the Simpson/linear-approximation phenomenon.

The minority position E. Only Case1 and Case3 argues that after partialling out X the coefficient is a positive weighted average of τ(X)>0, essentially identifying Cov(Y,D-E[D|X])>0 and conflating D-E[D|X] with D-Proj(D|1,X). The correct objection is the linear vs conditional expectation distinction: OLS uses the linear residual, not D-p(X), so sign is not guaranteed without linearity of p(X) and of m0(X).

Current belief: with no parametric restriction beyond stated independence and τ_i>0 a.s., the strictly positive population D coefficient is guaranteed only under unconditional randomisation. Case 2 is not signed, Case 3 is not signed in general because linear control does not remove non-linear selection on m0(X). The consensus A camp in this round matches the previous reflection. The persistent disagreement is whether Case 3 should be deemed signed; the mathematics above shows the sign reversal is valid under the stated non-parametric assumptions. Unresolved is whether the problem intends the linear projection to be treated as the non-parametric partial effect, but as stated ‘regress Y on a constant, D and X’ is the linear projection, so A. Only Case 1 remains the supported answer.

Cov(Y,D⊥)=E[Var(D|X)τ(X)]+Cov(m0(X)+p(X)τ(X),w(X)).
The first term >0. The second term =Cov(m0(X),w(X))+Cov(p(X)τ(X),w(X)) is unrestricted. w(X) is orthogonal to 1,X but p(X) can be non-linear, so w≠0 and can be correlated with any non-linear function of X.

Hence βD = Cov(Y,D⊥)/Var(D⊥) can be made arbitrarily negative while keeping τ(X)>0 and D⊥Y0,Y1|X. Discrete version X∈{-1,0,1} with p(-1)=p(1)=1,p(0)=0 gives βD<0 for large m0(0). The confusion arises from replacing the linear residual D-p̂(X) with the non-parametric residual D-p(X). With the non-parametric residual Cov(Y,D-p(X))=E[Var(D|X)τ(X)]>0, but OLS uses the linear residual.

Thus the linear coefficient is sign-identified only under unconditional randomisation. The “E. Only Case1 and Case3” camp treats the linear projection as if it partials out X non-parametrically, i.e. assumes Cov(Y,D⊥)=E[Var(D|X)τ(X)]>0. That is false without linearity of m0 and p. With the stated no parametric assumptions the sign can flip in Case3.

Hence the only case where positivity must hold in population is Case1. A. Only Case1.

$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$, $E[Y|X]=m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X)$.

Case 1 $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$.  
$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$.  Unconditional randomisation makes the OLS intercept-slope the ATE and the sign is forced. Uncontroversial.

$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_{0}|D=1]-E[m_{0}|D=0]$ can dominate.  E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(1)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$.  So the marginal OLS slope can be negative.  All agree Case 2 is not signed.

$\beta_{D}=E[Y\tilde D]/E[\tilde D^{2}]$,

$E[Y\tilde D|X]=m_{0}(X)w(X)+\tau(X)E[D\tilde D|X]$,

so

$E[Y\tilde D]=E[w(X)m_{0}(X)]+E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+E[\tau(X)p(X)(1-a-bX)]$.

$E[\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\tilde D|X)]=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$, but

$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E[\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\tilde D|X)]+\operatorname{Cov}(E[Y|X],E[\tilde D|X])$

and $E[\tilde D|X]=w(X)\neq0$ when $p(X)$ is non-linear.  The term $E[w m_{0}]=\operatorname{Cov}(m_{0}(X),p(X)-a-bX)$ is unrestricted.  Hence the sign of $\beta_{D}$ is the sign of $E[w m_{0}]$ plus a positive term and can be made arbitrarily negative.

Without linearity of $p(X)$ and $m_{0}(X)$ the sign is not identified.

Thus with no parametric restriction beyond the stated randomisation, positivity of the population OLS $D$ coefficient is guaranteed only under unconditional randomisation. Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but $D\not\perp X$. 
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The selection bias $E[m_{0}|D=1]-E[m_{0}|D=0]=\operatorname{Cov}(m_{0},D)/\operatorname{Var}(D)$ can dominate the positive $\tau$ term.
E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $m_{0}(1)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$. So the unadjusted difference in means / OLS on $1,D$ is not signed.

Case 3. Population linear projection on $1,D,X$. Let $\hat p(X)=\operatorname{Proj}(D|1,X)$, $D_{\perp}=D-\hat p(X)$, $w(X)=p(X)-\hat p(X)=E[D_{\perp}|X]$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$.
$\beta_{D}= \operatorname{Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})/\operatorname{Var}(D_{\perp})$.
$E[Y D_{\perp}|X]=m_{0}(X)w(X)+\tau(X)E[D D_{\perp}|X]$ so
$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})=E[\tau(X)\operatorname{Var}(D|X)]+ \operatorname{Cov}\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),w(X)\big)$.
The first term $>0$ is the non-parametric partial covariance $E[(D-E[D|X])(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[\operatorname{Var}(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$.
The second term is $\operatorname{Cov}(m_{0},w)+\operatorname{Cov}(p\tau,w)$. With no linearity restriction $w(X)$ is the linear approximation error of the propensity $p(X)$. $w$ can be made arbitrarily negatively correlated with $m_{0}$ while keeping $\tau>0$ and $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$.

Standard counterexamples: $X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $\hat p\equiv0.5$, $w(x)=0.4x^{2}-0.4E[x^{2}]$, $m_{0}(x)=-M x^{2}$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives $\beta_{D}=1- M\, \operatorname{Cov}(x^{2},p)/\operatorname{Var}(D_{\perp})\to -\infty$ as $M\to\infty$ while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$.
Discrete version $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$ equiprobable, $p(-1)=p(1)=0.9,p(0)=0.1$, $m_{0}(0)=10,m_{0}(\pm1)=0$, $\tau=1$ gives $\beta_{D}<0$.

Hence the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$ gives a positive covariance, but the OLS residual $D-\operatorname{Proj}(D|1,X)$ retains a term $\operatorname{Cov}(m_{0},p-\operatorname{Proj}(p))$ which is unrestricted under the stated non-parametric assumptions. The sign reversal is the usual linear-projection Simpson phenomenon.

The E-camp argues $\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})=E[\operatorname{Var}(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$ because they effectively replace the linear residual by the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$. That requires linearity of $E[Y|X]$ and/or $p(X)$ in $X$, which is not permitted.

Current belief is therefore: positivity is guaranteed only under unconditional randomisation. Case 2 and Case 3 are not guaranteed without parametric linearity. That is answer A. Only Case 1. Disagreement persists with colleagues claiming Case 3 is signed; their argument conflates the non-parametric partial effect with the linear projection.

reflection_text.3:
The potential-outcome model is $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_i=Y_{1i}-Y_{0i}>0$ a.s., $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, $p(X)=E[D|X]$ and under conditional randomisation $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ so $E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$ and $E[Y|X,D]-E[Y|X,D=0]=\tau(X)>0$ pointwise.

*Case 1.* $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. Then the OLS intercept-slope projection is the difference in means
$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}]-E[Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$. Unconditional randomisation forces the sign.

*Case 2.* $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$. 
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_{0}|D=1]-E[m_{0}|D=0]=Cov(m_{0}(X),D)/Var(D)$ can dominate the positive $\tau$ term. E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $m_{0}(1)\gg m_{0}(0)$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$. Uncontrolled difference in means is not sign identified.

*Case 3.* Linear projection $Y=\alpha+\beta D+\gamma X+\varepsilon$. With $D_{\perp}=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}(D)$,
$\beta_{3}=Cov(Y,D_{\perp})/Var(D_{\perp})$.
$Cov(Y,D_{\perp}|X)=\tau(X)Var(D|X)>0$ so $E[Cov(Y,D_{\perp}|X)]>0$, but
$Cov(Y,D_{\perp})=E[Cov(Y,D_{\perp}|X)]+Cov(E[Y|X],E[D_{\perp}|X])$
$=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),\,p(X)-\hat p(X)\big)$
where $\hat p(X)$ is the linear projection of $p(X)$ on $1,X$ and $r(X)=p(X)-\hat p(X)$ is orthogonal to $1,X$ in the $L^{2}$ sense.
The term $Cov(m_{0}(X),r(X))$ is unrestricted under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ alone. With a non-linear propensity $p(\cdot)$ the linear residual $r(X)\neq0$ and can be made arbitrarily negatively correlated with $m_{0}(X)$ while keeping $\tau(X)>0$. Then $Cov(Y,D_{\perp})$ can be made negative.

Standard examples: $X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $\hat p\equiv0.5$, $m_{0}(x)=-M x^{2}$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives $\beta_{D}=1-M\,Cov(x^{2},p)/Var(D_{\perp})\to-\infty$ as $M\to\infty$; discrete $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$ with $p(\pm1)=0.9$, $p(0)=0.1$, $m_{0}(0)=M$, $m_{0}(\pm1)=0$ yields $\beta_{D}=1-10M<0$. The non-parametric partial covariance $E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$ is positive, but OLS uses the linear residual $D-\hat p(X)$, not $D-p(X)$. Hence the linear projection can suffer the usual Simpson/linear-sign-reversal.

The colleagues arguing for E/Only Case1 and Case3 conflate $D-E[D|X]$ with the linear residual $D-{\rm Proj}(D|1,X)$ and assume positivity of the Frisch-Waugh coefficient is inherited from the within-$X$ positivity. That requires linearity of $p(X)$ and $m_{0}(X)$ in $X$, which is not allowed.

Thus under the stated non-parametric assumptions positivity of the population OLS coefficient on $D$ is forced only by unconditional randomisation. Case 2 is false by selection bias, Case 3 is false by non-linear $p(X)$ and $m_{0}(X)$ interacting with the linear projection residual. Current belief: A. Only Case 1.
reflection_text.4:
The population OLS coefficient is the linear projection coefficient, not the conditional mean coefficient. Write $Y=Y_0+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., $m_0(X)=E[Y_0|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, $p(X)=E[D|X]$. Under $D\perp Y_0,Y_1|X$, $E[Y|X,D]=m_0(X)+\tau(X)D$ and $E[Y|X]=m_0(X)+p(X)\tau(X)$.

Case 1. $D\perp Y_0,Y_1$. Then $\beta_1=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_1-Y_0]=E[\tau]>0$. Unconditional randomisation makes the intercept–slope regression the ATE, sign is guaranteed.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_0,Y_1|X$ but $D\not\perp X$. $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$. The selection term $\operatorname{Cov}(m_0(X),D)$ can dominate. With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_0(X)$ increasing, e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $m_0(1)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$, $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$. The uncontrolled difference in means is not sign identified.

Case 3. Linear projection on $1,D,X$. Let $\hat D=\operatorname{Proj}(D|1,X)$, $D_\perp=D-\hat D$, $w(X)=p(X)-\hat p(X)$ with $E[w]=E[wX]=0$. Then $\beta_D=\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D_\perp)/\operatorname{Var}(D_\perp)$ and

$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D_\perp)=E[\tau(X)\operatorname{Var}(D|X)]+E[w(X)\{m_0(X)+p(X)\tau(X)\}]$.

The first term $>0$, but $E[w(X)m_0(X)]$ is the covariance of $m_0(X)$ with the linear residual of the propensity. With a non-linear $p(X)$ $w(X)\neq0$ and can be made arbitrarily negatively correlated with $m_0(X)$ while keeping $\tau(X)>0$ and $D\perp Y_0,Y_1|X$. E.g. $X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^2$, $m_0(x)=-M x^2$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives $\beta_D=1-M\,{\rm Cov}(x^2,p)/\operatorname{Var}(D_\perp)\to-\infty$ as $M\to\infty$, while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for all $X$. Discrete examples $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$ with $p(-1)=p(1)=1,p(0)=0$, $m_0(0)=10$, $\tau=1$ give $\beta_D=-9<0$.

The non-parametric partial covariance $E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[\tau(X)\operatorname{Var}(D|X)]>0$ would be positive, i.e. controlling for $X$ non-parametrically preserves sign. The OLS residual is $D-\hat p(X)$, not $D-p(X)$. The confusion in the E camp is the replacement of the linear residual by the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$. Without a linearity restriction on $m_0(X)$ and $p(X)$ the linear projection on $1,D,X$ does not inherit pointwise positivity.

Hence positivity is guaranteed only under unconditional randomisation. Case 2 and Case 3 can be negative despite $\tau_i>0$ a.s. and $D\perp Y_0,Y_1|X$. Current belief: A. Only Case 1. The split in the room is between those using $D-E[D|X]$ and those using $D-\operatorname{Proj}(D|1,X)$.

reflection_text.16:
The individual effect is $Y_{1}(i)-Y_{0}(i)>0$ a.s.  Write $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, $p(X)=E[D|X]$.  Under $D\perp Y_{0},\tau|X$,

$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$, $E[Y|X]=m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X)$.

Case 1 $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$.  
$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$.  Unconditional randomisation makes the OLS intercept-slope the ATE and the sign is forced. Uncontroversial.

Case 2 $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but $X$ uncontrolled.  
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_{0}|D=1]-E[m_{0}|D=0]$ can dominate.  E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(1)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$.  So the marginal OLS slope can be negative.  All agree Case 2 is not signed.

$\beta_{D}=E[Y\tilde D]/E[\tilde D^{2}]$,

$E[Y\tilde D|X]=m_{0}(X)w(X)+\tau(X)E[D\tilde D|X]$,

so

$E[Y\tilde D]=E[w(X)m_{0}(X)]+E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+E[\tau(X)p(X)(1-a-bX)]$.

$E[\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\tilde D|X)]=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$, but

$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E[\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\tilde D|X)]+\operatorname{Cov}(E[Y|X],E[\tilde D|X])$

and $E[\tilde D|X]=w(X)\neq0$ when $p(X)$ is non-linear.  The term $E[w m_{0}]=\operatorname{Cov}(m_{0}(X),p(X)-a-bX)$ is unrestricted.  Hence the sign of $\beta_{D}$ is the sign of $E[w m_{0}]$ plus a positive term and can be made arbitrarily negative.

The latter retains $E[w m_{0}]$ and can be negatively correlated with a non-linear $m_{0}(X)$.  Claims that Case 3 must be positive conflate the conditional mean monotonicity $E[Y|D=1,X]>E[Y|D=0,X]$ with the linear projection coefficient. Without linearity of $p(X)$ and $m_{0}(X)$ the sign is not identified.

Thus with no parametric restriction beyond the stated randomisation, positivity of the population OLS $D$ coefficient is guaranteed only under unconditional randomisation.  Case 1 is guaranteed, Cases 2 and 3 are not.  The correct answer is A. Only Case 1.  The disagreement in the round is precisely the linear-projection vs conditional-mean distinction for Case 3; the sign-reversal examples show the linear-projection argument is false without a linearity assumption.

$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$ and $E[Y|X]=m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X)$. Hence $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ pointwise.

$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The selection bias $E[m_{0}|D=1]-E[m_{0}|D=0]=\operatorname{Cov}(m_{0},D)/\operatorname{Var}(D)$ can dominate the positive $\tau$ term.

$\beta_{D}= \operatorname{Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})/\operatorname{Var}(D_{\perp})$.
$E[Y D_{\perp}|X]=m_{0}(X)w(X)+\tau(X)E[D D_{\perp}|X]$ so
$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})=E[\tau(X)\operatorname{Var}(D|X)]+ \operatorname{Cov}\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),w(X)\big)$.
The first term $>0$ is the non-parametric partial covariance $E[(D-E[D|X])(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[\operatorname{Var}(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$.
The second term is $\operatorname{Cov}(m_{0},w)+\operatorname{Cov}(p\tau,w)$. With no linearity restriction $w(X)$ is the linear approximation error of the propensity $p(X)$. $w$ can be made arbitrarily negatively correlated with $m_{0}$ while keeping $\tau>0$ and $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$.

The sign reversal is the usual linear-projection Simpson phenomenon.
