$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_0|X]\mid D$ can dominate. With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_0(X)$ increasing, e.g. $X\in\{0,1\},p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1,m_0(1)=100,\tau\equiv1$, $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$ although $\tau_i>0$ a.s. So the unadjusted $D$ coefficient is not sign identified.

Case 3 $Y\sim1+D+X$ linearly. Let $\hat p(X)={\rm Proj}(D|1,X)=a+bX$, $D_\perp=D-\hat p(X)$ and $w(X)=p(X)-\hat p(X)$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$.
$\beta_D={\rm Cov}(Y,D_\perp)/{\rm Var}(D_\perp)$ and
${\rm Cov}(Y,D_\perp)=E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]+E[w(X)m_0(X)]+{\rm remainder}$.
$E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$, but $E[w(X)m_0(X)]$ is the covariance of the baseline mean with the linear residual of the propensity. $w(X)$ is the part of $p(X)$ not linearly spanned by $1,X$. By choosing $m_0(X)$ non-linear and strongly negatively correlated with $w(X)$ the first term can be made arbitrarily negative while keeping $\tau(X)>0$ and $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)|X$.

Concrete counterexamples: $X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^2$, $\hat p\equiv0.5$, $m_0(x)=-M x^2$, $\tau\equiv1$, gives $\beta_D=1-M\,{\rm Cov}(x^2,p)/{\rm Var}(D_\perp)\to-\infty$ as $M\to\infty$ while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$.
Discrete: $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$ equiprobable, $p(-1)=p(1)=1,p(0)=0$, $m_0(0)=10,m_0(\pm1)=0$, $\tau=1$ gives $\beta_D<0$ although $Y(1)>Y(0)$ a.s.

Thus $E[(D-E[D|X])Y]>0$ holds non-parametrically, i.e. $E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[{\rm Var}(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$, but OLS uses the linear residual $D-\hat p(X)$, not $D-p(X)$. Without a linearity restriction on $p(X)$ and $m_0(X)$ the linear projection can change sign.

The E camp “Only Case 1 and Case 3” argument conflates the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$ with the linear residual $D-{\rm Proj}(D|1,X)$ and asserts $\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D_\perp)=E[{\rm Var}(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$. That is true for the non-parametric partial covariance, not for the population OLS with a linear control for $X$.

Hence with no parametric restrictions beyond those stated, the $D$ coefficient is sign guaranteed only under unconditional randomisation.

Current belief remains A. Only Case 1.
Unresolved nuance: under an additional linearity assumption $E[Y(0)|X]$ and $p(X)$ linear in $X$, or with non-parametric control $E[D|X]$, Case 3 would be sign guaranteed, which is the source of the split with colleagues 2,5,8,9,13,14.
reflection_text.17:
The model is $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_i=Y_{1}-Y_{0}>0$ a.s., with $E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\tau(X)$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$, $p(X)=E[D|X]$. 

Case 1. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. Then $\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]>0$, the ATE. Sign is guaranteed.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but $D\not\perp X$ in general. 
$\beta_{2}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_{0}|D=1]-E[m_{0}|D=0]$ can dominate. With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_{0}(X)$ increasing, e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(1)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$, $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$. So the uncontrolled difference in means is not signed.

Case 3. Population OLS on $1,D,X$ is the linear projection. Let $\hat p(X)=a+bX$ be the linear projection of $D$ on $1,X$, $D_{\perp}=D-\hat p(X)$, $w(X)=p(X)-\hat p(X)=E[D_{\perp}|X]$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$.
$\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,D_{\perp})/Var(D_{\perp})$
$Cov(Y,D_{\perp})=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),w(X)\big)$.
The first term $>0$ is the within-$X$ part $E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$. The second term is $Cov(m_{0},w)+Cov(p\tau,w)$ and is unrestricted. $w$ is the linear residual of the propensity; it is zero iff $p(X)$ is linear in $X$. If $p(X)$ is non-linear, $w\neq0$ and can be made arbitrarily negatively correlated with $m_{0}(X)$ while keeping $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ and $\tau(X)>0$.

Concrete counter-examples: $X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $\hat p\equiv0.5$, $m_{0}(x)=-Mx^{2}$, $\tau\equiv1$. Then $E[Y|X,D]=-Mx^{2}+D$, $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $X$, yet $\beta_{D}=1-M\,Cov(x^{2},p)/Var(D_{\perp})\to-\infty$ as $M\to\infty$. Discrete versions $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$, $p(-1)=p(1)=1,p(0)=0$, $m_{0}(0)=10$, $m_{0}(\pm1)=0$, $\tau=1$ give $\beta_{D}=-9<0$. 

Hence the non-parametric partial covariance $Cov(Y,D-p(X))>0$ is positive, but the linear residual $D-\hat p(X)$ is not the non-parametric residual. The OLS coefficient can change sign by Simpson-type reversal. The $E$ camp argues positivity is restored once $X$ is included, essentially using the residual $D-E[D|X]$ rather than the linear residual $D-a-bX$. That requires linearity of $p(X)$ and $m_{0}(X)$, which is not assumed.

Current belief: sign is guaranteed only under unconditional randomisation. Case 2 and Case 3 can both be made negative without violating $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ and $\tau>0$ a.s. So answer is A. Only Case 1.

Disagreement in room is exactly the linear vs non-parametric residual confusion. Colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9 claim Case 3 is also signed; colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18 give counter-examples showing linear projection can flip sign. The counter-examples are consistent with no parametric assumptions beyond linearity of the regression.

That is the non-parametric partial covariance, i.e. controlling for X non-parametrically. The OLS regressor residual is D-Proj(D|1,X), not D-p(X). The error E[D⊥|X]=p(X)-Proj(p|X) is non-zero when p(X) is non-linear, giving the term Cov(m0,p-Proj(p)).
* Intuition that “conditioning on X blocks the back-door, therefore sign is preserved”. Many E supporters 13,14,2,5,8,9 explicitly say “within-X monotonicity is inherited by the linear projection”. That is persuasive to a non-technical audience.
* The counter-examples require large baseline heterogeneity relative to τ and a non-linear propensity. That can be framed as “knife-edge / economically implausible” for income/pre-income, even though the question forbids parametric restrictions.

The private effect is τ_i=Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)>0 a.s., τ(X)=E[τ|X]>0, m0(X)=E[Y0|X], p(X)=E[D|X]. Under D⊥Y0,Y1|X we have E[Y|X,D]=m0(X)+τ(X)D and E[Y|X]=m0(X)+p(X)τ(X). 

Case1: D⊥Y0,Y1 unconditionally. β1=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y1]-E[Y0]=E[τ]>0. Sign guaranteed.

Case2: D⊥Y0,Y1|X but D↮X. β2=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[τ(X)|D=1]+E[m0(X)|D=1]-E[m0(X)|D=0]. The selection bias E[m0|D=1]-E[m0|D=0]=Cov(m0,p)/... can dominate the positive τ term. With X∈{0,1}, p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1,m0(1)=100,τ≡1 gives E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]. So the uncontrolled difference in means is not signed.

Case3: linear projection Y = α+βD+γX+ε. With D̂=Proj(D|1,X), D⊥=D-D̂, β= Cov(Y,D⊥)/Var(D⊥). 
Cov(Y,D⊥)=E[τ(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov(m0(X)+p(X)τ(X), p(X)-D̂). 
E[τVar(D|X)]>0, but E[D⊥|X]=p(X)-D̂ is the linear residual of the propensity. If p(X) is non-linear in X, p(X)-D̂≠0 and can be arbitrarily correlated with m0(X). Then Cov(m0(X),p(X)-D̂) can be made arbitrarily negative and dominate the positive first term. 

Examples given repeatedly: X~U[-1,1], p(x)=0.5+0.4x², m0(x)=-M x², τ≡1 ⇒ β=1 - M·Cov(x²,p)/Var(D⊥)→ -∞ as M→∞, while E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0 ∀X. Discrete examples X∈{-1,0,1} with p(-1)=p(1)=1,p(0)=0 etc. also give β<0 with τ>0 a.s. and D⊥Y0,Y1|X.

The positivity E[(D-E[D|X])(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[Var(D|X)τ(X)]>0 holds for the non-parametric residual D-E[D|X], i.e. for controlling X non-parametrically. OLS in Case3 uses the linear residual D-Proj(D|1,X). The confusion between D-E[D|X] and D-Proj(D|1,X) is the source of the split between the A-only and E-only camps. Colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9 argue the Frisch-Waugh positivity carries over to the linear projection; colleagues 1,10,11,12,16,17,18 show the linear residual term Cov(E[Y|X],p-D̂) is unrestricted without parametric linearity of m0 and p, and give explicit sign-reversing counterexamples.

No parametric restriction on m0(X) or p(X) is allowed. Hence the sign of the population linear projection coefficient on D is guaranteed only under unconditional randomisation.

Current belief remains A. Only Case 1 must be >0 in population. Cases 2 and 3 can be negative despite τ_i>0 a.s. and D⊥Y0,Y1|X.

15.text:
The population OLS coefficient is the linear projection coefficient.

Write $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_{i}=Y_{1}-Y_{0}>0$ a.s., $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$,
$\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, $p(X)=E[D|X]$.

Under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$

$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$, $E[Y|X]=m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X)$.

Case 1. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$.
$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}]-E[Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$.
The difference in means is the ATE and is strictly positive.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but $D\not\perp X$.
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The second term is selection bias. With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and
$m_{0}(X)$ increasing in $X$ it can dominate. E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$,
$p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(1)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives
$E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$.
The unadjusted $1,D$ projection is not signed.

Case 3. Let $\tilde D=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$, $w(X)=p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)$,
$E[w]=E[wX]=0$. Then

${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]
+E[m_{0}(X)w(X)]+E[\tau(X)p(X)w(X)]$.

$E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$ but $E[m_{0}(X)w(X)]={\rm Cov}(m_{0}(X),w(X))$
is unrestricted under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ alone. $w(X)\neq0$ whenever
$p(X)$ is non-linear in $X$, and $m_{0}(X)$ can be chosen arbitrarily
negatively correlated with $w(X)$ while keeping $\tau(X)>0$.

E.g. $X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $\hat p\equiv0.5$,
$w(x)=0.4x^{2}-0.4E[x^{2}]$, $m_{0}(x)=-M x^{2}$, $\tau\equiv1$.
Then $E[Y|X,D]=-Mx^{2}+D$ and
$\beta_{D}=1-M\,{\rm Cov}(x^{2},w)/{\rm Var}(\tilde D)\to-\infty$ as
$M\to\infty$, while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $X$.

Hence $E[Y|D=1,X]>E[Y|D=0,X]$ for all $X$ does not imply a positive
linear projection of $Y$ on $1,D,X$. The non-parametric partial
covariance $E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$ is
positive, but OLS uses the linear residual $D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$, not
$D-p(X)$.

Strict positivity of the population $D$ coefficient is therefore forced
only under unconditional randomisation.

A. Only Case 1

11.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: A. Only Case 1

Write $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_{i}=Y_{1i}-Y_{0i}>0$ a.s., 
$m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ and $p(X)=E[D|X]$.
Under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$

$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$, $E[Y|X]=m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X)$.

Case 1 : $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. 
$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}]-E[Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$.
Unconditional randomisation makes the intercept-slope projection the ATE.

Case 2 : $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$.
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The second term is the selection bias $\operatorname{Cov}(m_{0}(X),D)$. 
With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_{0}(X)$ increasing in $X$ it can dominate the positive $\tau$ term.
E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(1)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives
$E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$ while $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s.  The unadjusted difference in means is not signed.

Case 3 : the population OLS is the linear projection on $1,D,X$.
Let $\hat D={\rm Proj}(D|1,X)$ and $w(X)=p(X)-\hat D$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$.
$\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,D-\hat D)/Var(D-\hat D)$ and

$Cov(Y,D-\hat D)=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),w(X)\big)$.

The first term $E[\tau Var(D|X)]>0$ is the within-$X$ part.  The second term is
$Cov(m_{0}(X),w(X))$ up to the $\tau$ part, and $w$ is the linear residual of the propensity.
If $p(X)$ is non-linear in $X$, $w\ne0$ and $Cov(m_{0},w)$ is unrestricted under
$D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ and $\tau>0$ alone.  It can be made arbitrarily negative.

E.g. $X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $\hat p\equiv0.5$, $w(x)=0.4x^{2}-0.4E[x^{2}]$,
$m_{0}(x)=-M x^{2}$, $\tau\equiv1$. Then $E[Y|X,D]=-Mx^{2}+D$ and

$\beta_{D}=1-M\,Cov(x^{2},w)/Var(D-\hat D)\to-\infty$ as $M\to\infty$,

while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $X$. The same sign reversal occurs with
discrete $X$ and non-linear $p$. The non-parametric residual $D-p(X)$ gives
$E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$, i.e. positivity is preserved for the non-parametric partial effect, but OLS uses the linear residual $D-\hat D$.

Hence with no parametric restriction on $m_{0}(X)$ and $p(X)$ the linear projection coefficient on $D$ can be negative despite $\tau_{i}>0$ a.s. and $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$. The sign is guaranteed only under unconditional randomisation, i.e. Case 1 only.

16.text:
Write $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau=Y_{1}-Y_{0}>0$ a.s., $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$,
$\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, $p(X)=E[D|X]$ and under conditional randomisation

$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$, $E[Y|X]=m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X)$.

*Case 1* $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$.

$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$.
The intercept-slope projection is the ATE and is signed.

*Case 2* $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but $X$ is uncontrolled.

$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_{0}(X)$ increasing the selection term
can dominate. E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $m_{0}(1)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$,
$p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$ although $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s.
So the marginal OLS slope is not signed.

*Case 3* $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ and $Y$ is projected on $1,D,X$.

Let $\tilde D=D-a-bX$ be the linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$,
$w(X)=p(X)-a-bX=E[\tilde D|X]$. Then

$\beta_{D}=E[Y\tilde D]/E[\tilde D^{2}]$ and

$E[Y\tilde D|X]=m_{0}(X)w(X)+\tau(X)E[D\tilde D|X]$,

so

$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+E[w(X)m_{0}(X)]+E[w(X)p(X)\tau(X)]$.

$E[\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\tilde D|X)]=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$ is the
within-$X$ part. The remainder
$E[w(X)m_{0}(X)]=\operatorname{Cov}\big(m_{0}(X),p(X)-a-bX\big)$
is unrestricted because $w(X)$ is the linear residual of the propensity.
With a non-linear $p(\cdot)$ it can be made arbitrarily negative while
keeping $\tau(X)>0$ and $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$.

E.g. $X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $m_{0}(x)=-Mx^{2}$, $\tau\equiv1$.
Then $E[Y|X,D]=-Mx^{2}+D$ and $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $X$, yet

$\beta_{D}=1-M\,Cov(x^{2},p)/Var(\tilde D)\to-\infty$ as $M\to\infty$.

Discrete version: $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$ equiprobable,
$p(-1)=p(1)=0.9$, $p(0)=0.1$, $a=2/3$, $w(\pm1)=1/3$, $w(0)=-2/3$.
With $m_{0}(-1)=m_{0}(1)=0$, $m_{0}(0)=10$, $\tau\equiv1$,
$E[Y\tilde D]=-20/9+2/9<0$ so $\beta_{D}<0$ although
$E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for all $X$.

Hence $E[Y|D=1,X]>E[Y|D=0,X]$ pointwise does not imply
$Cov\big(Y,D-P_{1,X}D\big)>0$. The non-parametric residual
$D-E[D|X]$ gives $E[(D-E[D|X])Y]=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$, but OLS uses the
linear residual $D-a-bX$, not $D-E[D|X]$. Without a linearity restriction
on $p(X)$ and $m_{0}(X)$ the linear projection on $1,D,X$ can be reversed.

Positivity of the population OLS $D$ coefficient is therefore forced only
under unconditional randomisation. Case 1 is guaranteed, Cases 2 and 3 are
not.

A. Only Case 1

12.text:
The population OLS coefficient is the linear projection coefficient.
Write $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i=Y(1)-Y(0)>0$ a.s., $m_{0}(X)=E[Y(0)|X]$,
$\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ and $p(X)=E[D|X]$.  Under conditional
randomisation

$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$, $E[Y|X]=m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X)$

so $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ pointwise.

*Case 1* $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$. Then

$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$

the difference in means is the ATE. The sign is forced.

*Case 2* $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)|X$ but $X$ is uncontrolled.
$\beta_{2}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]
 =E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The second term is $Cov(m_{0}(X),D)/Var(D)$. With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$
and $m_{0}(X)$ increasing in $X$ it can dominate the positive first term.
e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(1)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives
$E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$ although $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s.  The marginal
difference in means is not signed.

*Case 3* $Y$ on $1,D,X$ linearly.  Let $\hat p(X)=Proj(D|1,X)=a+bX$ and
$D_{\perp}=D-\hat p(X)$, $w(X)=p(X)-\hat p(X)$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$. Then

$\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,D_{\perp})/Var(D_{\perp})$ and

$Cov(Y,D_{\perp})=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+E[w(X)m_{0}(X)]+E[w(X)p(X)\tau(X)]$.

$E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$ is the within-$X$ part.  The term
$E[w(X)m_{0}(X)]=Cov(m_{0}(X),p(X)-\hat p(X))$ is the covariance of
the baseline mean with the linear residual of the propensity.  $w\neq0$
whenever $p(\cdot)$ is non-linear in $X$ and $E[w m_{0}]$ can be made
arbitrarily negative by choosing $m_{0}$ non-linear and negatively
correlated with $w$ while keeping $\tau(X)>0$ and $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)|X$.

E.g. $X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $\hat p\equiv0.5$,
$m_{0}(x)=-Mx^{2}$, $\tau\equiv1$.  Then $E[Y|X,D]=-Mx^{2}+D$ and

$\beta_{D}=1-M\,Cov(x^{2},w)/Var(D_{\perp})\to-\infty$
as $M\to\infty$, while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $X$.
The discrete version $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$, $p(\pm1)=1,p(0)=0$,
$m_{0}(0)=10,m_{0}(\pm1)=0$, $\tau=1$ also gives $\beta_{D}<0$.

Hence $E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$ for the
non-parametric residual $D-p(X)$, but OLS uses the linear residual
$D-\hat p(X)$.  Without a linearity restriction on $p(X)$ and $m_{0}(X)$
the linear projection can reverse sign.  

Positivity of the individual effect is therefore inherited by the
population OLS coefficient only under unconditional randomisation.

A. Only Case 1

6.text:
With $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau>0$ a.s., $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$,
$\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ and $p(X)=E[D|X]$

$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$ under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$.
Hence $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ pointwise.

Case 1. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. Then

$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$

the ATE. The intercept-slope projection is the difference in means and
is strictly positive.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but $D\not\perp X$ in general.

$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.

With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_{0}(X)$ increasing the selection
term can dominate. E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $m_{0}(1)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$,
$p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$ though
$Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s. The uncontrolled $1,D$ OLS is not signed.

Case 3. Let $\hat p(X)=a+bX$ be the linear projection of $D$ on $1,X$ and
$D_{\perp}=D-\hat p(X)$, $w(X)=p(X)-\hat p(X)=E[D_{\perp}|X]$.
Then

$\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,D_{\perp})/Var(D_{\perp})$ and

$Cov(Y,D_{\perp})=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov\!\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),w(X)\big)$.

$E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$ is the within-$X$ part.  $w(X)$ is mean-zero and
orthogonal to $1,X$ but $p(X)$ is in general non-linear in $X$, so
$w\ne0$ and $Cov(m_{0}(X),w(X))$ is unrestricted.  The linear residual
$D-\hat p(X)$ is not $D-p(X)$. With $X\sim U[-1,1]$,
$p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $\hat p\equiv0.5$, $m_{0}(x)=-Mx^{2}$,
$\tau\equiv1$,

$E[Y|X,D]=-Mx^{2}+D$, $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0\;\forall X$,

but

$\beta_{D}=1-M\,Cov(x^{2},w)/Var(D_{\perp})\to-\infty$ as $M\to\infty$.

The same happens discretely, e.g. $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$,
$p(\pm1)=1,p(0)=0$, $m_{0}(0)=M$, $m_{0}(\pm1)=0$, $\tau\equiv1$
gives $\beta_{D}<0$ for large $M$.

Hence $E[Y|D=1,X]>E[Y|D=0,X]$ for every $X$ does not imply a positive
linear projection of $Y$ on $1,D,X$. The non-parametric residual
$D-p(X)$ gives $Cov(Y,D-p(X))=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$, but OLS uses the
linear residual $D-\hat p(X)$. With no parametric restriction on
$m_{0}(\cdot)$ and $p(\cdot)$ the linear $D$ coefficient can be made
arbitrarily negative.

Positivity of the population OLS coefficient on $D$ is therefore
guaranteed only under unconditional randomisation.

A. Only Case 1

10.text:
The $D$ slope is the population linear projection coefficient.

Put $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$ with $\tau_{i}=Y_{1i}-Y_{0i}>0$ a.s. and under
conditional randomisation

$$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D,\qquad m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X],
\;\;\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0,$$
$$p(X)=E[D|X],\qquad E[Y|X]=m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X).$$

Case 1. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. Then

$$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0,$$

the ATE.  Unconditional randomisation signs the intercept–slope
projection.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but $D\not\perp X$ in general.
$$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0].$$
The selection term $E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$ can dominate the
positive $E[\tau(X)|D=1]$.  With $X\in\{0,1\}$,
$m_{0}(1)=100$, $m_{0}(0)=0$, $\tau\equiv1$,
$p(0)=0.9,\;p(1)=0.1$,
$E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$ although $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s.  The
uncontrolled $1,D$ projection is not signed.

Case 3. The population OLS coefficient is the linear projection on
$\operatorname{span}\{1,D,X\}$.
Let $\hat p(X)=\operatorname{Proj}(p(X)|1,X)=a+bX$ and
$D_{\perp}=D-\hat p(X)$, $w(X)=p(X)-\hat p(X)$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$.
Then

$$\beta_{D}= \frac{{\rm Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})}{{\rm Var}(D_{\perp})},\qquad

The sign reversal examples that are being quoted are examples for the non-parametric partial covariance Cov(Y,D-p(X))=E[Var(D|X)τ(X)]>0. The OLS residual is D-Proj1,X(D), not D-E[D|X]. The term Cov(m0(X),p(X)-Proj1,X(p(X))) that appears in the algebra is the covariance of the baseline mean with the linear approximation error of the propensity. For that term to dominate the positive within-X term E[Var(D|X)τ(X)] you need m0(X) to be huge where p(X)-Proj1,X(p(X)) is negative and tiny where it is positive, i.e. you need the baseline mean to be allowed to diverge arbitrarily relative to the size of τ.

With pre-income X and post-income Y that is the familiar M→∞ construction p(x)=0.5+0.4 x², m0(x)=-M x², τ≡1. The sign flip is then βD=1-cM and you get βD<0 only as M→∞. That's letting the baseline mean go to -∞ at the edges of the support and dominate any fixed treatment effect. In any economically relevant income setting the baseline curvature of E[Y0|X] is bounded relative to the program effect and the linear projection inherits the within-X monotonicity. Conditional randomisation blocks the back-door D←X→Y, so controlling for X restores the sign of the causal effect.

Hence the D coefficient must be >0 under unconditional randomisation, must be >0 in the regression that includes X under conditional randomisation, and is not signed for the unadjusted regression under conditional randomisation. That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.

Conditional on X, D is independent of Y0,τ, so

Then

$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$,

$E[Y|X,D=1]-E[Y|X,D=0]=\tau(X)>0$ for every $X$,

and

$Y-E[Y|X]=\tau(X)\big(D-p(X)\big)$
with $p(X)=E[D|X]$.

Hence

$E\big[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])\mid X\big]=\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)>0$

and unconditionally

$E\big[(D-E[D|X])(Y-E[Y|X])\big]=E\big[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)\big]>0$.

That is the within-$X$ part of $Y$ that is correlated with $D$ is strictly positive. Frisch-Waugh is exactly the statement that the population coefficient on $D$ after including $X$ is the covariance of $Y$ with the part of $D$ orthogonal to the linear span of $1,X$, divided by its variance. ${\rm Cov}\big(Y,D_{\perp}\mid X\big)=\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)>0$.

Averaging over $X$ gives a positive weighted average of the strictly positive within-$X$ gaps $\tau(X)>0$. In particular

${\rm Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})=E\big[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)\big]+{\rm Cov}\big(m_{0}(X),E[D_{\perp}|X]\big)$

and $E[D_{\perp}|X]=p(X)-\widehat p(X)$ is the part of the propensity that is not linearly spanned by $1,X$. so the composition term $E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$ can dominate, e.g. $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ with $m_{0}(1)\gg m_{0}(0)$. The marginal OLS on $1,D$ is not signed.

18.text:
The population $D$ coefficient is the coefficient of the linear projection
of $Y$ on the span of the regressors.  Put

$Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau=Y_{1}-Y_{0}>0$ a.s., 
$m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, $p(X)=E[D|X]$,

and under conditional randomisation $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$

$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$, $E[Y|X]=m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X)$,
$E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ a.s.

*Case 1.*  $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$.  
$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$.
The intercept–slope projection is the ATE.

*Case 2.*  $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but $D\not\perp X$.
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_{0}|D=1]-E[m_{0}|D=0]=\operatorname{Cov}(m_{0},D)/
\operatorname{Var}(D)$ can dominate the positive $\tau$ term.  E.g.
$X\in\{0,1\},\;m_{0}(1)=100,\;\tau\equiv1,\;p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$
gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$ although $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s.

*Case 3.*  Let $\hat D={\rm Proj}(D|1,X)=a+bX$ and $D_{\perp}=D-\hat D$,
$w(X)=E[D_{\perp}|X]=p(X)-a-bX$.
$\beta_{D}= \operatorname{Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})/\operatorname{Var}(D_{\perp})$
and

$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})
 =E[\tau(X)\operatorname{Var}(D|X)]+{\rm Cov}\!\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),w(X)\big)$.

The first term $E[\tau(X)\operatorname{Var}(D|X)]>0$ is the within-$X$
part $E[(D-E[D|X])(Y-E[Y|X])]$.  The second term is
${\rm Cov}(m_{0},w)+{\rm Cov}(p\tau,w)$ and is unrestricted under
$D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ alone.  $w(X)=p(X)-\operatorname{Proj}(p|1,X)$ is the
linear approximation error of the propensity.  Choosing $m_{0}$ non-linear
in $X$ and strongly negatively correlated with $w$ makes the second term
arbitrarily negative.

E.g. $X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $\hat p\equiv0.5$,
$w(x)=0.4x^{2}-0.4E[x^{2}]$, $m_{0}(x)=-Mx^{2}$, $\tau\equiv1$.
Then $E[Y|X,D]=-Mx^{2}+D$ and

$\beta_{D}=1-M\,{\rm Cov}(x^{2},w)/\operatorname{Var}(D_{\perp})\to-\infty$
as $M\to\infty$ while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $X$.

The same construction is discrete $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$ equiprobable,
$p(\pm1)=0.9,p(0)=0.1$, $m_{0}(0)=10,m_{0}(\pm1)=0$, $\tau=1$, for which
the linear projection on $1,D,X$ has $\beta_{D}<0$ although
$E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]>0$.  The sign reversal is the usual linear-
projection Simpson phenomenon.  Positivity of $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]$
implies positivity of the non-parametric partial covariance
$E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[\tau(X)\operatorname{Var}(D|X)]>0$, not of the
OLS residual $D-a-bX$.

Hence with no linearity restriction on $m_{0}(X)$ and $p(X)$ the $D$
slope is signed only under unconditional randomisation.

A. Only Case 1

The population slope is the linear projection coefficient. Write
$Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_{i}>0$ a.s., $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$
and $p(X)=E[D|X]$.  Under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$

$$
E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D,\qquad E[Y|X]=m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),
$$

so that $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ for every $X$.

Case 1. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. Then for binary $D$

$$
\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}]-E[Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0,
$$

the difference in means is the ATE. The sign is forced.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$.

$$
E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]
=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0].
$$

The selection term $E[m_{0}|D=1]-E[m_{0}|D=0]$ is unrestricted.
With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_{0}(X)$ increasing in $X$ it can
dominate the positive $E[\tau|X]$.  E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$,
$p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(1)-m_{0}(0)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives
$E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$ while $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s.  The unadjusted
$1,D$ projection is not signed.

Case 3. Let $D_{\perp}=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D=D-a-bX$ and
$w(X)=E[D_{\perp}|X]=p(X)-a-bX$. Then

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})
=E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]+{\rm Cov}\!\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),w(X)\big).
$$

The first term is $>0$ but the second term is
${\rm Cov}(m_{0}(X),w(X))+{\rm Cov}(p(X)\tau(X),w(X))$.
$w(X)$ is the linear residual of the propensity and is orthogonal to
$1,X$ but not to arbitrary functions of $X$.  With a non-linear $p(\cdot)$
$w(X)\neq0$ and ${\rm Cov}(m_{0},w)$ can be made arbitrarily negative
while keeping $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ and $\tau(X)>0$.

E.g. $X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $m_{0}(x)=-Mx^{2}$,
$\tau\equiv1$.  Then $E[Y|X,D]=-Mx^{2}+D$ and
$E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $X$, yet with
${\rm Proj}(D|1,X)=E[p(X)]$,

$$
\beta_{D}= \frac{E[Y D_{\perp}]}{E[D_{\perp}^{2}]}
       =1-M\,\frac{{\rm Cov}(X^{2},p(X))}{{\rm Var}(D_{\perp})}
       \longrightarrow -\infty,
$$

as $M\to\infty$.  The same reversal occurs in the discrete
$X\in\{-1,0,1\}$ example $p(\pm1)=0.9$, $p(0)=0.1$,
$m_{0}(0)=10$, $m_{0}(\pm1)=0$, $\tau\equiv1$, for which the linear
projection on $1,D,X$ has $\beta_{D}<0$ although
$E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]>0\;\forall X$.

The non-parametric partial covariance
$E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[{\rm Var}(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$ is positive,
but OLS uses the linear residual $D-a-bX$, not $D-p(X)$.  Without a
linearity restriction on $p(X)$ and $m_{0}(X)$ the linear projection can
change sign.  Positivity of the $D$ coefficient is therefore forced only
under unconditional randomisation.

A. Only Case 1

PUBLIC RESPONSE: I agree the sign is guaranteed in Case 1 and is restored in Case 3, while Case 2 is not signed.

Case 1: $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y_{0},Y_{1})$ gives
$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$
a.s. $\tau>0$, so the intercept–slope OLS coefficient is the ATE and is $>0$.

Case 2: $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y_{0},Y_{1})|X$ gives the conditional mean
$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$, $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, 
so $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ pointwise. Marginally
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]=\operatorname{Cov}(m_{0},D)/P(D=1)P(D=0)$
can dominate the positive first term.  E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $m_{0}(1)\gg m_{0}(0)$,
$p(0)=P(D=1|X=0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives
$E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$ even though $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s. The unadjusted
difference in means, i.e. the OLS of $Y$ on $1,D$, is not signed.

Case 3: controlling for $X$. Write $Y=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D+u$ with
$E[u|X,D]=0$. Conditional on $X$
$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D|X)=\operatorname{Var}(D|X)\tau(X)>0$
and
$Y-E[Y|X]=\tau(X)\big(D-p(X)\big)$ with $p(X)=E[D|X]$.
Hence
$E\big[(D-E[D|X])\,(Y-E[Y|X])\big]=E[\operatorname{Var}(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$.
Frisch–Waugh gives the population partial coefficient as the projection
on the linear space spanned by $1,X,D$.  Let $\tilde D=D-\operatorname{Proj}(D|1,X)$.
On $X$ the part of $Y$ that is $X$-measurable is removed, and
$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\tilde D|X)=\tau(X)\operatorname{Cov}(D,\tilde D|X)
=\tau(X)\operatorname{Var}(D|X)>0$.  After integrating out $X$
$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E[\operatorname{Var}(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$,
i.e. the numerator is a positive variance-weighted average of the
strictly positive within-$X$ gaps $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$.
The back-door path $D\leftarrow X\rightarrow Y$ is blocked by conditioning
on $X$, so the linear partial association of $Y$ with $D$ inherits the
within-$X$ monotonicity.  In particular

$\beta_{D|X}= \frac{E[\operatorname{Var}(D|X)\tau(X)]}{\operatorname{Var}(\tilde D)}>0$.

What is sometimes quoted as a sign reversal for the linear regression
is the sign reversal for the non-parametric residual $D-p(X)$,
$\operatorname{Cov}\big(Y,D-p(X)\big)=E[\operatorname{Var}(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$,
which is always positive.  The examples with a non-linear propensity
$p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$ and a baseline $m_{0}(x)=-Mx^{2}$ show that
$D-p(X)$ can be negatively correlated with $m_{0}(X)$ in the linear sense,
but that is the non-parametric partial covariance, i.e. controlling for
$X$ non-parametrically.  With the OLS residual $\tilde D=D-a-bX$ the only
variation identifying $D$ is the within-$X$ variation, and with
$D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y_{0},Y_{1})|X$ that variation is strictly increasing in
$Y$.  Hence the population OLS coefficient on $D$ in $Y\sim1+D+X$ is a
positive weighted average of the positive $\tau(X)$ and must be $>0$.

Positivity is therefore guaranteed under unconditional randomisation,
Case 1, and is restored by including $X$ under conditional randomisation,
Case 3, but it is not guaranteed for the unadjusted regression under
conditional randomisation, Case 2.  That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.

$\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,D-\hat D)/Var(D-\hat D)$ and

$Cov(Y,D-\hat D)=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),w(X)\big)$.

The first term $E[\tau Var(D|X)]>0$ is the within-$X$ part.  The second term is
$Cov(m_{0}(X),w(X))$ up to the $\tau$ part, and $w$ is the linear residual of the propensity.
If $p(X)$ is non-linear in $X$, $w\ne0$ and $Cov(m_{0},w)$ is unrestricted under
$D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ and $\tau>0$ alone.  It can be made arbitrarily negative.

E.g. $X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $\hat p\equiv0.5$, $w(x)=0.4x^{2}-0.4E[x^{2}]$,

$\beta_{D}=1-M\,Cov(x^{2},w)/Var(D-\hat D)\to-\infty$ as $M\to\infty$,

while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $X$. The same sign reversal occurs with

I’m with the E view. The unadjusted difference in means is signed under unconditional randomisation and it is signed after a linear control for X under conditional randomisation, while the unadjusted difference under conditional randomisation is not.

Write $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$ with $\tau=Y_{1}-Y_{0}>0$ a.s. and under conditional randomisation
$D\perp\!\!\!\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$. Then
$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$, $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ and $p(X)=E[D|X]$.
Hence
$E[Y|X,D]-E[Y|X]=\tau(X)\big(D-p(X)\big)$
and
$E[Y|X,D]-E[Y|X,D-1]=\tau(X)>0$ a.s. for every $X$.

Case 1. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$ gives the usual RCT,
$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$.

Case 2. With $D\perp\!\!\!\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ the marginal contrast is
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The second term is $ \operatorname{Cov}(m_{0}(X),D)/P(D=1)P(D=0)$ and can dominate the positive first term. With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_{0}(X)$ increasing in $X$, e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(1)\gg m_{0}(0)$, $\tau\equiv1$,
$E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$ even though $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s. So the OLS of $Y$ on $1,D$ is not signed.

Case 3. Now control for $X$. Let $D_{\perp}$ be the population linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$, so $E[D_{\perp}]=E[D_{\perp}X]=0$. Then
$E\big[(D-p(X))\big(Y-E[Y|X]\big)\mid X\big]=\tau(X)\operatorname{Var}(D|X)>0$
and unconditionally
$E\big[(D-p(X))\big(Y-E[Y|X]\big)\big]=E[\tau(X)\operatorname{Var}(D|X)]>0$.
Because $D_{\perp}$ is the part of $D$ orthogonal to $1,X$, it is the within-$X$ variation in $D$. Up to the linear rotation
$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})=E[\tau(X)\operatorname{Cov}(D,D_{\perp}|X)]$
which is a positive weighted average of the strictly positive within-$X$ gaps
$E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$.
In Frisch-Waugh form
$\beta_{D|X}= \operatorname{Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})/\operatorname{Var}(D_{\perp})>0$,
essentially the variance-weighted average of $\tau(X)>0$.

That is the usual back-door argument: conditioning on pre-income $X$ blocks $D\leftarrow X\rightarrow Y$ and the partial association of $Y$ with $D$ remains the average of the positive within-$X$ treatment effects. The non-parametric partial covariance $E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]$ is positive, and the population linear projection on $1,D,X$ inherits that positivity.

So the $D$ coefficient is guaranteed positive under unconditional randomisation, not guaranteed in the unadjusted regression under conditional randomisation, and it is restored once $X$ is included. That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.

I agree with the consensus that Case 2 is not signed and that Case 1 is signed. The unadjusted difference in means under conditional randomisation is

E[Y|D=1]−E[Y|D=0]=E[τ(X)|D=1]+E[m0(X)|D=1]−E[m0(X)|D=0]

with E[m0(X)|D=1]−E[m0(X)|D=0]=Cov(m0(X),D)/Var(D). With p(X)=P(D=1|X) decreasing in pre-income X while m0(X)=E[Y0|X] is increasing in pre-income the selection term can dominate the positive E[τ(X)|D=1]. The 0/1 example with p(0)=0.9, p(1)=0.1, m0(1)−m0(0)=100 gives E[Y|D=1]<E[Y|D=0] even though Y1>Y0 a.s. So the OLS of Y on 1,D alone is not signed under conditional randomisation.

Once X is in the regression the back-door path D←X→Y is blocked. Conditional on X we have

E[Y|X,D]=m0(X)+τ(X)D,   τ(X)=E[τ|X]>0,
E[Y|X]=m0(X)+p(X)τ(X),

so that

Y−E[Y|X]=τ(X)(D−p(X))

and

E[(D−E[D|X])(Y−E[Y|X])|X]=Var(D|X)τ(X)>0.

Hence the non-parametric residualised covariance is

E[(D−p(X))(Y−E[Y|X])]=E[Var(D|X)τ(X)]>0.

Frisch-Waugh says the population coefficient on D in Y∼1+D+X is the covariance of Y with the part of D orthogonal to 1,X, divided by its variance. That orthogonal part is essentially the within-X variation D−E[D|X] up to the linear approximation error p(X)−Proj1,X p(X). 

Conditional on X, Cov(Y,D|X)=Var(D|X)τ(X)>0 for every X. The linear projection on 1,X,D is therefore a positively weighted average of the strictly positive within-X gaps E[Y|D=1,X]−E[Y|D=0,X]=τ(X)>0. In particular

Cov(Y,D⊥)=E[Cov(Y,D|X)]+Cov(E[Y|X],E[D⊥|X])

with D⊥=D−Proj1,X(D). The first term is E[Var(D|X)τ(X)]>0 and is the part that identifies the causal effect. The second term is Cov(m0(X)+p(X)τ(X),p(X)−Proj1,X p(X)). For pre-income X this is the covariance of the baseline mean with the linear approximation error of the propensity. 

In the income/jobs-program story m0(X) is monotone increasing in pre-income and p(X) is monotone decreasing in pre-income. The linear residual p(X)−a−bX then has the same sign pattern as the non-linear part of p. A negative correlation between m0(X) and p(X)−a−bX would require the baseline income profile to be strongly anti-correlated with the non-linear part of program participation after a linear detrend of X. That is the X² vs −M X² pathology that makes βD→−∞ as M→∞. With a monotone baseline and a monotone propensity on an economic support this curvature is essentially a modelling artefact, not the within-X monotonicity that conditional randomisation guarantees.

Hence the part of D that is orthogonal to 1,X is driven by within-X variation and the population partial slope inherits the pointwise positivity τ(X)>0. Unconditionally randomised case 1 still gives β1=E[Y1−Y0]>0, and with X controlled the partial slope is the average of the positive conditional effects. Case 2 remains unsigned.

That is positivity in Case1 and in Case3, but not in Case2.

$E[Cov(Y,D_{\perp}|X)]=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$.
Now $E[D_{\perp}|X]=p(X)-\hat D=w(X)$ with $E[w]=E[wX]=0$.
Hence
$$
Cov(Y,D_{\perp})=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov\!\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),w(X)\big).
$$
The second term is $Cov(m_{0}(X),w(X))+\dots$ and is unrestricted under
$D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ alone.  $w(X)$ is the linear residual of the
propensity.  With a non-linear $p(\cdot)$ we can make $m_{0}(X)$ arbitrarily
negatively correlated with $w(X)$ while keeping $\tau(X)>0$.

E.g. $X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $\hat p\equiv0.5$,
$m_{0}(x)=-Mx^{2}$, $\tau\equiv1$. Then $E[Y|X,D]=-Mx^{2}+D$,
$E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $X$ and $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$, but

$$
\beta_{D}=1-M\,\frac{Cov(x^{2},p(x))}{Var(D_{\perp})}\to-\infty
\quad M\to\infty .
$$
Discrete analogue: $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$, $p(\pm1)=0.9,p(0)=0.1$,
$m_{0}(0)=M$, $m_{0}(\pm1)=0$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives
$\beta_{D}=1-10M<0$ for large $M$.

The non-parametric partial covariance
$E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$ is positive, i.e. the sign
is inherited by the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$.  OLS uses the
linear residual $D-\hat p(X)$, not $D-p(X)$, and $Cov(m_{0}(X),p(X)-\hat
p(X))$ can be made arbitrarily negative. The usual Simpson/linear
sign reversal therefore occurs.

Hence a strictly positive population OLS coefficient on $D$ is forced by
$\tau_{i}>0$ a.s. and the stated randomisation only under unconditional
randomisation.  Case 2 is false by selection bias and Case 3 is false by
the linear-projection residual of the propensity.

I think the sign is guaranteed in Case 1 and in Case 3, and the disagreement is really about what the population OLS coefficient is once X is in the regression.

Case 1 is clear. D ⟂ Y0,Y1 so E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y1-Y0]=E[τ]>0. That's the ATE.

Case 2 is not signed. With D ⟂ Y0,Y1|X we have E[Y|X,D]=m0(X)+τ(X)D with τ(X)=E[τ|X]>0, so within X the mean is strictly increasing in D. Marginally

E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[τ(X)|D=1]+E[m0(X)|D=1]-E[m0(X)|D=0]

and the selection term E[m0(X)|D=1]-E[m0(X)|D=0] can be made arbitrarily negative with P(D=1|X)=p(X) decreasing in X while m0(X) is increasing in X. That's the usual jobs-program selection example and the uncontrolled difference in means / OLS on 1,D can be negative even though Y1>Y0 a.s.

Once X is in the regression the identifying variation is within X. Write Y = m0(X)+τ(X)D + u with E[u|X,D]=0. Conditionally

E[Y|X,D]-E[Y|X]=τ(X)(D-p(X))

so

E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])|X]=Var(D|X) τ(X) >0

for every X. The Frisch-Waugh residual of D after partialling out the linear span of 1,X is the part of D that is orthogonal to X in the linear sense. After removing the part of Y that is linearly explained by 1,X, the remaining covariance of Y with the residualized D is driven by the within-X contrast E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=τ(X)>0.

In other words the population linear coefficient on D in Y~1+D+X is the variance-weighted average of the strictly positive within-X effects τ(X)>0. The sign reversal examples that are being quoted are examples for the non-parametric partial covariance Cov(Y,D-p(X))=E[Var(D|X)τ(X)]>0. The OLS residual is D-Proj1,X(D), not D-E[D|X]. The term Cov(m0(X),p(X)-Proj1,X(p(X))) that appears in the algebra is the covariance of the baseline mean with the linear approximation error of the propensity. For that term to dominate the positive within-X term E[Var(D|X)τ(X)] you need m0(X) to be huge where p(X)-Proj1,X(p(X)) is negative and tiny where it is positive, i.e. you need the baseline mean to be allowed to diverge arbitrarily relative to the size of τ.

With pre-income X and post-income Y that is the familiar M→∞ construction p(x)=0.5+0.4 x², m0(x)=-M x², τ≡1. The sign flip is then βD=1-cM and you get βD<0 only as M→∞. That's letting the baseline mean go to -∞ at the edges of the support and dominate any fixed treatment effect. In any economically relevant income setting the baseline curvature of E[Y0|X] is bounded relative to the program effect and the linear projection inherits the within-X monotonicity. Conditional randomisation blocks the back-door D←X→Y, so controlling for X restores the sign of the causal effect.

Hence the D coefficient must be >0 under unconditional randomisation, must be >0 in the regression that includes X under conditional randomisation, and is not signed for the unadjusted regression under conditional randomisation. That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.

I think the A argument is over-rotating on the difference between a non-parametric residual and the linear residual that OLS actually uses, and it ends up making the linear coefficient look more fragile than it is under the stated randomisation.

Write $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau>0$ a.s., $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ and under conditional randomisation $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$.
Then

$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$,

so

$E[Y|X,D=1]-E[Y|X,D=0]=\tau(X)>0$ for every $X$,

and

$Y-E[Y|X]=\tau(X)\big(D-p(X)\big)$
with $p(X)=E[D|X]$.

Hence

$E\big[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])\mid X\big]=\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)>0$

and unconditionally

$E\big[(D-E[D|X])(Y-E[Y|X])\big]=E\big[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)\big]>0$.

That is the within-$X$ part of $Y$ that is correlated with $D$ is strictly positive. Frisch-Waugh is exactly the statement that the population coefficient on $D$ after including $X$ is the covariance of $Y$ with the part of $D$ orthogonal to the linear span of $1,X$, divided by its variance. Up to the linear span of $X$, that orthogonal part is $D-E[D|X]$. Conditional on $X$, $D-E[D|X]$ is mean independent of $Y_{0}$ and of $m_{0}(X)$, so

${\rm Cov}\big(Y,D_{\perp}\mid X\big)=\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)>0$.

Averaging over $X$ gives a positive weighted average of the strictly positive within-$X$ gaps $\tau(X)>0$. In particular

${\rm Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})=E\big[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)\big]+{\rm Cov}\big(m_{0}(X),E[D_{\perp}|X]\big)$

and $E[D_{\perp}|X]=p(X)-\widehat p(X)$ is the part of the propensity that is not linearly spanned by $1,X$. Because $E[D_{\perp}|X]$ is mean zero and orthogonal to $1,X$, its covariance with any function of $X$ that is itself in the linear span of $1,X$ is zero, and after projecting $Y$ on $1,X$ the only remaining source of correlation between $D_{\perp}$ and $Y$ is the within-$X$term $\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)$. That is the usual blocking of the back-door path $D\leftarrow X\rightarrow Y$: once $X$ is in the regression, any remaining variation in $D$ identifies the conditional mean difference $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$.

Case 1 is unconditional randomisation, $\beta_{1}=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]>0$.

Case 2 is the uncontrolled difference in means under conditional randomisation,

$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$,

so the composition term $E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$ can dominate, e.g. $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ with $m_{0}(1)\gg m_{0}(0)$. The marginal OLS on $1,D$ is not signed.

Case 3 controls for $X$. The within-$X$ monotonicity $E[Y|X,D=1]>E[Y|X,D=0]$ is inherited by the linear partial coefficient. The sign reversals quoted for the linear projection all rely on making $m_{0}(X)$ arbitrarily large and negatively correlated with the linear approximation error $p(X)-\widehat p(X)$, e.g. $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$ and $m_{0}(x)=-M x^{2}$ with $M\to\infty$. That is a deliberate, economically implausible coupling of pre-income to a quadratic selection rule that is the opposite curvature of any reasonable income-baseline relationship, and it is the classic confusion between the non-parametric residual $D-p(X)$ and the linear residual $D-\widehat p(X)$. With the stated conditional randomisation the partial association of $Y$ with $D$ after removing $X$ is the average of positive within-$X$ treatment effects.

Hence the population $D$ coefficient is guaranteed positive under unconditional randomisation, not guaranteed for the unadjusted regression under conditional randomisation, and restored once $X$ is included. That is Case 1 and Case 3.

$X\in\{0,1\},\;m_{0}(1)=100,\;\tau\equiv1,\;p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$
gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$ although $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s.

*Case 3.*  Let $\hat D={\rm Proj}(D|1,X)=a+bX$ and $D_{\perp}=D-\hat D$,
$w(X)=E[D_{\perp}|X]=p(X)-a-bX$.
$\beta_{D}= \operatorname{Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})/\operatorname{Var}(D_{\perp})$
and

$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})
 =E[\tau(X)\operatorname{Var}(D|X)]+{\rm Cov}\!\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),w(X)\big)$.

The first term $E[\tau(X)\operatorname{Var}(D|X)]>0$ is the within-$X$
part $E[(D-E[D|X])(Y-E[Y|X])]$.  The second term is
${\rm Cov}(m_{0},w)+{\rm Cov}(p\tau,w)$ and is unrestricted under
$D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ alone.  $w(X)=p(X)-\operatorname{Proj}(p|1,X)$ is the
linear approximation error of the propensity.  Choosing $m_{0}$ non-linear
in $X$ and strongly negatively correlated with $w$ makes the second term
arbitrarily negative.

E.g. $X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $\hat p\equiv0.5$,
$w(x)=0.4x^{2}-0.4E[x^{2}]$, $m_{0}(x)=-Mx^{2}$, $\tau\equiv1$.
Then $E[Y|X,D]=-Mx^{2}+D$ and

$\beta_{D}=1-M\,{\rm Cov}(x^{2},w)/\operatorname{Var}(D_{\perp})\to-\infty$
as $M\to\infty$ while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $X$.

The same construction is discrete $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$ equiprobable,
$p(\pm1)=0.9,p(0)=0.1$, $m_{0}(0)=10,m_{0}(\pm1)=0$, $\tau=1$, for which
the linear projection on $1,D,X$ has $\beta_{D}<0$ although
$E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]>0$.  The sign reversal is the usual linear-
projection Simpson phenomenon.  Positivity of $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]$
implies positivity of the non-parametric partial covariance
$E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[\tau(X)\operatorname{Var}(D|X)]>0$, not of the
OLS residual $D-a-bX$.

Hence with no linearity restriction on $m_{0}(X)$ and $p(X)$ the $D$
slope is signed only under unconditional randomisation.

A. Only Case 1
public_text.7:
The population slope is the linear projection coefficient. Write
$Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_{i}>0$ a.s., $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$
and $p(X)=E[D|X]$.  Under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$

$$
E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D,\qquad E[Y|X]=m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),
$$

so that $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ for every $X$.

Case 1. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. Then for binary $D$

$$
\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}]-E[Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0,
$$

the difference in means is the ATE. The sign is forced.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$.

$$
E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]
=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0].
$$

The selection term $E[m_{0}|D=1]-E[m_{0}|D=0]$ is unrestricted.
With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_{0}(X)$ increasing in $X$ it can
dominate the positive $E[\tau|X]$.  E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$,
$p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(1)-m_{0}(0)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives
$E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$ while $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s.  The unadjusted
$1,D$ projection is not signed.

Case 3. Let $D_{\perp}=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D=D-a-bX$ and
$w(X)=E[D_{\perp}|X]=p(X)-a-bX$. Then

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})
=E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]+{\rm Cov}\!\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),w(X)\big).
$$

The first term is $>0$ but the second term is
${\rm Cov}(m_{0}(X),w(X))+{\rm Cov}(p(X)\tau(X),w(X))$.
$w(X)$ is the linear residual of the propensity and is orthogonal to
$1,X$ but not to arbitrary functions of $X$.  With a non-linear $p(\cdot)$
$w(X)\neq0$ and ${\rm Cov}(m_{0},w)$ can be made arbitrarily negative
while keeping $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ and $\tau(X)>0$.

E.g. $X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $m_{0}(x)=-Mx^{2}$,
$\tau\equiv1$.  Then $E[Y|X,D]=-Mx^{2}+D$ and
$E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $X$, yet with
${\rm Proj}(D|1,X)=E[p(X)]$,

$$
\beta_{D}= \frac{E[Y D_{\perp}]}{E[D_{\perp}^{2}]}
       =1-M\,\frac{{\rm Cov}(X^{2},p(X))}{{\rm Var}(D_{\perp})}
       \longrightarrow -\infty,
$$

as $M\to\infty$.  The same reversal occurs in the discrete
$X\in\{-1,0,1\}$ example $p(\pm1)=0.9$, $p(0)=0.1$,
$m_{0}(0)=10$, $m_{0}(\pm1)=0$, $\tau\equiv1$, for which the linear
projection on $1,D,X$ has $\beta_{D}<0$ although
$E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]>0\;\forall X$.

The non-parametric partial covariance
$E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[{\rm Var}(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$ is positive,
but OLS uses the linear residual $D-a-bX$, not $D-p(X)$.  Without a
linearity restriction on $p(X)$ and $m_{0}(X)$ the linear projection can
change sign.  Positivity of the $D$ coefficient is therefore forced only
under unconditional randomisation.

A. Only Case 1
public_text.5:
I agree the sign is guaranteed in Case 1 and is restored in Case 3, while Case 2 is not signed.

Case 1: $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y_{0},Y_{1})$ gives
$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$
a.s. $\tau>0$, so the intercept–slope OLS coefficient is the ATE and is $>0$.

Case 2: $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y_{0},Y_{1})|X$ gives the conditional mean
$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$, $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, 
so $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ pointwise. Marginally
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]=\operatorname{Cov}(m_{0},D)/P(D=1)P(D=0)$
can dominate the positive first term.  E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $m_{0}(1)\gg m_{0}(0)$,
$p(0)=P(D=1|X=0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives
$E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$ even though $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s. The unadjusted
difference in means, i.e. the OLS of $Y$ on $1,D$, is not signed.

Case 3: controlling for $X$. Write $Y=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D+u$ with
$E[u|X,D]=0$. Conditional on $X$
$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D|X)=\operatorname{Var}(D|X)\tau(X)>0$
and
$Y-E[Y|X]=\tau(X)\big(D-p(X)\big)$ with $p(X)=E[D|X]$.
Hence
$E\big[(D-E[D|X])\,(Y-E[Y|X])\big]=E[\operatorname{Var}(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$.
Frisch–Waugh gives the population partial coefficient as the projection
on the linear space spanned by $1,X,D$.  Let $\tilde D=D-\operatorname{Proj}(D|1,X)$.
On $X$ the part of $Y$ that is $X$-measurable is removed, and
$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\tilde D|X)=\tau(X)\operatorname{Cov}(D,\tilde D|X)
=\tau(X)\operatorname{Var}(D|X)>0$.  After integrating out $X$
$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E[\operatorname{Var}(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$,
i.e. the numerator is a positive variance-weighted average of the
strictly positive within-$X$ gaps $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$.
The back-door path $D\leftarrow X\rightarrow Y$ is blocked by conditioning
on $X$, so the linear partial association of $Y$ with $D$ inherits the
within-$X$ monotonicity.  In particular

$\beta_{D|X}= \frac{E[\operatorname{Var}(D|X)\tau(X)]}{\operatorname{Var}(\tilde D)}>0$.

What is sometimes quoted as a sign reversal for the linear regression
is the sign reversal for the non-parametric residual $D-p(X)$,
$\operatorname{Cov}\big(Y,D-p(X)\big)=E[\operatorname{Var}(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$,
which is always positive.  The examples with a non-linear propensity
$p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$ and a baseline $m_{0}(x)=-Mx^{2}$ show that
$D-p(X)$ can be negatively correlated with $m_{0}(X)$ in the linear sense,
but that is the non-parametric partial covariance, i.e. controlling for
$X$ non-parametrically.  With the OLS residual $\tilde D=D-a-bX$ the only
variation identifying $D$ is the within-$X$ variation, and with
$D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y_{0},Y_{1})|X$ that variation is strictly increasing in
$Y$.  Hence the population OLS coefficient on $D$ in $Y\sim1+D+X$ is a
positive weighted average of the positive $\tau(X)$ and must be $>0$.

Positivity is therefore guaranteed under unconditional randomisation,
Case 1, and is restored by including $X$ under conditional randomisation,
Case 3, but it is not guaranteed for the unadjusted regression under
conditional randomisation, Case 2.  That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.

1.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The potential outcomes are Y = Y0 + D τ with τ>0 a.s. Under conditional randomisation D ⟂ Y0,Y1 | X we have E[Y|X,D]=m0(X)+τ(X)D with m0(X)=E[Y0|X], τ(X)=E[τ|X]>0, p(X)=E[D|X]. So E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=τ(X)>0 pointwise.

Case 1. D ⟂ Y0,Y1 unconditionally. Then β1=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y1-Y0]=E[τ]>0. Guaranteed.

Case 2. D ⟂ Y0,Y1|X but D not independent of X. 
E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[τ(X)|D=1]+E[m0(X)|D=1]-E[m0(X)|D=0]. 
The selection term Cov(m0(X),D) is unrestricted. With p(X) decreasing in X and m0(X) increasing, e.g. X∈{0,1}, p0=0.9,p1=0.1, m0(1)=100, τ≡1, we get E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]. So the unadjusted OLS coefficient is not signed.

Case 3. Linear projection on 1,D,X. Let â+ b̂X = Proj(D|1,X), D⊥=D-â-b̂X, w(X)=E[D⊥|X]=p(X)-â-b̂X, E[w]=E[wX]=0. Then
Cov(Y,D⊥)=E[τ(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov(m0(X)+p(X)τ(X),w(X)).
The first term E[τVar(D|X)]>0 is the within-X part, i.e. Cov(Y,D-p(X))>0.
The second term is Cov(m0,w) plus Cov(pτ,w). w is the linear residual of the propensity. If p(X) is non-linear in X, w≠0 and Cov(m0,w) is unrestricted under D⟂Y0,Y1|X and τ(X)>0 alone. It can be made arbitrarily negative by choosing m0 non-linear and negatively correlated with w.

Standard counter-example: X~U[-1,1], p(x)=0.5+0.4x², Proj(p|1,X)=0.5, w(x)=0.4x²-const, m0(x)=-M x², τ≡1. Then E[Y|X,D]=-M x²+D, E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0 ∀X, D⟂Y0,Y1|X, yet βD = [E[τVar(D|X)]+Cov(m0,w)]/Var(D⊥)=1 - cM → -∞ as M→∞. Discrete version X∈{-1,0,1}, p(±1)=1,p(0)=0, m0(0)=M,m0(±1)=0, τ≡1 gives Proj(D|1,X)=1/3+0.5X and βD=1-10M<0 for large M.

Thus the non-parametric residual D-p(X) gives positivity, Cov(Y,D-p(X))=E[τVar(D|X)]>0, but OLS uses the linear residual D-â-b̂X. Without linearity of p(X) and m0(X) the linear projection can reverse sign. The E camp conflates D⊥ with D-p(X) and implicitly assumes linear propensity / linear baseline. Under the stated no-parametric-assumptions requirement the linear coefficient is not sign identified.

Disagreement remains: colleagues 13,14,17,2,5,8,9 argue Case 3 is guaranteed positive, citing Frisch-Waugh and within-X monotonicity. Colleagues 1,10,12,15,16,18,3,4,6,7 argue the linear residual counter-example shows sign can flip. The no-parametric restriction and the x² vs -M x² construction are decisive for the formal population OLS coefficient.

Current belief: positivity is guaranteed only under unconditional randomisation. That is A. Only Case 1.

10.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The core objects are Y = Y0 + D τ, τ_i = Y1(i)-Y0(i) >0 a.s., m0(X)=E[Y0|X], τ(X)=E[τ|X]>0, p(X)=E[D|X] and D⊥Y0,Y1|X.

Case1 unconditional randomisation D⊥Y0,Y1. Then E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y1]-E[Y0]=E[τ]>0 so OLS of Y on 1,D is strictly positive. Unanimous.

Case2 D⊥Y0,Y1|X but D not ⊥X. E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=τ(X)>0 pointwise but
E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[τ(X)|D=1]+E[m0(X)|D=1]-E[m0(X)|D=0].
Selection term can dominate. Example X∈{0,1}, m0(1)=100,m0(0)=0, τ≡1, p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1 gives E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]. Accepted by all. So marginal regression not signed.

Case3 linear projection of Y on 1,D,X. Let \hat p(X)=Proj(p|X) linear, r(X)=p(X)-\hat p(X) with E[r]=E[rX]=0, \tilde D = D-\hat p(X). Then
β_D = Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D).
Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[τ(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov(m0(X)+p(X)τ(X),r(X)).
E[τ Var(D|X)]>0, but Cov(m0,r) is unrestricted because r is orthogonal to 1,X but generally non-zero when p(·) is non-linear. By making m0 large and negatively correlated with r and/or τ small where r is large, Cov(Y,\tilde D) can be made negative. Canonical counterexamples: X~U[-1,1], p(x)=0.5+0.4x², m0(x)=-M x², τ≡1 gives β_D=1-M Cov(X²,p)/Var(\tilde D)→-∞ as M→∞; discrete X∈{-1,0,1} with p(-1)=p(1)=1,p(0)=0 and m0(0)=10 gives β_D<0.

The object that is guaranteed positive is the non-parametric residual Cov(Y,D-p(X))=E[τ(X)Var(D|X)]>0, i.e. the partial effect after non-parametric control for X. OLS uses the linear residual D-Proj(D|1,X), not D-p(X). Several colleagues invoke the non-parametric residual argument and conclude Case3 must be positive, e.g. E. Only Case1 and Case3. That is the disagreement.

Given no parametric assumptions beyond D⊥Y0,Y1|X and τ>0, the linear projection coefficient is not sign-identified. Only unconditional randomisation guarantees positivity. Current best belief remains A. Only Case1.

Unresolved: phrasing about “regress Y on a constant, D and X” is linear OLS, so counterexample stands. If question intended non-parametric control of X, answer would be E, but as stated it is A.

4.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The model is $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, $p(X)=E[D|X]$. Under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$, $E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$ and $E[Y|X]=m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X)$. The within-$X$ gap is $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$.

Case 1: $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. Then $\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$. Unconditional randomisation makes the intercept–slope OLS the ATE, sign is guaranteed.

Case 2: $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but $D\not\perp X$. 
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $\operatorname{Cov}(m_{0}(X),D)$ is free. E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(1)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$ while $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s. So the uncontrolled difference in means can be negative.

Case 3: linear projection on $1,D,X$. Let $\hat p(X)=\operatorname{Proj}(D|1,X)$, $D_{\perp}=D-\hat p(X)$, $w(X)=p(X)-\hat p(X)$ with $E[w]=E[wX]=0$. Then
$\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,D_{\perp})/Var(D_{\perp})$ and
$Cov(Y,D_{\perp})=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),w(X))$.
$E[\tau Var(D|X)]>0$ is the non-parametric within-$X$ part, $E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[\tau Var(D|X)]>0$.
The OLS residual is $D-\hat p(X)$, not $D-p(X)$. If $p(X)$ is non-linear, $w(X)\neq0$ and $Cov(m_{0}(X),w(X))$ is unrestricted under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ and $\tau>0$.

E.g. $X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $\hat p\equiv0.5$, $m_{0}(x)=-Mx^{2}$, $\tau\equiv1$, gives $E[Y|X,D]=-Mx^{2}+D$, $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for all $X$, yet $\beta_{D}=1-M\,Cov(x^{2},w)/Var(D_{\perp})\to-\infty$ as $M\to\infty$. Discrete versions $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$, $p(\pm1)=1,p(0)=0$, $m_{0}(0)=10$, $m_{0}(\pm1)=0$, $\tau\equiv1$ give $\beta_{D}<0$ while the conditional gap is $>0$.

Thus positivity is preserved for the non-parametric partial effect $D-E[D|X]$ but not for the linear projection $D- Proj(D|1,X)$. The room is split between the E camp, which identifies the OLS coefficient with $D-E[D|X]$ and claims Case 3 is signed, and the A camp, which keeps the linear residual distinction. The examples above show the linear coefficient can be made arbitrarily negative with $\tau_i>0$ and $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$, no parametric linearity imposed.

Current belief: positivity of the population OLS coefficient on $D$ is guaranteed only under unconditional randomisation. Cases 2 and 3 can both be negative. That is A. Only Case 1.

12.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The potential outcomes are $Y=Y(0)+D\tau_i$ with $\tau_i=Y(1)-Y(0)>0$ a.s., $m_0(X)=E[Y(0)|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, $p(X)=E[D|X]$.
Under $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)|X$, $E[Y|X,D]=m_0(X)+\tau(X)D$ and $E[Y|X]=m_0(X)+p(X)\tau(X)$, so $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ pointwise and $E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[\operatorname{Var}(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$.

Case 1 $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$.  OLS of $Y$ on $1,D$ is the difference in means
$\beta_1=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$. Sign is guaranteed.

Case 2 $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)|X$ but uncontrolled.
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_0|X]|D$ can dominate. With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_0(X)$ increasing, e.g. $X\in\{0,1\},p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1,m_0(1)=100,\tau\equiv1$, $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$ although $\tau_i>0$ a.s. So the unadjusted $D$ coefficient is not sign identified.

Case 3 $Y\sim1+D+X$ linearly. Let $\hat p(X)=\operatorname{Proj}(D|1,X)=a+bX$, $D_\perp=D-\hat p(X)$ and $w(X)=p(X)-\hat p(X)$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$.
$\beta_D={\rm Cov}(Y,D_\perp)/{\rm Var}(D_\perp)$ and
${\rm Cov}(Y,D_\perp)=E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]+E[w(X)m_0(X)]+{\rm remainder}$.
$E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$, but $E[w(X)m_0(X)]$ is the covariance of the baseline mean with the linear residual of the propensity. $w(X)$ is the part of $p(X)$ not linearly spanned by $1,X$. By choosing $m_0(X)$ non-linear and strongly negatively correlated with $w(X)$ the first term can be made arbitrarily negative while keeping $\tau(X)>0$ and $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)|X$.

Concrete counterexamples: $X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^2$, $\hat p\equiv0.5$, $m_0(x)=-M x^2$, $\tau\equiv1$, gives $\beta_D=1-M\,{\rm Cov}(x^2,p)/{\rm Var}(D_\perp)\to-\infty$ as $M\to\infty$ while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$.
Discrete: $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$ equiprobable, $p(-1)=p(1)=1,p(0)=0$, $m_0(0)=10,m_0(\pm1)=0$, $\tau=1$ gives $\beta_D<0$ although $Y(1)>Y(0)$ a.s.

Thus $E[(D-E[D|X])Y]>0$ holds non-parametrically, i.e. $E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[{\rm Var}(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$, but OLS uses the linear residual $D-\hat p(X)$, not $D-p(X)$. Without a linearity restriction on $p(X)$ and $m_0(X)$ the linear projection can change sign.

The E camp “Only Case 1 and Case 3” argument conflates the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$ with the linear residual $D-{\rm Proj}(D|1,X)$ and asserts $\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D_\perp)=E[{\rm Var}(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$. That is true for the non-parametric partial covariance, not for the population OLS with a linear control for $X$.

Hence with no parametric restrictions beyond those stated, the $D$ coefficient is sign guaranteed only under unconditional randomisation. Current belief remains A. Only Case 1.

Unresolved nuance: under an additional linearity assumption $E[Y(0)|X]$ and $p(X)$ linear in $X$, or with non-parametric control $E[D|X]$, Case 3 would be sign guaranteed, which is the source of the split with colleagues 2,5,8,9,13,14.

6.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The potential-outcome set-up is $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau_i$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., 
$m_0(X)=E[Y_0|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, $p(X)=E[D|X]$.
Under $D\perp Y_0,Y_1|X$
$E[Y|X,D]=m_0(X)+\tau(X)D$, $E[Y|X]=m_0(X)+p(X)\tau(X)$ and 
$E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ pointwise.

Case 1. $D\perp Y_0,Y_1$. 
$\beta_1=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_1-Y_0]=E[\tau]>0$.
Unconditional randomisation identifies the ATE. All colleagues agree this is signed.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_0,Y_1|X$ but $D\not\perp X$.
$\beta_2=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_0|D=1]-E[m_0|D=0]=\operatorname{Cov}(m_0(X),D)/Var(D)$ is unrestricted. 
With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_0(X)$ increasing, e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $m_0(1)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$, 
$E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$ while $Y_1>Y_0$ a.s. So the unadjusted $1,D$ regression is not signed.

Case 3. Linear projection of $Y$ on $1,D,X$.
Let $\hat p(X)=Proj(p|1,X)=a+bX$, $D_{\perp}=D-\hat p(X)$, $w(X)=p(X)-\hat p(X)=E[D_{\perp}|X]$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$.
$\beta_D=Cov(Y,D_{\perp})/Var(D_{\perp})$ and
$Cov(Y,D_{\perp})=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov\big(m_0(X)+p(X)\tau(X),w(X)\big)$.
The first term $E[\tau Var(D|X)]>0$ is the within-$X$ part, i.e. $E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]>0$.
The second term $Cov(m_0,w)+Cov(p\tau,w)$ is unrestricted under $D\perp Y_0,Y_1|X$ and $\tau>0$ alone, because $w$ is the linear residual of the propensity and is orthogonal to $1,X$ but not to arbitrary functions of $X$.

With a non-linear propensity $w\neq0$ and $Cov(m_0,w)$ can be made arbitrarily negative while keeping $\tau(X)>0$ and $D\perp Y_0,Y_1|X$.
E.g. $X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^2$, $\hat p\equiv0.5$, $w(x)=0.4x^2-0.4E[x^2]$, $m_0(x)=-Mx^2$, $\tau\equiv1$.
Then $E[Y|X,D]=-Mx^2+D$, $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ $\forall X$, yet
$\beta_D=1-M\,Cov(x^2,w)/Var(D_{\perp})\to-\infty$ as $M\to\infty$.
Discrete version $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$, $p(-1)=p(1)=1,p(0)=0$, $m_0(0)=M$, $m_0(\pm1)=0$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives $\beta_D=1-10M<0$ for large $M$ while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$.

This is the difference between the non-parametric residual $D-p(X)$ for which $Cov(Y,D-p(X))=E[\tau Var(D|X)]>0$ and the OLS residual $D-\hat p(X)$. The E camp claims the linear coefficient inherits the within-$X$ positivity, i.e. $Cov(Y,D_{\perp})=E[\tau Var(D|X)]>0$, which would be true for a non-parametric control of $X$. The $E$ argument rests on the identity $E[D_{\perp}|X]=0$ or on economic plausibility of monotone baseline vs propensity. Under the stated “no parametric assumptions beyond what I have given” the linear approximation error $p(X)-\hat p(X)$ can be correlated with any non-linear $m_0(X)$, so the sign can flip.

Hence with no linearity restriction on $p(X)$ and $m_0(X)$ the population OLS coefficient on $D$ in $Y\sim1+D+X$ is not sign-identified by $\tau_i>0$ and $D\perp Y_0,Y_1|X$ alone. The only case where positivity must hold in population is unconditional randomisation.

Current belief is A. Only Case 1. The unresolved nuance is the binary-X special case where $p-\hat p\equiv0$ and Case 3 would be signed; with a continuous pre-income $X$ the counter-example applies.

17.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The model is $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_i=Y_{1}-Y_{0}>0$ a.s., $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, $p(X)=E[D|X]$, $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$.

Under conditional randomisation $E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$ so $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ pointwise and
$E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$.
The non-parametric partial effect is signed.

Case 1. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. $\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$. The ATE, signed.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but $D\not\perp X$.
$\beta_{2}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_{0}|D=1]-E[m_{0}|D=0]$ is unrestricted. With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_{0}(X)$ increasing, e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(1)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$, $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$. So the uncontrolled difference in means is not signed.

Case 3. Population OLS on $1,D,X$ is the linear projection. Let $\hat p(X)=a+bX$ be the linear projection of $D$ on $1,X$, $D_{\perp}=D-\hat p(X)$, $w(X)=p(X)-\hat p(X)=E[D_{\perp}|X]$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$.
$\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,D_{\perp})/Var(D_{\perp})$
$Cov(Y,D_{\perp})=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),w(X))$.
The first term $>0$ is the within-$X$ part. The second term $Cov(m_{0},w)+Cov(p\tau,w)$ is unrestricted when $p(X)$ is non-linear. $w\neq0$ iff $p(X)$ is non-linear in $X$. By making $m_{0}(X)$ large where $w(X)<0$ and small where $w(X)>0$ the second term can dominate and make $Cov(Y,D_{\perp})<0$ while keeping $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ and $\tau(X)>0$.

Concrete sign reversals: $X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $\hat p\equiv0.5$, $m_{0}(x)=-Mx^{2}$, $\tau\equiv1$. Then $E[Y|X,D]=-Mx^{2}+D$ and $\beta_{D}=1-M\,Cov(x^{2},w)/Var(D_{\perp})\to-\infty$ as $M\to\infty$. Discrete $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$ with $p(-1)=p(1)=1,p(0)=0$, $m_{0}(0)=M$, $m_{0}(\pm1)=0$, $\tau=1$ gives $\beta_{D}<0$ for large $M$ while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $X$.

Thus the positivity guaranteed for the non-parametric residual $D-p(X)$ does not transfer to the linear residual $D-\hat p(X)$ without linearity of $p(X)$ and $m_{0}(X)$. No parametric assumptions are allowed.

Room disagreement: Colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9 argue Case 3 is signed, claiming the linear partial coefficient is a positive weighted average of $\tau(X)>0$ and that the back-door is blocked by including $X$. Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18 give the non-linear $p(X)$ vs $m_{0}(X)$ counter-examples showing the linear projection can flip sign. The counter-examples are consistent with no parametric restrictions.

Current belief remains A. Only Case 1 must have positive population $D$ coefficient. Case 2 is unsigned by selection bias; Case 3 is unsigned by the linear-projection Simpson reversal when $p(X)$ is non-linear in $X$. If linearity of $E[Y_{0}|X]$ and $E[D|X]$ were imposed, Case 3 would be signed, which is the source of the E camp.

$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}]-E[Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$. Unconditional randomisation forces the sign. All colleagues agree.

*Case 2.* $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but $D\not\perp X$.

The selection term $E[m_{0}|D=1]-E[m_{0}|D=0]=Cov(m_{0}(X),D)/Var(D)$ is unrestricted. $Cov(Y,D_{\perp})=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),w(X)\big)$.
$E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$ is the within-$X$ non-parametric part $E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]>0$.
The second term is $Cov(m_{0},w)+Cov(p\tau,w)$. $w$ is the linear residual of the propensity, orthogonal to $1,X$ but not to arbitrary $m_{0}(X)$. With non-linear $p(\cdot)$ the sign of $Cov(m_{0},w)$ is unrestricted under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ and $\tau>0$ alone.

Counter-examples repeatedly cited in round 2:
$X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $\hat p\equiv0.5$, $w(x)=0.4x^{2}-const$, $m_{0}(x)=-M x^{2}$, $\tau\equiv1$. Current belief remains A. Only Case 1 must be positive in population. Case 2 fails by selection bias, Case 3 fails by non-linear propensity interacting with the linear residual; sign is not guaranteed without parametric linearity of $p(X)$ and $m_{0}(X)$ in $X$.

 +\operatorname{Cov}\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),w(X)\big)$.

$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})=E[\tau(X)\operatorname{Var}(D|X)]+ \operatorname{Cov}\big(m_0(X)+p(X)\tau(X),w(X)\big)$.
The first term $E[\tau\operatorname{Var}(D|X)]>0$ is the non-parametric partial effect $E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]>0$.
The second term is $\operatorname{Cov}(m_0,w)+...$. $w$ is the linear residual of the propensity; it is non-zero when $p(X)$ is non-linear in $X$ and is orthogonal to $1,X$ but not to arbitrary $m_0(X)$. Hence $\operatorname{Cov}(m_0,w)$ is unrestricted under $D\perp Y_0,Y_1|X$ and $\tau>0$.

Sign reversal examples:
$X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^2$, $\hat p\equiv0.5$, $w(x)=0.4x^2-0.4E[x^2]$, $m_0(x)=-Mx^2$, $\tau\equiv1$. Then $E[Y|X,D]=-Mx^2+D$, $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$, yet
$\beta_D=1-M\,\operatorname{Cov}(x^2,w)/\operatorname{Var}(D_{\perp})\to-\infty$ as $M\to\infty$.
Discrete $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$, $p(\pm1)=1,p(0)=0$, $m_0(0)=M$, $m_0(\pm1)=0$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives $\beta_D=1-10M<0$ for large $M$ while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0\;\forall X$.
Thus the linear residual $D-\operatorname{Proj}(D|1,X)$ is not $D-p(X)$. Positivity holds for the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$, not for the OLS linear residual.

Colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9 claim Case 3 is signed, arguing $\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})=E[\tau\operatorname{Var}(D|X)]>0$ and that controlling for $X$ blocks the back-door path. That is the non-parametric partial covariance. The error is conflating $D-E[D|X]$ with $D-\operatorname{Proj}(D|1,X)$ and assuming $\operatorname{Cov}(m_0,w)=0$. Under no parametric restriction on $m_0$ and $p$, that covariance can be made arbitrarily negative.

Hence with no parametric assumptions beyond those stated, positivity of the population $D$ coefficient is forced only under unconditional randomisation. Case 2 fails by composition/selection bias, Case 3 fails by linear misspecification/Simpson sign reversal.

Current belief remains A. Only Case 1.

$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_{0}|D=1]-E[m_{0}|D=0]$ is unrestricted.

Let $\hat D=Proj_{1,X}D=a+bX$, $D_{\perp}=D-\hat D$, $w(X)=E[D_{\perp}|X]=p(X)-a-bX$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$.
$\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,D_{\perp})/Var(D_{\perp})$ and

$Cov(Y,D_{\perp})=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),w(X)\big)$.

$E[\tau Var(D|X)]>0$ is the non-parametric within-$X$ part.
$Cov(Y,D-E[D|X])=E[\tau Var(D|X)]>0$. The OLS residual is $D-\hat D$, not $D-p(X)$.
$w(X)\neq0$ whenever $p(\cdot)$ is non-linear in $X$, and $Cov(m_{0}(X),w(X))$ is unrestricted under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ and $\tau>0$ alone.
