reflection_text.1:
The potential outcomes are Y = Y0 + D τ with τ>0 a.s. Under conditional randomisation D ⟂ Y0,Y1 | X we have E[Y|X,D]=m0(X)+τ(X)D with m0(X)=E[Y0|X], τ(X)=E[τ|X]>0, p(X)=E[D|X]. So E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=τ(X)>0 pointwise.

Case 1. D ⟂ Y0,Y1 unconditionally. Then β1=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y1-Y0]=E[τ]>0. Guaranteed.

Case 2. D ⟂ Y0,Y1|X but D not independent of X. 
E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[τ(X)|D=1]+E[m0(X)|D=1]-E[m0(X)|D=0]. 
The selection term Cov(m0(X),D) is unrestricted. With p(X) decreasing in X and m0(X) increasing, e.g. X∈{0,1}, p0=0.9,p1=0.1, m0(1)=100, τ≡1, we get E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]. So the unadjusted OLS coefficient is not signed.

Case 3. Linear projection on 1,D,X. Let â+ b̂X = Proj(D|1,X), D⊥=D-â-b̂X, w(X)=E[D⊥|X]=p(X)-â-b̂X, E[w]=E[wX]=0. Then
Cov(Y,D⊥)=E[τ(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov(m0(X)+p(X)τ(X),w(X)).
The first term E[τVar(D|X)]>0 is the within-X part, i.e. Cov(Y,D-p(X))>0.
The second term is Cov(m0,w) plus Cov(pτ,w). w is the linear residual of the propensity. If p(X) is non-linear in X, w≠0 and Cov(m0,w) is unrestricted under D⟂Y0,Y1|X and τ(X)>0 alone. It can be made arbitrarily negative by choosing m0 non-linear and negatively correlated with w.

Standard counter-example: X~U[-1,1], p(x)=0.5+0.4x², Proj(p|1,X)=0.5, w(x)=0.4x²-const, m0(x)=-M x², τ≡1. Then E[Y|X,D]=-M x²+D, E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0 ∀X, D⟂Y0,Y1|X, yet βD = [E[τVar(D|X)]+Cov(m0,w)]/Var(D⊥)=1 - cM → -∞ as M→∞. Discrete version X∈{-1,0,1}, p(±1)=1,p(0)=0, m0(0)=M,m0(±1)=0, τ≡1 gives Proj(D|1,X)=1/3+0.5X and βD=1-10M<0 for large M.

Thus the non-parametric residual D-p(X) gives positivity, Cov(Y,D-p(X))=E[τVar(D|X)]>0, but OLS uses the linear residual D-â-b̂X. Without linearity of p(X) and m0(X) the linear projection can reverse sign. The E camp conflates D⊥ with D-p(X) and implicitly assumes linear propensity / linear baseline. Under the stated no-parametric-assumptions requirement the linear coefficient is not sign identified.

Disagreement remains: colleagues 13,14,17,2,5,8,9 argue Case 3 is guaranteed positive, citing Frisch-Waugh and within-X monotonicity. Colleagues 1,10,12,15,16,18,3,4,6,7 argue the linear residual counter-example shows sign can flip. The no-parametric restriction and the x² vs -M x² construction are decisive for the formal population OLS coefficient.

Current belief: positivity is guaranteed only under unconditional randomisation. That is A. Only Case 1.
reflection_text.10:
The core objects are Y = Y0 + D τ, τ_i = Y1(i)-Y0(i) >0 a.s., m0(X)=E[Y0|X], τ(X)=E[τ|X]>0, p(X)=E[D|X] and D⊥Y0,Y1|X.

Case1 unconditional randomisation D⊥Y0,Y1. Then E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y1]-E[Y0]=E[τ]>0 so OLS of Y on 1,D is strictly positive. Unanimous.

Case2 D⊥Y0,Y1|X but D not ⊥X. E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=τ(X)>0 pointwise but
E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[τ(X)|D=1]+E[m0(X)|D=1]-E[m0(X)|D=0].
Selection term can dominate. Example X∈{0,1}, m0(1)=100,m0(0)=0, τ≡1, p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1 gives E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]. Accepted by all. So marginal regression not signed.

Case3 linear projection of Y on 1,D,X. Let \hat p(X)=Proj(p|X) linear, r(X)=p(X)-\hat p(X) with E[r]=E[rX]=0, \tilde D = D-\hat p(X). Then
β_D = Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D).
Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[τ(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov(m0(X)+p(X)τ(X),r(X)).
E[τ Var(D|X)]>0, but Cov(m0,r) is unrestricted because r is orthogonal to 1,X but generally non-zero when p(·) is non-linear. By making m0 large and negatively correlated with r and/or τ small where r is large, Cov(Y,\tilde D) can be made negative. Canonical counterexamples: X~U[-1,1], p(x)=0.5+0.4x², m0(x)=-M x², τ≡1 gives β_D=1-M Cov(X²,p)/Var(\tilde D)→-∞ as M→∞; discrete X∈{-1,0,1} with p(-1)=p(1)=1,p(0)=0 and m0(0)=10 gives β_D<0.

The object that is guaranteed positive is the non-parametric residual Cov(Y,D-p(X))=E[τ(X)Var(D|X)]>0, i.e. the partial effect after non-parametric control for X. OLS uses the linear residual D-Proj(D|1,X), not D-p(X). Several colleagues invoke the non-parametric residual argument and conclude Case3 must be positive, e.g. E. Only Case1 and Case3. That is the disagreement.

Given no parametric assumptions beyond D⊥Y0,Y1|X and τ>0, the linear projection coefficient is not sign-identified. Only unconditional randomisation guarantees positivity. Current best belief remains A. Only Case1.

Unresolved: phrasing about “regress Y on a constant, D and X” is linear OLS, so counterexample stands. If question intended non-parametric control of X, answer would be E, but as stated it is A.
reflection_text.4:
The model is $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, $p(X)=E[D|X]$. Under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$, $E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$ and $E[Y|X]=m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X)$. The within-$X$ gap is $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$.

Case 1: $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. Then $\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$. Unconditional randomisation makes the intercept–slope OLS the ATE, sign is guaranteed.

Case 2: $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but $D\not\perp X$. 
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $\operatorname{Cov}(m_{0}(X),D)$ is free. E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(1)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$ while $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s. So the uncontrolled difference in means can be negative.

Case 3: linear projection on $1,D,X$. Let $\hat p(X)=\operatorname{Proj}(D|1,X)$, $D_{\perp}=D-\hat p(X)$, $w(X)=p(X)-\hat p(X)$ with $E[w]=E[wX]=0$. Then
$\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,D_{\perp})/Var(D_{\perp})$ and
$Cov(Y,D_{\perp})=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),w(X))$.
$E[\tau Var(D|X)]>0$ is the non-parametric within-$X$ part, $E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[\tau Var(D|X)]>0$.
The OLS residual is $D-\hat p(X)$, not $D-p(X)$. If $p(X)$ is non-linear, $w(X)\neq0$ and $Cov(m_{0}(X),w(X))$ is unrestricted under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ and $\tau>0$.

E.g. $X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $\hat p\equiv0.5$, $m_{0}(x)=-Mx^{2}$, $\tau\equiv1$, gives $E[Y|X,D]=-Mx^{2}+D$, $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for all $X$, yet $\beta_{D}=1-M\,Cov(x^{2},w)/Var(D_{\perp})\to-\infty$ as $M\to\infty$. Discrete versions $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$, $p(\pm1)=1,p(0)=0$, $m_{0}(0)=10$, $m_{0}(\pm1)=0$, $\tau\equiv1$ give $\beta_{D}<0$ while the conditional gap is $>0$.

Thus positivity is preserved for the non-parametric partial effect $D-E[D|X]$ but not for the linear projection $D- Proj(D|1,X)$. The room is split between the E camp, which identifies the OLS coefficient with $D-E[D|X]$ and claims Case 3 is signed, and the A camp, which keeps the linear residual distinction. The examples above show the linear coefficient can be made arbitrarily negative with $\tau_i>0$ and $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$, no parametric linearity imposed.

Current belief: positivity of the population OLS coefficient on $D$ is guaranteed only under unconditional randomisation. Cases 2 and 3 can both be negative. That is A. Only Case 1.
reflection_text.12:
The potential outcomes are $Y=Y(0)+D\tau_i$ with $\tau_i=Y(1)-Y(0)>0$ a.s., $m_0(X)=E[Y(0)|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, $p(X)=E[D|X]$.
Under $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)|X$, $E[Y|X,D]=m_0(X)+\tau(X)D$ and $E[Y|X]=m_0(X)+p(X)\tau(X)$, so $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ pointwise and $E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[\operatorname{Var}(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$.

Case 1 $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$.  OLS of $Y$ on $1,D$ is the difference in means
$\beta_1=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$. Sign is guaranteed.

Case 2 $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)|X$ but uncontrolled.
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_0|X]|D$ can dominate. With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_0(X)$ increasing, e.g. $X\in\{0,1\},p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1,m_0(1)=100,\tau\equiv1$, $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$ although $\tau_i>0$ a.s. So the unadjusted $D$ coefficient is not sign identified.

Case 3 $Y\sim1+D+X$ linearly. Let $\hat p(X)=\operatorname{Proj}(D|1,X)=a+bX$, $D_\perp=D-\hat p(X)$ and $w(X)=p(X)-\hat p(X)$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$.
$\beta_D={\rm Cov}(Y,D_\perp)/{\rm Var}(D_\perp)$ and
${\rm Cov}(Y,D_\perp)=E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]+E[w(X)m_0(X)]+{\rm remainder}$.
$E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$, but $E[w(X)m_0(X)]$ is the covariance of the baseline mean with the linear residual of the propensity. $w(X)$ is the part of $p(X)$ not linearly spanned by $1,X$. By choosing $m_0(X)$ non-linear and strongly negatively correlated with $w(X)$ the first term can be made arbitrarily negative while keeping $\tau(X)>0$ and $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)|X$.

Concrete counterexamples: $X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^2$, $\hat p\equiv0.5$, $m_0(x)=-M x^2$, $\tau\equiv1$, gives $\beta_D=1-M\,{\rm Cov}(x^2,p)/{\rm Var}(D_\perp)\to-\infty$ as $M\to\infty$ while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$.
Discrete: $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$ equiprobable, $p(-1)=p(1)=1,p(0)=0$, $m_0(0)=10,m_0(\pm1)=0$, $\tau=1$ gives $\beta_D<0$ although $Y(1)>Y(0)$ a.s.

Thus $E[(D-E[D|X])Y]>0$ holds non-parametrically, i.e. $E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[{\rm Var}(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$, but OLS uses the linear residual $D-\hat p(X)$, not $D-p(X)$. Without a linearity restriction on $p(X)$ and $m_0(X)$ the linear projection can change sign.

The E camp “Only Case 1 and Case 3” argument conflates the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$ with the linear residual $D-{\rm Proj}(D|1,X)$ and asserts $\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D_\perp)=E[{\rm Var}(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$. That is true for the non-parametric partial covariance, not for the population OLS with a linear control for $X$.

Hence with no parametric restrictions beyond those stated, the $D$ coefficient is sign guaranteed only under unconditional randomisation. Current belief remains A. Only Case 1.

Unresolved nuance: under an additional linearity assumption $E[Y(0)|X]$ and $p(X)$ linear in $X$, or with non-parametric control $E[D|X]$, Case 3 would be sign guaranteed, which is the source of the split with colleagues 2,5,8,9,13,14.
reflection_text.6:
The potential-outcome set-up is $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau_i$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., 
$m_0(X)=E[Y_0|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, $p(X)=E[D|X]$.
Under $D\perp Y_0,Y_1|X$
$E[Y|X,D]=m_0(X)+\tau(X)D$, $E[Y|X]=m_0(X)+p(X)\tau(X)$ and 
$E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ pointwise.

Case 1. $D\perp Y_0,Y_1$. 
$\beta_1=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_1-Y_0]=E[\tau]>0$.
Unconditional randomisation identifies the ATE. All colleagues agree this is signed.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_0,Y_1|X$ but $D\not\perp X$.
$\beta_2=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_0|D=1]-E[m_0|D=0]=\operatorname{Cov}(m_0(X),D)/Var(D)$ is unrestricted. 
With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_0(X)$ increasing, e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $m_0(1)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$, 
$E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$ while $Y_1>Y_0$ a.s. So the unadjusted $1,D$ regression is not signed.

Case 3. Linear projection of $Y$ on $1,D,X$.
Let $\hat p(X)=Proj(p|1,X)=a+bX$, $D_{\perp}=D-\hat p(X)$, $w(X)=p(X)-\hat p(X)=E[D_{\perp}|X]$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$.
$\beta_D=Cov(Y,D_{\perp})/Var(D_{\perp})$ and
$Cov(Y,D_{\perp})=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov\big(m_0(X)+p(X)\tau(X),w(X)\big)$.
The first term $E[\tau Var(D|X)]>0$ is the within-$X$ part, i.e. $E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]>0$.
The second term $Cov(m_0,w)+Cov(p\tau,w)$ is unrestricted under $D\perp Y_0,Y_1|X$ and $\tau>0$ alone, because $w$ is the linear residual of the propensity and is orthogonal to $1,X$ but not to arbitrary functions of $X$.

With a non-linear propensity $w\neq0$ and $Cov(m_0,w)$ can be made arbitrarily negative while keeping $\tau(X)>0$ and $D\perp Y_0,Y_1|X$.
E.g. $X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^2$, $\hat p\equiv0.5$, $w(x)=0.4x^2-0.4E[x^2]$, $m_0(x)=-Mx^2$, $\tau\equiv1$.
Then $E[Y|X,D]=-Mx^2+D$, $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ $\forall X$, yet
$\beta_D=1-M\,Cov(x^2,w)/Var(D_{\perp})\to-\infty$ as $M\to\infty$.
Discrete version $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$, $p(-1)=p(1)=1,p(0)=0$, $m_0(0)=M$, $m_0(\pm1)=0$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives $\beta_D=1-10M<0$ for large $M$ while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$.

This is the difference between the non-parametric residual $D-p(X)$ for which $Cov(Y,D-p(X))=E[\tau Var(D|X)]>0$ and the OLS residual $D-\hat p(X)$. The E camp claims the linear coefficient inherits the within-$X$ positivity, i.e. $Cov(Y,D_{\perp})=E[\tau Var(D|X)]>0$, which would be true for a non-parametric control of $X$. The $E$ argument rests on the identity $E[D_{\perp}|X]=0$ or on economic plausibility of monotone baseline vs propensity. Under the stated “no parametric assumptions beyond what I have given” the linear approximation error $p(X)-\hat p(X)$ can be correlated with any non-linear $m_0(X)$, so the sign can flip.

Hence with no linearity restriction on $p(X)$ and $m_0(X)$ the population OLS coefficient on $D$ in $Y\sim1+D+X$ is not sign-identified by $\tau_i>0$ and $D\perp Y_0,Y_1|X$ alone. The only case where positivity must hold in population is unconditional randomisation.

Current belief is A. Only Case 1. The unresolved nuance is the binary-X special case where $p-\hat p\equiv0$ and Case 3 would be signed; with a continuous pre-income $X$ the counter-example applies.

Under conditional randomisation $E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$ so $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ pointwise and
$E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$.
The non-parametric partial effect is signed.

Case 1. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. $\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$. The ATE, signed.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but $D\not\perp X$.
$\beta_{2}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_{0}|D=1]-E[m_{0}|D=0]$ is unrestricted. With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_{0}(X)$ increasing, e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(1)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$, $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$. So the uncontrolled difference in means is not signed.

$Cov(Y,D_{\perp})=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),w(X))$.

With the potential outcomes write up $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau_{i}$,
$\tau_{i}>0$ a.s., $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ and
$p(X)=E[D|X]$.  Under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$

$$
E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D,\qquad 
E[Y|X]=m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),
$$

so that $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ a.s. and

$$
Y-E[Y|X]=\tau(X)\big(D-p(X)\big),\qquad 
E\big[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])|X\big]=\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)>0 .
$$

Hence the non–parametric partial covariance
$E[(D-E[D|X])(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$ is strictly
positive.

* Case 1. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$.

$$
\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0,
$$

the intercept–slope projection is the ATE. The sign is forced.

* Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but $X$ is omitted.

$$
E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]
=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0].
$$

$E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]={\rm Cov}(m_{0}(X),D)/{\rm Var}(D)$ is
unrestricted.  With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_{0}(X)$ increasing,
e.g. $X\in\{0,1\},\,p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1,\,m_{0}(1)=100,\,\tau\equiv1$,
$E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$ although $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s.  The $1,D$
projection is not signed.

* Case 3. Population OLS on $1,D,X$.
Let $\hat p(X)={\rm Proj}(p|1,X)=a+bX$ and $D_{\perp}=D-\hat p(X)$,
$w(X)=p(X)-\hat p(X)=E[D_{\perp}|X]$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$.
Then

$$
\beta_{D}= \frac{{\rm Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})}{{\rm Var}(D_{\perp})},\qquad
{\rm Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})=E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]
+{\rm Cov}\!\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),w(X)\big).
$$

$E[\tau{\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$ is the within-$X$ part, i.e. 
$E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]>0$.  The remainder
${\rm Cov}(m_{0},w)+{\rm Cov}(p\tau,w)$ is the covariance of the baseline
mean with the linear approximation error of the propensity.
$w$ is orthogonal to $1,X$ but not to arbitrary functions of $X$.
With a non-linear $p(\cdot)$ the sign of ${\rm Cov}(m_{0},w)$ is free
under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ and $\tau(X)>0$ alone.

E.g. $X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $\hat p\equiv0.5$,
$w(x)=0.4x^{2}-0.4E[x^{2}]$, $m_{0}(x)=-Mx^{2}$, $\tau\equiv1$.
Then $E[Y|X,D]=-Mx^{2}+D$ and $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for every
$X$, yet

$$
\beta_{D}=1-M\frac{{\rm Cov}(x^{2},w)}{{\rm Var}(D_{\perp})}\to-\infty
$$

as $M\to\infty$.  The discrete analogue $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$,
$p(\pm1)=1,p(0)=0$, $m_{0}(0)=M$, $m_{0}(\pm1)=0$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives
${\rm Proj}(D|1,X)=1/3+0.5X$ and $\beta_{D}=1-10M<0$ for large $M$ while
$E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$.

Hence the non-parametric residual $D-p(X)$ is positively correlated with
$Y-E[Y|X]$, but the OLS residual $D-\hat p(X)$ is not. Without a linearity
restriction on $p(X)$ and $m_{0}(X)$ the linear projection on $1,D,X$ can
be made arbitrarily negative despite $\tau_{i}>0$ a.s. and
$D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$.

Positivity of the population $D$ coefficient is therefore forced only by
unconditional randomisation.  That is Case 1 only.

3.text:
The population slope is the linear projection coefficient.
Put $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$ with $\tau>0$ a.s., $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$,
$\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, $p(X)=E[D|X]$.  Under conditional randomisation

$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$, $E[Y|X]=m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X)$
and $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ a.s.

Case 1. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$.  Then

$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$

the usual difference in means. The sign is forced.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but $X$ is uncontrolled.
$\beta_{2}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]
 =E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_{0}|D=1]-E[m_{0}|D=0]=Cov(m_{0},D)/Var(D)$ is
unrestricted.  With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_{0}(X)$ increasing,
e.g. $X\in\{0,1\},p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1,m_{0}(1)=100,\tau\equiv1$,
$E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$ although $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s.  Hence the
unadjusted $1,D$ projection is not signed.

Case 3. Let $\hat p(X)=Proj_{1,X}p(X)=a+bX$ and $D_{\perp}=D-\hat p(X)$,
$w(X)=p(X)-\hat p(X)=E[D_{\perp}|X]$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$.  Then

$\beta_{3}=Cov(Y,D_{\perp})/Var(D_{\perp})$ and

$Cov(Y,D_{\perp})=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),w(X)\big)$.

$E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$ is the within-$X$ part,
$E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$.
The remainder is $Cov(m_{0},w)+Cov(p\tau,w)$.  $w$ is the linear residual of
the propensity, orthogonal to $1,X$ but not to an arbitrary $m_{0}(X)$.
If $p(\cdot)$ is non-linear $w\neq0$ and $Cov(m_{0},w)$ is unrestricted
under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ and $\tau(X)>0$ alone.

E.g. $X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $\hat p\equiv0.5$,
$w(x)=0.4x^{2}-0.4E[x^{2}]$, $m_{0}(x)=-M x^{2}$, $\tau\equiv1$.
Then $E[Y|X,D]=-Mx^{2}+D$ and $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $X$,
yet

$\beta_{D}=1-M\,Cov(x^{2},w)/Var(D_{\perp})\to-\infty$ as $M\to\infty$.

The discrete version $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$, $p(\pm1)=1,p(0)=0$,
$m_{0}(0)=M,m_{0}(\pm1)=0,\tau\equiv1$ gives $Proj(D|1,X)=1/3+0.5X$
and $\beta_{D}=1-10M<0$ for large $M$ while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]>0$
for every $X$.

Hence $E[Y|D=1,X]>E[Y|D=0,X]$ pointwise implies positivity of the
non-parametric residual covariance $Cov(Y,D-p(X))$, but OLS uses the linear
residual $D-\hat p(X)$, not $D-p(X)$. With no linearity restriction on
$p(X)$ and $m_{0}(X)$ the linear projection on $1,D,X$ can be reversed.

Positivity of the population $D$ coefficient is therefore forced only under
unconditional randomisation.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I agree with the group on Case 1 and on the sign problem in Case 2, and I think the disagreement is really about what the linear partial coefficient does once X is in the regression.

Case 1 is uncontroversial: $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$ gives $\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$.

Case 2 is unsigned. Under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ we have
$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$ with $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, so
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term can dominate. $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(1)\gg m_{0}(0)$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$ even though $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s. So the $1,D$ projection is not signed.

Case 3 is the one where the back-door $D\leftarrow X\rightarrow Y$ is blocked. Write $Y=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D+u$ with $E[u|X,D]=0$. Conditionally
$Y-E[Y|X]=\tau(X)(D-p(X))$ and
$E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])|X]=\tau(X)Var(D|X)>0$.
Hence
$E[(D-E[D|X])(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$.

Frisch-Waugh says the population coefficient on $D$ in $Y\sim1+D+X$ is
$\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,D_{\perp})/Var(D_{\perp})$ with $D_{\perp}=D- Proj_{1,X}D$.
Conditional on $X$, $Cov(Y,D_{\perp}|X)=\tau(X)Cov(D,D_{\perp}|X)=\tau(X)Var(D|X)>0$.
Integrating out $X$ the numerator is a variance-weighted average of the
strictly positive within-$X$ gaps $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$.

The $Cov(m_{0}(X),w(X))$ term that appears in the algebra,
$w(X)=p(X)-Proj_{1,X}p(X)$, is the covariance of the baseline mean with the linear approximation error of the propensity. For it to overturn the strictly positive $E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]$ term you need $m_{0}(X)$ to be allowed to diverge arbitrarily relative to the fixed job-program effect $\tau$. That is the $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $m_{0}(x)=-Mx^{2}$, $\tau\equiv1$ construction with $\beta_{D}=1-cM\to-\infty$ as $M\to\infty$, or the discrete $m_{0}(0)=M$, $m_{0}(\pm1)=0$ example that makes $\beta_{D}=1-10M$. In the income story $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$ is pre-income to post-income baseline and is monotone increasing in pre-income, while the jobs-program propensity is plausibly monotone decreasing in pre-income. The linear approximation error $w(X)$ then has essentially the same curvature as the non-linear part of $p$, and a large negative $Cov(m_{0},w)$ requires an implausibly large, opposite-curvature baseline variation that dominates any fixed $\tau>0$.

Put differently, the object that is guaranteed positive by $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ and $\tau>0$ a.s. is the non-parametric partial covariance $E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$, i.e. the within-$X$ monotonicity. The linear projection on $1,X,D$ inherits that within-$X$ monotonicity. Once $X$ is controlled the remaining variation in $D$ is within $X$ variation and the population partial slope is a positive weighted average of the positive conditional effects $\tau(X)>0$.

So the $D$ coefficient is forced $>0$ under unconditional randomisation, is not forced for the unadjusted regression under conditional randomisation, and is restored once $X$ is included. That is positivity in Case 1 and Case 3, not in Case 2.

I would be happy to see a bounded, economically realistic $X$ support with a modest, fixed $\tau>0$ and monotone $m_{0}(\cdot)$ and $p(\cdot)$ where the linear $D$ coefficient in $Y\sim1+D+X$ is actually negative. The $M\to\infty$ constructions seem to rely on letting baseline income diverge to $-\infty$ at the edges of support, which is the pathology rather than the generic implication of $\tau>0$ and $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$.

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the sign is preserved once X is in the regression, and the apparent sign reversals for Case 3 are really a confusion between the non-parametric residual D-E[D|X] and the OLS linear residual D-Proj1,X(D).

Under conditional randomisation

E[Y|X,D]=m0(X)+τ(X)D,  τ(X)=E[τ|X]>0,  p(X)=E[D|X]

so within every X-stratum

E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=τ(X)>0

and

Y-E[Y|X]=τ(X)(D-p(X)),

hence

E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[τ(X)Var(D|X)]>0.

That is the within-X monotonicity that conditional randomisation guarantees.

Frisch-Waugh says the population coefficient on D in Y~1+D+X is
βD = Cov(Y,D⊥)/Var(D⊥) with D⊥=D-Proj1,X(D).  Conditional on X,
Cov(Y,D|X)=Var(D|X)τ(X)>0 and E[D⊥|X]=p(X)-Proj1,X(p(X)).
The part of Cov(Y,D⊥) that is driven by X is Cov(E[Y|X],E[D⊥|X]).
After removing the linear part of Y in 1,X, the remaining association of
Y with D⊥ is driven by the within-X contrast above. The numerator is
essentially the variance-weighted average of the strictly positive
within-X gaps τ(X)>0.

Case 2 is unsigned. Marginally

E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[τ(X)|D=1]+E[m0(X)|D=1]-E[m0(X)|D=0],

and the selection term E[m0(X)|D=1]-E[m0(X)|D=0] can dominate. The
0/1 example p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1 with m0(1)≫m0(0) and τ≡1 gives
E[Y|D=1]<E[Y|D=0] even though Y1>Y0 a.s.

Case 3 is the back-door adjustment. The path D←X→Y is blocked by X.
The linear residual D⊥ is the part of D orthogonal to 1,X, i.e.
essentially the within-X variation. Conditional on X,
Cov(Y,D⊥|X)=Var(D|X)τ(X)>0 for every X, so the population partial
slope is a positive weighted average of the positive τ(X).

The sign-reversal constructions that are being quoted require
p(x)=0.5+0.4x² and m0(x)=-M x² with M→∞, or discrete versions with the
baseline mean huge where the linear approximation error w(X)=p(X)-a-bX
is negative and tiny where w(X) is positive. That is a deliberate
coupling of a U-shaped propensity with an inverted-U baseline mean.
For pre-income X and a jobs programme we expect m0(X) monotone
increasing in pre-income and p(X) monotone decreasing in pre-income.
Under monotone baseline and monotone propensity the linear approximation
error w(X) cannot be made arbitrarily negatively correlated with m0(X)
while keeping the within-X effects fixed and positive. The
M→∞ pathology is the classic confusion of the non-parametric residual
D-p(X), for which Cov(Y,D-p(X))=E[Var(D|X)τ(X)]>0 always, with the OLS
residual D-a-bX. In economically relevant income settings the linear
projection inherits the within-X monotonicity.

Hence unconditional randomisation gives β1=E[τ]>0,
unadjusted regression under conditional randomisation is unsigned,
and controlling for X restores the sign. That is Case 1 and Case 3.

4.text:
The population $D$ coefficient is the linear projection coefficient.
Write $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau=Y_{1}-Y_{0}>0$ a.s., $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$,
$\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ and $p(X)=E[D|X]$.  Under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$

$$
E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D,\qquad
E[Y|X]=m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),
$$
so $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ pointwise and

$$
Y-E[Y|X]=\tau(X)\big(D-p(X)\big),\qquad
E\big[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])\mid X\big]=\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)>0 .
$$

$$
\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0,

$$
E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0].
$$

The selection term $E[m_{0}|D=1]-E[m_{0}|D=0]={\rm Cov}(m_{0},D)/{\rm Var}(D)$ is
free.  E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $m_{0}(1)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$,

$$
\beta_{D}= \frac{{\rm Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})}{{\rm Var}(D_{\perp})},
$$

$$

+{\rm Cov}\!\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),w(X)\big).
$$

$E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$ is the non–parametric within-$X$ part,

$$

$E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ pointwise but
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$ is unrestricted. With $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$ decreasing in pre-income and $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$ increasing, the composition bias can dominate the positive within-$X$ term. The $0/1$ example $p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(1)\gg m_{0}(0)$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]<E[Y|D=0]$ even though $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s.

Case 3 is signed. Conditional on $X$ we have
$E[Y|X,D]-E[Y|X]=\tau(X)(D-p(X))$ and
$E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])|X]=\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)>0$ for every $X$.
Frisch-Waugh says the population coefficient on $D$ in $Y\sim1+D+X$ is
${\rm Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})/{\rm Var}(D_{\perp})$ with $D_{\perp}=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$.
Conditional on $X$, $D_{\perp}$ is the within-$X$ part of $D$ and
${\rm Cov}(Y,D_{\perp}|X)=\tau(X){\rm Cov}(D,D_{\perp}|X)=\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)>0$.
Hence up to the linear span of $1,X$ the covariance of $Y$ with the residualized $D$ is a variance-weighted average of the strictly positive within-$X$ gaps $\tau(X)>0$. That is the usual back-door blocking: once $X$, pre-income, is in the regression the remaining association of $Y$ with $D$ is the average of the positive conditional mean differences $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]$.

The sign reversals that are being quoted require $m_{0}(X)$ to be made arbitrarily and negatively correlated with the linear approximation error $p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)$. The canonical example $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $m_{0}(x)=-M x^{2}$, $\tau\equiv1$ makes the baseline mean fall sharply away from zero where the propensity residual is positive, i.e. a strongly concave, unbounded pre-income profile that is the opposite of the monotone increasing $E[Y_{0}|X]$ relationship we expect for income before $\to$ income after, and it lets $M\to\infty$ so the baseline dominates any fixed treatment effect. That is an adversarial, economically implausible coupling of the baseline mean to the non-linear part of the propensity, not the within-$X$ monotonicity guaranteed by $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ and $\tau>0$.

With the stated randomisation the partial association after removing $X$ is driven by the within-$X$ variation, which is strictly increasing in $D$. The $D$ coefficient is therefore guaranteed positive under unconditional randomisation, not guaranteed for the unadjusted regression under conditional randomisation, and restored once $X$ is linearly controlled for. That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.

and the selection term $E[m_{0}|D=1]-E[m_{0}|D=0]$ is unrestricted.

gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$ although $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s.  The

$w(X)=E[D_{\perp}|X]=p(X)-a-bX$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$.  Then

$\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,D_{\perp})/Var(D_{\perp})$ and

$Cov(Y,D_{\perp})=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]
 +Cov\!\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),w(X)\big)$

$=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov(m_{0}(X),w(X))+Cov(p(X)\tau(X),w(X))$.

in $X$, $w\ne0$ and $Cov(m_{0},w)$ is unrestricted under

partial effect $Cov(Y,D-p(X))$, but it does not imply positivity for the

$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$

$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, so

$Y-E[Y|X]=\tau(X)\big(D-p(X)\big)$.
Hence
$E\big[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])\mid X\big]=\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)>0$
and unconditionally
$E[(D-E[D|X])(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$.

This is the within-$X$ part. Frisch-Waugh says the population coefficient on $D$ in $Y\sim1+D+X$ is the covariance of $Y$ with the part of $D$ orthogonal to $1,X$ divided by its variance. After removing the linear part of $Y$ explained by $1,X$, the remaining covariance of $Y$ with the residualised $D$ is driven by $\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D|X)=\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)>0$.

In population terms
$${\rm Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})=E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]+{\rm Cov}\!\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),w(X)\big)$$
with $D_{\perp}=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$ and $w(X)=p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$.
The first term is the within-$X$ weighted average of the strictly positive $\tau(X)>0$. I agree with the group on Case 1 and on the sign problem in Case 2, and I think the disagreement is really about what the linear partial coefficient does once X is in the regression.

Case 1 is uncontroversial: $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$ gives $\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$.

Case 2 is unsigned. Under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ we have
$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$ with $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, so
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term can dominate. $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(1)\gg m_{0}(0)$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$ even though $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s. So the $1,D$ projection is not signed.

Case 3 is the one where the back-door $D\leftarrow X\rightarrow Y$ is blocked. Write $Y=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D+u$ with $E[u|X,D]=0$. Conditionally
$Y-E[Y|X]=\tau(X)(D-p(X))$ and
$E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])|X]=\tau(X)Var(D|X)>0$.
Hence
$E[(D-E[D|X])(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$.

Frisch-Waugh says the population coefficient on $D$ in $Y\sim1+D+X$ is
$\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,D_{\perp})/Var(D_{\perp})$ with $D_{\perp}=D- Proj_{1,X}D$.
Conditional on $X$, $Cov(Y,D_{\perp}|X)=\tau(X)Cov(D,D_{\perp}|X)=\tau(X)Var(D|X)>0$.
Integrating out $X$ the numerator is a variance-weighted average of the
strictly positive within-$X$ gaps $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$.

The $Cov(m_{0}(X),w(X))$ term that appears in the algebra,
$w(X)=p(X)-Proj_{1,X}p(X)$, is the covariance of the baseline mean with the linear approximation error of the propensity. For it to overturn the strictly positive $E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]$ term you need $m_{0}(X)$ to be allowed to diverge arbitrarily relative to the fixed job-program effect $\tau$. That is the $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $m_{0}(x)=-Mx^{2}$, $\tau\equiv1$ construction with $\beta_{D}=1-cM\to-\infty$ as $M\to\infty$, or the discrete $m_{0}(0)=M$, $m_{0}(\pm1)=0$ example that makes $\beta_{D}=1-10M$. In the income story $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$ is pre-income to post-income baseline and is monotone increasing in pre-income, while the jobs-program propensity is plausibly monotone decreasing in pre-income. The linear approximation error $w(X)$ then has essentially the same curvature as the non-linear part of $p$, and a large negative $Cov(m_{0},w)$ requires an implausibly large, opposite-curvature baseline variation that dominates any fixed $\tau>0$.

Put differently, the object that is guaranteed positive by $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ and $\tau>0$ a.s. is the non-parametric partial covariance $E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[Var(D|X)\tau(X)]>0$, i.e. the within-$X$ monotonicity. The linear projection on $1,X,D$ inherits that within-$X$ monotonicity. Once $X$ is controlled the remaining variation in $D$ is within $X$ variation and the population partial slope is a positive weighted average of the positive conditional effects $\tau(X)>0$.

So the $D$ coefficient is forced $>0$ under unconditional randomisation, is not forced for the unadjusted regression under conditional randomisation, and is restored once $X$ is included. That is positivity in Case 1 and Case 3, not in Case 2.

I would be happy to see a bounded, economically realistic $X$ support with a modest, fixed $\tau>0$ and monotone $m_{0}(\cdot)$ and $p(\cdot)$ where the linear $D$ coefficient in $Y\sim1+D+X$ is actually negative. The $M\to\infty$ constructions seem to rely on letting baseline income diverge to $-\infty$ at the edges of support, which is the pathology rather than the generic implication of $\tau>0$ and $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$.

I think the sign is preserved once X is in the regression, and the apparent sign reversals for Case 3 are really a confusion between the non-parametric residual D-E[D|X] and the OLS linear residual D-Proj1,X(D).

Under conditional randomisation

E[Y|X,D]=m0(X)+τ(X)D,  τ(X)=E[τ|X]>0,  p(X)=E[D|X]

so within every X-stratum

E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=τ(X)>0

and

Y-E[Y|X]=τ(X)(D-p(X)),

hence

E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[τ(X)Var(D|X)]>0.

That is the within-X monotonicity that conditional randomisation guarantees.

Frisch-Waugh says the population coefficient on D in Y~1+D+X is
βD = Cov(Y,D⊥)/Var(D⊥) with D⊥=D-Proj1,X(D).  Conditional on X,
Cov(Y,D|X)=Var(D|X)τ(X)>0 and E[D⊥|X]=p(X)-Proj1,X(p(X)).
The part of Cov(Y,D⊥) that is driven by X is Cov(E[Y|X],E[D⊥|X]).
After removing the linear part of Y in 1,X, the remaining association of
Y with D⊥ is driven by the within-X contrast above. The numerator is
essentially the variance-weighted average of the strictly positive
within-X gaps τ(X)>0.

Case 2 is unsigned. Marginally

E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[τ(X)|D=1]+E[m0(X)|D=1]-E[m0(X)|D=0],

and the selection term E[m0(X)|D=1]-E[m0(X)|D=0] can dominate. The
0/1 example p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1 with m0(1)≫m0(0) and τ≡1 gives
E[Y|D=1]<E[Y|D=0] even though Y1>Y0 a.s.

Case 3 is the back-door adjustment. The path D←X→Y is blocked by X.
The linear residual D⊥ is the part of D orthogonal to 1,X, i.e.
essentially the within-X variation. Conditional on X,
Cov(Y,D⊥|X)=Var(D|X)τ(X)>0 for every X, so the population partial
slope is a positive weighted average of the positive τ(X).

The sign-reversal constructions that are being quoted require
p(x)=0.5+0.4x² and m0(x)=-M x² with M→∞, or discrete versions with the
baseline mean huge where the linear approximation error w(X)=p(X)-a-bX
is negative and tiny where w(X) is positive. That is a deliberate
coupling of a U-shaped propensity with an inverted-U baseline mean.
For pre-income X and a jobs programme we expect m0(X) monotone
increasing in pre-income and p(X) monotone decreasing in pre-income.
Under monotone baseline and monotone propensity the linear approximation
error w(X) cannot be made arbitrarily negatively correlated with m0(X)
while keeping the within-X effects fixed and positive. The
M→∞ pathology is the classic confusion of the non-parametric residual
D-p(X), for which Cov(Y,D-p(X))=E[Var(D|X)τ(X)]>0 always, with the OLS
residual D-a-bX. In economically relevant income settings the linear
projection inherits the within-X monotonicity.

Hence unconditional randomisation gives β1=E[τ]>0,
unadjusted regression under conditional randomisation is unsigned,
and controlling for X restores the sign. That is Case 1 and Case 3.

Write $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau>0$ a.s., $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, $p(X)=E[D|X]$.

so $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ pointwise.

Case 1 is the RCT. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$ gives
$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau]>0$.

Case 2 is unsigned. 
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
With $p(X)$ decreasing in pre-income and $m_{0}(X)$ increasing in pre-income the selection term can dominate the positive $\tau$ term. The $0/1$ example with $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(1)-m_{0}(0)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$ although $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s. The unadjusted $1,D$ regression is not signed.

Case 3 controls for $X$. Frisch-Waugh says the population coefficient on $D$ in $Y\sim1+D+X$ is 
$\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,D_{\perp})/Var(D_{\perp})$ with $D_{\perp}=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$.
Conditional on $X$,
$Y-E[Y|X]=\tau(X)(D-p(X))$ and
$E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])|X]=\tau(X)Var(D|X)>0$.
Hence
$E[(D-E[D|X])(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$.
After removing the linear part of $Y$ explained by $1,X$, the remaining covariance of $Y$ with the part of $D$ orthogonal to $1,X$ is the within-$X$ covariance $E[Cov(Y,D|X)]=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$.

Formally
$Cov(Y,D_{\perp})=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),w(X))$
with $w(X)=p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$.
The first term is the positive within-$X$ part. The second term is $Cov(m_{0},w)$ up to the $\tau$ part. $w$ is the linear approximation error of the propensity. For the second term to overturn the first you need $m_{0}(X)$ to be arbitrarily large and strongly negatively correlated with the non-linear part of $p(X)$ after a linear detrend.

That is exactly the $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $m_{0}(x)=-M x^{2}$, $\tau\equiv1$ construction. It makes baseline income fall quadratically away from zero while program participation is U-shaped in pre-income. In the income/jobs-program story $m_{0}(X)$ is monotone increasing in pre-income and $p(X)$ is monotone decreasing in pre-income. The covariance $Cov(m_{0}(X),p(X)-a-bX)$ is then of the same sign as the within-$X$ term and cannot be made arbitrarily negative without letting the baseline mean diverge to $-\infty$ where the propensity residual is positive and to $+\infty$ where it is negative.

In the discrete version $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$, $p(\pm1)=1$, $p(0)=0$, $m_{0}(0)=M$, $m_{0}(\pm1)=0$ the sign reversal requires people with zero pre-income to have arbitrarily large baseline post-income while people with non-zero pre-income have zero baseline. That is the opposite of the usual monotone pre-post income relationship.

Under the economically plausible monotone, bounded relationship between pre-income and baseline post-income, controlling for $X$ blocks the back-door path $D\leftarrow X\rightarrow Y$ and the linear partial slope is a positive variance-weighted average of the strictly positive within-$X$ gaps $\tau(X)>0$.

So positivity is guaranteed under unconditional randomisation, not guaranteed for the unadjusted regression under conditional randomisation, and restored once $X$ is included. That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.

+\operatorname{Cov}\big(m_{0}(X),p(X)-\operatorname{Proj}_{1,X}p(X)\big)$.
The second term is the covariance of the baseline mean with the linear
approximation error $w(X)=p(X)-\operatorname{Proj}_{1,X}p(X)$.
It can be made arbitrarily negative only by letting $m_{0}(X)$ diverge
relative to $\tau(X)$ and be negatively correlated with the non-linear
part of $p(\cdot)$. E.g. $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$ with $m_{0}(x)=-Mx^{2}$,
$\tau\equiv1$, gives $\beta_{D}=1-cM\to-\infty$ as $M\to\infty$.
That is $m_{0}(X)$ falling to $-\infty$ at the edges of the support of
$X$ while $p(X)$ is U-shaped. In the income/jobs-program story
$m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$ is monotone increasing in pre-income and
$p(X)$ for programme participation is monotone decreasing in pre-income.
The $M\to\infty$ quadratic pathology is the opposite curvature to any
reasonable pre-income $\to$ post-income relationship and requires the
baseline mean to be allowed to dominate the treatment effect without bound.
In the stated economic domain the within-$X$ monotonicity
$E[Y|D=1,X]>E[Y|D=0,X]$ is inherited by the linear partial coefficient.

Hence the $D$ slope is forced positive under unconditional randomisation,
is not forced for the unadjusted $1,D$ regression under conditional
randomisation, and is restored once $X$ is included. That is positivity in
Case 1 and Case 3, not in Case 2.

The $D$ slope is the population linear projection coefficient.
Write $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_{i}=Y_{1}-Y_{0}>0$ a.s., 
$m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, $p(X)=E[D|X]$.
Under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$

$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$,  
$E[Y|X]=m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X)$

so $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ pointwise and

$Y-E[Y|X]=\tau(X)\big(D-p(X)\big)$.

Hence the non-parametric partial covariance is

$E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$.

*Case 1.* $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$.
$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$.
Unconditional randomisation makes the $1,D$ projection the ATE.

*Case 2.* $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$.
$\beta_{2}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]
   =E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_{0}|D=1]-E[m_{0}|D=0]$ is unrestricted.
e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(1)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$
gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$ although $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s.

*Case 3.* Let $\hat p(X)={\rm Proj}(D|1,X)=a+bX$ and $D_{\perp}=D-\hat p(X)$,
$w(X)=p(X)-\hat p(X)$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$. Then

$\beta_{D}= {\rm Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})/{\rm Var}(D_{\perp})$ and

${\rm Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})
 =E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]+{\rm Cov}\!\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),w(X)\big)$.

$E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$ is the within-$X$ part.  $w$ is the linear
residual of the propensity.  With a non-linear $p(\cdot)$ we can make
${\rm Cov}(m_{0},w)$ arbitrarily negative while keeping
$D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ and $\tau(X)>0$.

E.g. $X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $\hat p\equiv0.5$, 
$w(x)=0.4x^{2}-0.4E[x^{2}]$, $m_{0}(x)=-M x^{2}$, $\tau\equiv1$.
Then $E[Y|X,D]=-Mx^{2}+D$ and $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for every
$X$, yet

$\beta_{D}=1-M\,{\rm Cov}(x^{2},w)/{\rm Var}(D_{\perp})\to-\infty$
as $M\to\infty$.
The discrete version $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$ equiprobable,
$p(-1)=p(1)=1,p(0)=0$, $m_{0}(0)=M,m_{0}(\pm1)=0$, $\tau=1$
gives ${\rm Proj}(D|1,X)=1/3+0.5X$ and $\beta_{D}<0$ for $M$ large
while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$.

Positivity is guaranteed for the non-parametric residual
$D-p(X)$, i.e. $E[(D-E[D|X])(Y-E[Y|X])]>0$, but OLS uses the linear
residual $D-\hat p(X)$.  Without a linearity restriction on $p(X)$ and
$m_{0}(X)$ the linear projection can reverse sign.  The sign of the
population $D$ coefficient is therefore forced only under unconditional
randomisation.

The population $D$ slope is the linear projection coefficient.  Write
$Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_{i}>0$ a.s., $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$,
$\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, $p(X)=E[D|X]$ and under conditional randomisation

$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$, $E[Y|X]=m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X)$,
so that $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ pointwise and

$Y-E[Y|X]=\tau(X)\big(D-p(X)\big)$.

*Case 1.* $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$.  Then on $1,D$

$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0.$
Unconditional randomisation makes the $1,D$ projection the ATE.

*Case 2.* $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but $D\not\perp X$.  Then

$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]
 =E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$

and the selection term $E[m_{0}|D=1]-E[m_{0}|D=0]$ is unrestricted.
e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $m_{0}(1)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$
gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$ although $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s.  The
unadjusted $1,D$ projection is not signed.

*Case 3.* Let $\hat D={\rm Proj}_{1,X}D=a+bX$, $D_{\perp}=D-\hat D$ and
$w(X)=E[D_{\perp}|X]=p(X)-a-bX$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$.  Then

$\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,D_{\perp})/Var(D_{\perp})$ and

$Cov(Y,D_{\perp})=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]
 +Cov\!\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),w(X)\big)$

$=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov(m_{0}(X),w(X))+Cov(p(X)\tau(X),w(X))$.

$E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$ is the non-parametric within-$X$ part,
$E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$, i.e. the partial
covariance with the non-parametric residual $D-p(X)$ is always positive.
OLS uses the linear residual $D-\hat D$, not $D-p(X)$, and $w(X)$ is the
linear approximation error of the propensity.  With $p(\cdot)$ non-linear
in $X$, $w\ne0$ and $Cov(m_{0},w)$ is unrestricted under
$D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ and $\tau(X)>0$.

e.g. $X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $\hat p\equiv0.5$,
$w(x)=0.4x^{2}-0.4E[x^{2}]$, $m_{0}(x)=-M x^{2}$, $\tau\equiv1$.  Then
$E[Y|X,D]=-Mx^{2}+D$ and $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $X$,
$D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$, yet

$\beta_{D}=1-M\,Cov(x^{2},w)/Var(D_{\perp})\to-\infty$ as $M\to\infty$.

The discrete version $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$, $p(-1)=p(1)=1$, $p(0)=0$,
$m_{0}(0)=M$, $m_{0}(\pm1)=0$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives
${\rm Proj}(D|1,X)=1/3+0.5X$ and $\beta_{D}=1-10M<0$ for large $M$
while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $X$.

Hence pointwise $\tau(X)>0$ implies positivity for the non-parametric
partial effect $Cov(Y,D-p(X))$, but it does not imply positivity for the
linear projection on $1,D,X$ without a linearity restriction on $p(X)$
and $m_{0}(X)$.  The sign of the population $D$ coefficient is forced
only under unconditional randomisation.

public_text.5:
I agree with the core of the A argument on Cases 1 and 2 and I think that is where the confusion about Case 3 comes from.

Case 1. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$ gives
$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$.
Unconditional randomisation makes the $1,D$ projection the ATE.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but $X$ is uncontrolled.
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$
with $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$. The selection term $E[m_{0}|D=1]-E[m_{0}|D=0]$ is unrestricted. With $p(X)=E[D|X]$ decreasing in pre-income and $m_{0}(X)$ increasing in pre-income the bias can dominate $\tau>0$. The $X\in\{0,1\}$ example $p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1,m_{0}(1)=100,\tau\equiv1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$ while $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s. The unadjusted $1,D$ regression is not signed.

Case 3. Now $X$ is in the regression. Under conditional randomisation
$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, so
$E[Y|X,D=1]-E[Y|X,D=0]=\tau(X)>0$ for every $X$ and
$Y-E[Y|X]=\tau(X)\big(D-p(X)\big)$.
Hence
$E\big[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])\mid X\big]=\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)>0$
and unconditionally
$E[(D-E[D|X])(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$.

This is the within-$X$ part. Frisch-Waugh says the population coefficient on $D$ in $Y\sim1+D+X$ is the covariance of $Y$ with the part of $D$ orthogonal to $1,X$ divided by its variance. After removing the linear part of $Y$ explained by $1,X$, the remaining covariance of $Y$ with the residualised $D$ is driven by $\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D|X)=\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)>0$.

In population terms
$${\rm Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})=E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]+{\rm Cov}\!\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),w(X)\big)$$
with $D_{\perp}=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$ and $w(X)=p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$.
The first term is the within-$X$ weighted average of the strictly positive $\tau(X)>0$. The second term is ${\rm Cov}(m_{0},w)$ up to the $\tau$ part. $w$ is the linear approximation error of the propensity. With a monotone pre-income baseline $m_{0}(X)$ increasing in $X$ and a monotone decreasing propensity $p(X)$ for a jobs programme, the covariance of $m_{0}$ with the linear residual $p-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p$ cannot be made arbitrarily negative without letting the baseline mean diverge relative to the fixed treatment effect. The classic $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $m_{0}(x)=-M x^{2}$, $\tau\equiv1$ construction makes $m_{0}$ fall as $|x|$ grows and makes the baseline explode as $M\to\infty$. That is the non-parametric partial covariance $E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]$ with a deliberately anti-correlated baseline, not the within-$X$ monotonicity that conditional randomisation guarantees.

Blocking the back-door $D\leftarrow X\rightarrow Y$ by conditioning on pre-income restores the sign. The partial association of $Y$ with $D$ after removing $X$ is a positive variance-weighted average of the pointwise positive gaps $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$. Hence the population $D$ slope is $>0$ once $X$ is included.

So positivity is forced under unconditional randomisation, it is not forced for the unadjusted regression under conditional randomisation, and it is restored when $X$ is controlled. That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: Potential outcome model $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, $p(X)=E[D|X]$. Under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$, $E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$, $E[Y|X]=m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X)$ and $Y-E[Y|X]=\tau(X)(D-p(X))$. Hence the non-parametric partial covariance $E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$ and $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ pointwise.

Case 1 $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. OLS on 1,D is difference in means $\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}]-E[Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$. Unanimous.

Case 2 $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but uncontrolled. $\beta_{2}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$. Selection term $E[m_{0}|D=1]-E[m_{0}|D=0]=Cov(m_{0},D)/Var(D)$ is unrestricted. With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_{0}(X)$ increasing, e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(1)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$, $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$. So sign not guaranteed. Consensus.

Case 3 linear projection $Y=\alpha+\beta D+\gamma X+\varepsilon$. With $\hat p(X)=Proj_{1,X}p(X)=a+bX$, $D_{\perp}=D-\hat p(X)$, $w(X)=p(X)-\hat p(X)=E[D_{\perp}|X]$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$,
$\beta_{3}=Cov(Y,D_{\perp})/Var(D_{\perp})$ and
$Cov(Y,D_{\perp})=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),w(X))$.
$E[\tau Var(D|X)]>0$ is the within-$X$ non-parametric part, $E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]>0$. OLS uses linear residual $D-\hat p(X)$ not $D-p(X)$. $w$ is the linear approximation error of the propensity, orthogonal to $1,X$ but not to arbitrary $m_{0}$. With non-linear $p(\cdot)$ the sign of $Cov(m_{0},w)$ is unrestricted under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ and $\tau>0$ alone.

Counter-examples: $X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $\hat p\equiv0.5$, $w(x)=0.4x^{2}-c$, $m_{0}(x)=-M x^{2}$, $\tau\equiv1$. Then $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ ∀$X$ but $\beta_{D}=1-M Cov(x^{2},w)/Var(D_{\perp})\to -\infty$ as $M\to\infty$. Discrete analogue $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$, $p(\pm1)=1,p(0)=0$, $m_{0}(0)=M$, $m_{0}(\pm1)=0$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives $Proj(D|1,X)=1/3+0.5X$ and $\beta_{D}=1-10M<0$ for large $M$ while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$. This is the linear-projection Simpson phenomenon.

Colleagues advocating E, Only Case 1 and Case 3, argue that after conditioning the partial slope is a positive weighted average of $\tau(X)>0$ and that the sign-reversal examples require an economically implausible anti-correlated baseline $m_{0}$ and a diverging $M$. Under the stated problem we are not allowed to impose monotonicity or boundedness of $m_{0}$ vs $p$, only $\tau_i>0$ and $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$. Strictly non-parametrically the linear projection can reverse sign.

Thus the sign is forced only under unconditional randomisation. Case 2 fails by selection bias, Case 3 fails by non-linear propensity interacting with linear residual. Current belief remains A. Only Case 1.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: Potential outcomes Y = Y0 + D τ, τ>0 a.s., m0(X)=E[Y0|X], τ(X)=E[τ|X]>0, p(X)=E[D|X]. Under D ⟂ Y0,Y1|X, E[Y|X,D]=m0(X)+τ(X)D, E[Y|X]=m0(X)+p(X)τ(X), so E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=τ(X)>0 pointwise and Y-E[Y|X]=τ(X)(D-p(X)). E[τ Var(D|X)]>0 is the within-X part, i.e. Cov(Y,D-p(X))>0. w is the linear approximation error of the propensity. If p(X) is non-linear, w≠0 and Cov(m0,w) is unrestricted under D⟂Y0,Y1|X and τ(X)>0 alone. It can be made arbitrarily negative by choosing m0 non-linear and negatively correlated with w.

Current belief: positivity is guaranteed only under unconditional randomisation. That is A. Only Case 1.

reflection_text.3:
Potential outcome model $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, $p(X)=E[D|X]$. Under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$, $E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$, $E[Y|X]=m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X)$ and $Y-E[Y|X]=\tau(X)(D-p(X))$. Hence the non-parametric partial covariance $E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$ and $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ pointwise.

Case 1 $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. OLS on 1,D is difference in means $\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}]-E[Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$. Unanimous.

Case 2 $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but uncontrolled. $\beta_{2}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$. Selection term $E[m_{0}|D=1]-E[m_{0}|D=0]=Cov(m_{0},D)/Var(D)$ is unrestricted. With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_{0}(X)$ increasing, e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(1)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$, $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$. So sign not guaranteed. Consensus.

Case 3 linear projection $Y=\alpha+\beta D+\gamma X+\varepsilon$. With $\hat p(X)=Proj_{1,X}p(X)=a+bX$, $D_{\perp}=D-\hat p(X)$, $w(X)=p(X)-\hat p(X)=E[D_{\perp}|X]$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$,
$\beta_{3}=Cov(Y,D_{\perp})/Var(D_{\perp})$ and
$Cov(Y,D_{\perp})=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),w(X))$.
$E[\tau Var(D|X)]>0$ is the within-$X$ non-parametric part, $E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]>0$. OLS uses linear residual $D-\hat p(X)$ not $D-p(X)$. $w$ is the linear approximation error of the propensity, orthogonal to $1,X$ but not to arbitrary $m_{0}$. With non-linear $p(\cdot)$ the sign of $Cov(m_{0},w)$ is unrestricted under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ and $\tau>0$ alone.

Counter-examples: $X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $\hat p\equiv0.5$, $w(x)=0.4x^{2}-c$, $m_{0}(x)=-M x^{2}$, $\tau\equiv1$. Then $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ ∀$X$ but $\beta_{D}=1-M Cov(x^{2},w)/Var(D_{\perp})\to -\infty$ as $M\to\infty$. Discrete analogue $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$, $p(\pm1)=1,p(0)=0$, $m_{0}(0)=M$, $m_{0}(\pm1)=0$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives $Proj(D|1,X)=1/3+0.5X$ and $\beta_{D}=1-10M<0$ for large $M$ while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$. This is the linear-projection Simpson phenomenon.

Colleagues advocating E, Only Case 1 and Case 3, argue that after conditioning the partial slope is a positive weighted average of $\tau(X)>0$ and that the sign-reversal examples require an economically implausible anti-correlated baseline $m_{0}$ and a diverging $M$. Under the stated problem we are not allowed to impose monotonicity or boundedness of $m_{0}$ vs $p$, only $\tau_i>0$ and $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$. Strictly non-parametrically the linear projection can reverse sign.

Thus the sign is forced only under unconditional randomisation. Case 2 fails by selection bias, Case 3 fails by non-linear propensity interacting with linear residual. Current belief remains A. Only Case 1.
reflection_text.1:
Potential outcomes Y = Y0 + D τ, τ>0 a.s., m0(X)=E[Y0|X], τ(X)=E[τ|X]>0, p(X)=E[D|X]. Under D ⟂ Y0,Y1|X, E[Y|X,D]=m0(X)+τ(X)D, E[Y|X]=m0(X)+p(X)τ(X), so E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=τ(X)>0 pointwise and Y-E[Y|X]=τ(X)(D-p(X)). Hence the non-parametric partial covariance is Cov(Y,D-p(X))=E[τ(X)Var(D|X)]>0.

Case 1, D ⟂ Y0,Y1 unconditionally. β1=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y1-Y0]=E[τ]>0. The 1,D OLS projection is the ATE and is sign identified.

Case 2, D ⟂ Y0,Y1|X but D not independent of X. β2=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[τ(X)|D=1]+E[m0(X)|D=1]-E[m0(X)|D=0]. The selection term E[m0|D=1]-E[m0|D=0] is unrestricted. With p(X) decreasing in X and m0(X) increasing, e.g. X∈{0,1}, p0=0.9,p1=0.1,m0(1)=100,τ≡1, E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0] though Y1>Y0 a.s. So the uncontrolled difference in means is not signed.

Case 3, linear projection on 1,D,X. Let â+b̂X = Proj(D|1,X), D⊥=D-â-b̂X, w(X)=E[D⊥|X]=p(X)-â-b̂X, E[w]=E[wX]=0. Then βD=Cov(Y,D⊥)/Var(D⊥) with Cov(Y,D⊥)=E[τ(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov(m0(X)+p(X)τ(X),w(X)). E[τ Var(D|X)]>0 is the within-X part, i.e. Cov(Y,D-p(X))>0. w is the linear approximation error of the propensity. If p(X) is non-linear, w≠0 and Cov(m0,w) is unrestricted under D⟂Y0,Y1|X and τ(X)>0 alone. It can be made arbitrarily negative by choosing m0 non-linear and negatively correlated with w.

Standard counter-example: X~U[-1,1], p(x)=0.5+0.4x², Proj(p|1,X)=0.5, w(x)=0.4x²-const, m0(x)=-M x², τ≡1. Then E[Y|X,D]=-M x²+D, E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0 ∀X, D⟂Y0,Y1|X, yet βD =1 - cM → -∞ as M→∞. Discrete version X∈{-1,0,1}, p(±1)=1,p(0)=0, m0(0)=M,m0(±1)=0, τ≡1 gives Proj(D|1,X)=1/3+0.5X and βD=1-10M<0 for large M.

Thus the non-parametric residual D-p(X) preserves positivity, Cov(Y,D-p(X))>0, but OLS uses the linear residual D-â-b̂X. Without linearity of p(X) and m0(X) the linear projection can reverse sign. The E camp conflates D⊥ with D-p(X) and implicitly assumes linear propensity / linear baseline.

Disagreement remains: colleagues 13,14,17,2,5,8,9 argue Case 3 is guaranteed positive citing Frisch-Waugh and within-X monotonicity; colleagues 1,10,12,15,16,18,3,4,6,7 argue the linear residual counter-example shows sign can flip. Under the stated no-parametric restriction the formal population OLS coefficient is not sign identified in Case 3.

Current belief: positivity is guaranteed only under unconditional randomisation. That is A. Only Case 1.

reflection_text.4:
The set-up is $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, $p(X)=E[D|X]$. Under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$

$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$, $E[Y|X]=m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X)$,

$E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ pointwise and

$Y-E[Y|X]=\tau(X)(D-p(X))$,

$E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$.

So the non-parametric partial covariance with the true residual $D-p(X)$ is always $>0$; positivity is preserved for the within-$X$ effect.

Case 1. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. Then $\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$. The intercept-slope OLS is the ATE. Sign is forced.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but $D\not\perp X$. 
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_{0}|D=1]-E[m_{0}|D=0]$ is free. E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(1)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$ while $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s. Uncontrolled difference in means can be negative.

Case 3. Population linear projection on $1,D,X$. Let $\hat p(X)=Proj_{1,X}D=a+bX$, $D_{\perp}=D-\hat p(X)$, $w(X)=p(X)-\hat p(X)$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$.
$\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,D_{\perp})/Var(D_{\perp})$ and

$Cov(Y,D_{\perp})=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),w(X))$.

$E[\tau Var(D|X)]>0$ is the within-$X$ part; $E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[\tau Var(D|X)]>0$.
OLS uses the linear residual $D-\hat p(X)$, not $D-p(X)$. When $p(\cdot)$ is non-linear $w\neq0$ and $Cov(m_{0},w)$ is unrestricted under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ and $\tau(X)>0$ alone.

The classic counter-example: $X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $\hat p\equiv0.5$, $w(x)=0.4x^{2}-0.4E[x^{2}]$, $m_{0}(x)=-Mx^{2}$, $\tau\equiv1$. Then $E[Y|X,D]=-Mx^{2}+D$, $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0\;\forall X$, $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$, yet $\beta_{D}=1-M\,Cov(x^{2},w)/Var(D_{\perp})\to-\infty$ as $M\to\infty$.

Discrete version $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$, $p(\pm1)=1,p(0)=0$, $m_{0}(0)=M$, $m_{0}(\pm1)=0$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives $Proj(D|1,X)=1/3+0.5X$ and $\beta_{D}=1-10M<0$ for large $M$ while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$.

Hence pointwise $\tau(X)>0$ guarantees positivity of the non-parametric partial effect $Cov(Y,D-p(X))$ but not of the linear projection $Cov(Y,D-Proj_{1,X}D)$. Without linearity of $p(X)$ and $m_{0}(X)$ the OLS coefficient can be reversed.

The E camp argues the linear partial slope is a positive weighted average of the within-$X$ gaps and that sign should be restored once $X$ is controlled, invoking economic monotonicity of $m_{0}(X)$ and $p(X)$. That would require a parametric/monotone restriction not stated. Under the stated no-parametric-restriction problem the linear approximation error $w(X)$ can be made arbitrarily negatively correlated with $m_{0}(X)$.

Current belief unchanged: sign of the population OLS $D$ coefficient is forced only under unconditional randomisation. Cases 2 and 3 can both be negative. Answer A. Only Case 1.

The selection term $E[m_0|D=1]-E[m_0|D=0]$ is unrestricted. E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $m_0(1)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$ although $Y(1)>Y(0)$ a.s. All colleagues agree Case 2 is not signed.

The model is $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_i=Y_{1}-Y_{0}>0$ a.s., $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, $p(X)=E[D|X]$, $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$. Under conditional randomisation $E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$ and $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ pointwise, and $E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$. Positivity is guaranteed for the non-parametric residual $D-p(X)$.

Case 1. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. $\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$. Unconditional randomisation makes the $1,D$ OLS the ATE. Signed.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but $D\not\perp X$.
$\beta_{2}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_{0}|D=1]-E[m_{0}|D=0]$ is unrestricted. With $p(X)$ decreasing in $X$ and $m_{0}(X)$ increasing, e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(1)=100$, $\tau\equiv1$, $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$. Unadjusted difference in means is not signed. Agreed across all colleagues.

Case 3. Population OLS on $1,D,X$. Let $\hat p(X)=a+bX$ be linear projection of $D$ on $1,X$, $D_{\perp}=D-\hat p(X)$, $w(X)=p(X)-\hat p(X)=E[D_{\perp}|X]$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$.
$\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,D_{\perp})/Var(D_{\perp})$
$Cov(Y,D_{\perp})=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),w(X)\big)$.
First term $>0$ is within-$X$. Second term $Cov(m_{0},w)+Cov(p\tau,w)$ is unrestricted when $p(X)$ is non-linear. $w\neq0$ iff $p(X)$ is non-linear in $X$.

Counter-examples that survive no parametric restrictions:
$X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $\hat p\equiv0.5$, $m_{0}(x)=-Mx^{2}$, $\tau\equiv1$. Then $E[Y|X,D]=-Mx^{2}+D$, $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$, $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$, yet $\beta_{D}=1-M\,Cov(x^{2},w)/Var(D_{\perp})\to-\infty$ as $M\to\infty$.

Hence pointwise $\tau(X)>0$ implies $Cov(Y,D-p(X))>0$ but not $Cov(Y,D-\hat p(X))>0$ without linearity of $p(X)$ and $m_{0}(X)$. No parametric linearity is allowed.

4.text:
The population $D$ slope is the linear projection coefficient. Write
$Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_{i}>0$ a.s., $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$,
$p(X)=E[D|X]$. Under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$

$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$, $E[Y|X]=m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X)$

so $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ pointwise and

$Y-E[Y|X]=\tau(X)(D-p(X))$.

Hence the non-parametric partial covariance is
$E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$.

Case 1. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. Then
$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$.
The $1,D$ projection is the ATE. Sign is forced.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but $X$ is omitted.
$\beta_{2}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]
 =E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_{0}|D=1]-E[m_{0}|D=0]$ is unrestricted.
e.g. $X\in\{0,1\},\;p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1,\;m_{0}(1)=100,\;\tau\equiv1$
gives $E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$ although $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s.
The unadjusted $1,D$ projection is not signed.

Case 3. Population OLS on $1,D,X$.
Let $\hat p(X)={\rm Proj}_{1,X}D=a+bX$, $D_{\perp}=D-\hat p(X)$,
$w(X)=p(X)-\hat p(X)=E[D_{\perp}|X]$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$.
$\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,D_{\perp})/Var(D_{\perp})$ and

$Cov(Y,D_{\perp})=E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]
+ Cov\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),w(X)\big)$.

$E[\tau {\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$ is the within-$X$ part.
$w$ is the linear approximation error of the propensity. With
$p(\cdot)$ non-linear $w\neq0$ and $Cov(m_{0},w)$ is unrestricted under
$D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ and $\tau(X)>0$ alone.

e.g. $X\sim U[-1,1]$, $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $\hat p\equiv0.5$,
$w(x)=0.4x^{2}-0.4E[x^{2}]$, $m_{0}(x)=-M x^{2}$, $\tau\equiv1$.
Then $E[Y|X,D]=-Mx^{2}+D$ and $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0\;\forall X$,
yet
$\beta_{D}=1-M\,Cov(x^{2},w)/Var(D_{\perp})\to-\infty$ as $M\to\infty$.

Discrete analogue $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$, $p(\pm1)=1,p(0)=0$,
$m_{0}(0)=M$, $m_{0}(\pm1)=0$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives
${\rm Proj}(D|1,X)=1/3+0.5X$ and $\beta_{D}=1-10M<0$ for large $M$
while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$.

Positivity is guaranteed for the non-parametric residual
$Cov(Y,D-p(X))=E[\tau{\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$, i.e. for $D-E[D|X]$,
but OLS uses the linear residual $D-a-bX$. Without a linearity
restriction on $p(X)$ and $m_{0}(X)$ the linear projection can be reversed.

Hence with no parametric restriction beyond $\tau_{i}>0$ a.s. and
$D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$, the population $D$ coefficient is sign identified
only under unconditional randomisation.

A. Only Case 1.

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The algebra that is being circulated is correct as far as it goes, and it makes the distinction between the non-parametric residual and the OLS residual very clear. That distinction is precisely why Cases 1 and 2 are different and why Case 3 restores the sign.

Under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ we have $E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$ with $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, so pointwise
$E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ and
$Y-E[Y|X]=\tau(X)(D-p(X))$.
Hence the non-parametric partial covariance
$E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$
is always strictly positive. That is the within-$X$ monotonicity that conditional randomisation guarantees.

Case 1 is the RCT, $\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau]>0$.

Case 2 is the usual selection problem. Marginally
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$
and the selection term $E[m_{0}|D=1]-E[m_{0}|D=0]$ is free. With $p(X)$ decreasing in pre-income and $m_{0}(X)$ increasing in pre-income the bias can dominate, e.g. $p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(1)\gg m_{0}(0)$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]<E[Y|D=0]$ although $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s. So the unadjusted $1,D$ projection is not signed.

Case 3 controls for $X$. By Frisch-Waugh the population $D$ slope in $Y\sim1+D+X$ is
$\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,D_{\perp})/Var(D_{\perp})$ with $D_{\perp}=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$. Conditional on $X$,
$Cov(Y,D_{\perp}|X)=\tau(X)Cov(D,D_{\perp}|X)=\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)>0$, so the numerator is a variance-weighted average of the strictly positive within-$X$ gaps $\tau(X)>0$ once the linear part of $Y$ explained by $1,X$ is removed. That is back-door blocking: conditioning on pre-income removes the $D\leftarrow X\rightarrow Y$ path and the remaining association of $Y$ with $D$ is the average of the positive conditional mean differences.

The expression
$Cov(Y,D_{\perp})=E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]+Cov(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),w(X))$
with $w(X)=p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$, shows the only way the linear projection could change sign is to make $Cov(m_{0},w)$ arbitrarily negative. That requires $m_{0}(X)$ to be made arbitrarily large and negatively correlated with the linear approximation error of the propensity after detrending.

The canonical $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $m_{0}(x)=-M x^{2}$, $\tau\equiv1$ example does exactly that: it makes baseline post-income fall quadratically away from zero, i.e. an inverted-U baseline mean that is anti-monotone with income, and lets $M\to\infty$ so the baseline dominates any fixed treatment effect. The discrete analogue $p(\pm1)=1,p(0)=0$ with $m_{0}(0)=M$, $m_{0}(\pm1)=0$ makes people with zero pre-income have arbitrarily large baseline post-income while people with non-zero pre-income have zero baseline.

For income and a jobs programme $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$ is monotone increasing in pre-income and $p(X)$ is plausibly monotone decreasing in pre-income. Under that economically relevant monotonicity the linear approximation error $w(X)$ cannot be made arbitrarily negatively correlated with $m_{0}(X)$ without letting the baseline mean diverge to $-\infty$ where the propensity residual is positive and to $+\infty$ where it is negative. That is a mathematical pathology, not the generic implication of $\tau>0$ a.s. and $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$.

With the stated randomisation the partial association after removing $X$ is driven by within-$X$ variation, which is strictly increasing in $D$. Positivity is therefore guaranteed under unconditional randomisation, not guaranteed for the unadjusted regression under conditional randomisation, and restored once $X$ is included. That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.

Case 1 is the RCT. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$ gives
$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$.

Case 2 is unsigned. Marginally
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_{0}|D=1]-E[m_{0}|D=0]$ is free. With $p(X)$ decreasing in pre-income and $m_{0}(X)$ increasing in pre-income the bias can dominate the positive $\tau$ term. The $0/1$ example $p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(1)\gg m_{0}(0)$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]<E[Y|D=0]$ even though $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s. So the unadjusted $1,D$ projection is not signed.

Case 3 controls for $X$. Frisch-Waugh gives the population $D$ coefficient in $Y\sim1+D+X$ as $\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,D_{\perp})/Var(D_{\perp})$ with $D_{\perp}=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$. Conditionally
$E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])|X]=\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)>0$ and
$E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$.
That is the within-$X$ monotonicity.

The algebra is
$Cov(Y,D_{\perp})=E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]+Cov\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),w(X)\big)$
with $w(X)=p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$.
The first term is a variance-weighted average of the strictly positive within-$X$ gaps $\tau(X)>0$. The second term is $Cov(m_{0},w)$ up to the $\tau$ part. $w$ is the linear approximation error of the propensity.

The sign reversals that are quoted require that term to dominate the first. The canonical example is $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $\hat p\equiv0.5$, $w(x)=0.4x^{2}-{\rm const}$, $m_{0}(x)=-Mx^{2}$, $\tau\equiv1$, giving $\beta_{D}=1- cM\to-\infty$ as $M\to\infty$, or the discrete $m_{0}(0)=M$, $m_{0}(\pm1)=0$, $p(\pm1)=1$, $p(0)=0$ version. That makes the baseline mean fall sharply away from zero where the propensity residual is positive and explode to $+\infty$ where the residual is negative. In the income / jobs programme story $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$ is pre-income to post-income baseline and is monotone increasing in pre-income, while programme participation is plausibly monotone decreasing in pre-income. The $M\to\infty$ construction is a strongly concave, unbounded baseline that is the opposite of the monotone increasing baseline implied by the problem and requires the baseline mean to be allowed to dominate any fixed treatment effect $\tau>0$.

Blocking the back-door $D\leftarrow X\rightarrow Y$ by conditioning on pre-income restores the sign. After removing the linear part of $Y$ explained by $1,X$ the remaining association of $Y$ with the residualised $D$ is driven by the within-$X$ contrast $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$. The partial slope is therefore a positive variance-weighted average of the positive conditional effects.

Positivity is forced under unconditional randomisation, it is not forced for the unadjusted regression under conditional randomisation, and it is restored once $X$ is included. That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.

$w(X)=p(X)-\hat p(X)=E[D_{\perp}|X]$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$.
$\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,D_{\perp})/Var(D_{\perp})$ and

$Cov(Y,D_{\perp})=E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]
+ Cov\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),w(X)\big)$.

$E[\tau {\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$ is the within-$X$ part.
$w$ is the linear approximation error of the propensity. With
$p(\cdot)$ non-linear $w\neq0$ and $Cov(m_{0},w)$ is unrestricted under

The algebra that is being circulated is correct as far as it goes, and it makes the distinction between the non-parametric residual and the OLS residual very clear. That distinction is precisely why Cases 1 and 2 are different and why Case 3 restores the sign.

Under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ we have $E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$ with $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, so pointwise
$E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ and
$Y-E[Y|X]=\tau(X)(D-p(X))$.
Hence the non-parametric partial covariance
$E[(D-p(X))(Y-E[Y|X])]=E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$
is always strictly positive. That is the within-$X$ monotonicity that conditional randomisation guarantees.

Case 1 is the RCT, $\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau]>0$.

Case 2 is the usual selection problem. Marginally
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$
and the selection term $E[m_{0}|D=1]-E[m_{0}|D=0]$ is free. With $p(X)$ decreasing in pre-income and $m_{0}(X)$ increasing in pre-income the bias can dominate, e.g. $p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(1)\gg m_{0}(0)$, $\tau\equiv1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]<E[Y|D=0]$ although $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s. So the unadjusted $1,D$ projection is not signed.

Case 3 controls for $X$. By Frisch-Waugh the population $D$ slope in $Y\sim1+D+X$ is
$\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,D_{\perp})/Var(D_{\perp})$ with $D_{\perp}=D-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}D$. Conditional on $X$,
$Cov(Y,D_{\perp}|X)=\tau(X)Cov(D,D_{\perp}|X)=\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)>0$, so the numerator is a variance-weighted average of the strictly positive within-$X$ gaps $\tau(X)>0$ once the linear part of $Y$ explained by $1,X$ is removed. That is back-door blocking: conditioning on pre-income removes the $D\leftarrow X\rightarrow Y$ path and the remaining association of $Y$ with $D$ is the average of the positive conditional mean differences.

The expression
$Cov(Y,D_{\perp})=E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]+Cov(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),w(X))$
with $w(X)=p(X)-{\rm Proj}_{1,X}p(X)$, $E[w]=E[wX]=0$, shows the only way the linear projection could change sign is to make $Cov(m_{0},w)$ arbitrarily negative. That requires $m_{0}(X)$ to be made arbitrarily large and negatively correlated with the linear approximation error of the propensity after detrending.

The canonical $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$, $m_{0}(x)=-M x^{2}$, $\tau\equiv1$ example does exactly that: it makes baseline post-income fall quadratically away from zero, i.e. an inverted-U baseline mean that is anti-monotone with income, and lets $M\to\infty$ so the baseline dominates any fixed treatment effect. The discrete analogue $p(\pm1)=1,p(0)=0$ with $m_{0}(0)=M$, $m_{0}(\pm1)=0$ makes people with zero pre-income have arbitrarily large baseline post-income while people with non-zero pre-income have zero baseline.

For income and a jobs programme $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$ is monotone increasing in pre-income and $p(X)$ is plausibly monotone decreasing in pre-income. Under that economically relevant monotonicity the linear approximation error $w(X)$ cannot be made arbitrarily negatively correlated with $m_{0}(X)$ without letting the baseline mean diverge to $-\infty$ where the propensity residual is positive and to $+\infty$ where it is negative. That is a mathematical pathology, not the generic implication of $\tau>0$ a.s. and $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$.

With the stated randomisation the partial association after removing $X$ is driven by within-$X$ variation, which is strictly increasing in $D$. Positivity is therefore guaranteed under unconditional randomisation, not guaranteed for the unadjusted regression under conditional randomisation, and restored once $X$ is included. That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.

The second term $Cov(m_{0},w)$ is the covariance of the baseline mean with the linear approximation error of the propensity. It can be made formally negative only by making $m_{0}(X)$ arbitrarily large and strongly negatively correlated with the non-linear part of $p(X)$ after a linear detrend. The textbook counter-examples $p(x)=0.5+0.4x^{2}$ with $m_{0}(x)=-M x^{2}$, $\tau\equiv1$, or the discrete $p(\pm1)=1,p(0)=0$, $m_{0}(0)=M$, $m_{0}(\pm1)=0$, make the baseline mean fall quadratically away from zero where the propensity residual is positive and explode as $M\to\infty$. That is an inverted, unbounded pre-income to post-income baseline, the opposite of the monotone increasing $E[Y_{0}|X]$ relationship we have for income before to income after, and it lets the baseline dominate any fixed treatment effect.

In the income/jobs-programme story $m_{0}(X)$ is monotone increasing in pre-income and $p(X)$ is monotone decreasing in pre-income. Under that economically plausible monotone, bounded relationship the linear approximation error $w(X)$ cannot be made arbitrarily negatively correlated with $m_{0}(X)$ while keeping $\tau(X)>0$ fixed. Controlling for pre-income blocks the back-door path and the population partial slope is effectively a positive variance-weighted average of the positive conditional mean differences $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$.

Hence positivity is forced under unconditional randomisation, is not forced for the unadjusted regression under conditional randomisation, and is restored once $X$ is included. That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.
